Usable as struct fields, enum variant payloads and method arguments, returns and properties: an enum I2cAddress { Seven(U7), Ten(U10) } with ww_repr = u1 takes 8 or 11 bits (see showcase)
  • Nibble-based variable length u32: unib32 (1 to 11 nibbles, four-bit alignment)
  • Byte-based variable length u32: uvlq32 (big endian VLQ, 1 to 5 bytes, one-byte alignment)
    • UVlq32Backfill: always written as 5 bytes, value can be filled in later and leading bytes dropped
    • TailSize<N>: right-justified in N bytes, filled in with the size of the rest of the enclosing value, which readers bound the value with (see wire format)
  • Byte-based variable length u64: uvlq64 (same VLQ encoding as uvlq32, 1 to 10 bytes, one-byte alignment)
  • Floating point numbers: f32, f64
  • Textual:
    • UTF-8 string String / &'i str
    • With a maximum length in bytes: MaxLen<String, N> / MaxLen<&'i str, N> (see bounded lists and strings)
  • Sequences:
    • Arrays:
      • Arbitrary length array: Vec<T>
      • Byte array: Vec<u8>
      • Arbitrary length array (no alloc): RefVec<'i, T>
      • Byte array (no alloc): RefVec<'i, u8>
      • Fixed sized array: [T; N], N a literal or any const expression
      • With a maximum length: MaxLen<Vec<T>, N> / MaxLen<RefVec<'i, T>, N> (see bounded lists and strings)
    • Compressed sequences, written bit by bit against the previous element (see wire format):
      • Integers as differences: Delta<'i, T> / DeltaOwned<T>, T any of u8..u64, i8..i64
      • Integers as differences of differences (timestamps): DeltaOfDelta<'i, T> / DeltaOfDeltaOwned<T>
      • Floats as XOR with the previous value: XorFloat<'i, T> / XorFloatOwned<T>, T is f32 or f64
      • Usable in derived types and in every API position; the dynamic client and Python see them as lists of numbers
  • Option<T> and Result<T, E>
  • Sparse slots of any types (no alloc, shrink_wrap level): OptionAnyVec<'i> - only the present values are written, after a header in the smallest of four modes; slots can be appended later (see wire format)
  • RefBox<T> for self-referential types.

  • User-defined:

    • Struct
    • Enum with or without data variants, multiple discriminant options:
      • Bit-aligned: u1, u2, ...
      • Nibble-aligned: nib
      • Byte-aligned: u8, u16, u32
      • Variable length unib32.
    • Tuple

  • Not yet supported or not decided whether to support:

    • Unicode character: char (4B)
    • ASCII character c_char (1B) (ASCII) and string: c_str
    • Map

items.title: Library types
items.text: There are a lot more types as a part of a standard library (date, time, version, numbers, SI units, etc.). See the overview.

items.title: Bounded lists and strings: MaxLen<T, N>
items.text:
MaxLen<T, N> wraps a list or a string (RefVec<'i, T>, Vec<T>, &'i str or String) and allows at most N elements (bytes for a string). It works everywhere a type can appear: struct and enum fields, method arguments and return types, properties, stream! and sink! items, and nested inside other lists (MaxLen<RefVec<'i, MaxLen<&'i str, 8>>, 4>).

pub const MAX_PIECE: usize = 256;

#[ww_trait]
trait Stage {
    fn write(offset: u32, last: bool, data: MaxLen<RefVec<'i, u8>, MAX_PIECE>);
    property!(rw label: MaxLen<&'i str, 32>);
}

In a #[ww_trait], N is an integer literal, {literal}, or the name of a const defined in the API crate's lib.rs. In a plain #[derive_shrink_wrap] type it is any const expression.

  • Checked both ways, never truncated. MaxLen::new refuses a value that is too long, serializing one (e.g. after changing it through DerefMut) fails with Error::MaxLenExceeded, and so does deserializing one, before any element is read. A server answers an over-long argument with an error, a client refuses to send one.
  • Same wire form as the unbounded type. Not a single byte changes: the bound only exists in the code on both ends. That is what keeps it evolvable: a bound can be added, raised, lowered or removed without a new wire format, and the evolution rules decide which of those old peers accept.
  • Visible in introspection. ww_self describes it as Type::MaxLen { max_len, ty }, so the dynamic client and the Python module check the bound too (Python raises ValueError: ... at most N ...).
  • Worst-case size at compile time. Every type has a SerializeShrinkWrap::MAX_SIZE: Option<MaxSize>, Some when every part of it is bounded (numbers, arrays, Option/Result, structs and enums of them, and MaxLen lists and strings of bounded elements) and None as soon as anything can grow without a limit (a plain Vec, RefVec, String, RefBox, compressed sequences). MaxSize::buffer_len_of(T::MAX_SIZE) is a buffer length any value of T always serializes into. It is an upper bound, not the exact worst case: every length is counted as at least four nibbles and every alignment as needed.

A generated no_alloc server also gets, per method, <METHOD>_REQUEST_MAX_LEN and <METHOD>_RESPONSE_MAX_LEN: Option<usize>: the longest request message that calls it and the longest reply, None when an argument or the return type is unbounded. A firmware can check at compile time that its message buffer is big enough:

const MAX_MESSAGE_LEN: usize = 512;
const _: () = assert!(matches!(
    api_server::WRITE_REQUEST_MAX_LEN,
    Some(len) if len <= MAX_MESSAGE_LEN
));

MaxLen bounds the length of one value. The number of resources in a resource array (stream!(adc[]: u16)) is a different thing, see arrays.

items.title: Self-referential types
items.text: Self-referential types are supported through the RefBox<T>, providing similar semantics to Rust Box<T> type, but without using heap allocation on no_std.

items.title: Alignment
items.text:
Some types are one- or four-bit aligned and the rest are one-byte aligned. Dense packing is used to save space, including in enum discriminants (which can even be U1). Byte arrays, strings, and Unsized objects are all one-byte aligned to limit code complexity and computations required. Unused bits are set to zero and can be reclaimed when evolving a type.

For example:

fn version1() {
    let mut buf = [0u8; 8];
    let mut wr = BufWriter::new(&mut buf[..]);
    wr.write_bool(true).unwrap();
    wr.write_u8(0xAA).unwrap();
    let bytes = wr.finish_and_take().unwrap();
    assert_eq!(bytes, &[0x80, 0xAA]);
}

In a future version while older one is still in use, it was decided to add some more data:

fn version1_1() {
    let mut buf = [0u8; 8];
    let mut wr = BufWriter::new(&mut buf[..]);
    wr.write_bool(true).unwrap();
    wr.write(&Some(U6::new(5).unwrap())).unwrap();
    wr.write_u8(0xAA).unwrap();
    let bytes = wr.finish_and_take().unwrap();
    assert_eq!(bytes, &[0xC5, 0xAA]);
}

Older code can still read new data and will skip the Option, and newer code can read old data, yielding None. All the while, the serialized size didn't even change (it could have though, it's just an example).

items.title: TODO: Subtypes (bounded numbers)
items.text:
Lengths of lists and strings are bounded with MaxLen.

Simple checked numbers where only a range of values is allowed:

  • u16<{1..=512}>

Set of allowed values:

  • u8<{0..=8}, 12, 16, 20, 24, 32, 48, 64>

Numbers are checked before serialization and after deserialization.

items.title: TODO: SI support
items.text:
Specify SI unit for any number:

  • current: f32<"A">
  • velocity: f32<"m/s">

Units are not transmitted over the wire, used as a hint for code generation and in UI tool.

items.title: Resources addressing
items.text:
Primary mode of addressing to uniquely identify a resource (method, property, stream or trait) is an array of indices, starting from an API root. It is the most efficient way as well, utilising UNib32 variable length numbers based on nibbles (e.g., [0, 1, 2] is only 2 bytes, including array length).

For example, turn_on address is [0] and turn_off is [1].

#[ww_trait]
trait ApiRoot {
    fn turn_on();
    fn turn_off();
}

As a user, you do not have to worry about these indices, as they are automatically assigned and actual names are used in generated code.

When a resource is an array, one more index is added, selecting the required one. On the server code side this index is passed as an additional argument to user handler function.

There could be multiple arrays on the way to a resource (e.g., array of trait implementations and then an array of resources inside said trait). Multiple indices are added in the appropriate positions in this case.

Using this scheme requires knowing exactly which API and it's exact version that peer implements. When this is not possible or not desired (e.g., if addressing multiple nodes at the same time) - trait addressing can be used.

items.title: Global trait addressing (FullVersion)
items.text:
There is a possibility to make API calls on "ww-traits", without knowing the exact resource address. For example one could make a "sleep" call on all devices in a CAN Bus network, that support "PowerManagement" trait. Or "get_fw_version" on any device supporting "FirmwareInfo" trait. In order to do so, instead of relying on resource address, FullVersion is sent instead.

Compared to resource addresses that can only take a few bytes, FullVersion is likely to take about 8-16 bytes or more and vary with the crate name. This is unfortunate for constrained systems, or if one wants to pack many calls into one packet.

The request carries the trait's crate name and version (FullVersion), the trait's name in that crate (a crate can define several, ww_dfu has five) and the path from the trait's root. The server finds the trait wherever it sits in its API tree and continues from there. It answers ErrorKind::TraitNotFound when it doesn't implement the trait, only implements an incompatible version of its crate (major and, before 1.0, minor have to match), or only implements it under a resource array (ww_impl!(port[]: ww_gpio::Bank): a global path can't select an index). When a trait is implemented several times, the first one in the tree (depth first, in resource id order) answers.

Global paths don't depend on the user API or its version, which makes them the way to talk to a device whose API the host doesn't know: a host built against a new API version can still reboot a device running an old one into its updater (ww_dfu::BootControl) or read its info traits. On the host, connect with traits_only and call through a trait client:

// any device, whatever its API and version: the user API check of link setup is skipped
let device = DynClient::traits_only(|c| c.usb().serial_eq(serial)).connect().await?;
// a client generated with `client = "trait_client"` for ww_dfu::BootControl, see tests/cross_version
let mut boot = BootControl::new(device.global_attachment(ww_dfu::BOOT_CONTROL_FULL_GID, "BootControl"));
boot.reboot(BootTarget::Updater).call().await?;

A traits_only connection refuses absolute paths (Error::AbsolutePathInTraitsOnly): without the device's API they could mean anything. ww dfu reboot in the CLI does exactly this.

items.title: Global trait addressing (CompactVersion)
items.text:
Solution to this is CompactVersion, which carries globally unique type id and major.minor version components only, all UNib32 encoded. The only downside is that guaranteeing globally unique IDs is not as simple as using crate's name anymore. IDs are manually assigned and tracked via git instead in ww_global registry.

Servers don't serve compact trait paths yet (ErrorKind::TraitNotFound): compact ids of traits are not in the API model, and none is assigned so far (API-20).

items.title: API report
items.text: TODO: export a file describing all levels of API with IDs

items.title: Arrays
items.text:
Any resource can also be an array - method, property, stream and even a trait implementation:

#[ww_trait]
trait ArrayOf {
    fn run<N: u32>();
    stream!(adc[]: u16);
    property!(led[]: bool);
    ww_impl!(motor[]: ww_motor_control "0.1.0" :: Motor);
}

TODO: bounds of the index (adc[8], motor[1..=4]). The length of a list or string inside a resource's type is bounded with MaxLen instead.

Traits inside other traits can also contain arrays, all the indices leading up to them are accumulated and passed as Rust array [u32; N] argument into a corresponding user handler.

That way generated code can be kept efficient and simple, because the whole API tree is essentially flattened and simple function calls are used to interface with user provided implementation. At least that is the case for now on no_std targets.

items.title: Array of resources vs resource of array
items.text:
Here, resource led is itself an array, when accessing it - an index will be added to the resource path. Each one of three bool's is accessed separately from each other.

#[ww_trait]
trait ArrayOfResources {
    property!(led[3]: bool);
}

On the other hand, here led is not an array, but its type is. All three boolean's are accessed in one go.

#[ww_trait]
trait ResourceOfArrays {
    property!(led: [bool; 3]);
}

Both can be used together as well, for example:

#[ww_trait]
trait ArrayOfArrays {
    property!(rgb_led[3]: [u8; 3]);
}

items.title: Errors
items.text:
A call to a device can fail in three different ways, and WireWeaver keeps them apart all the way to your code:

  • The device said no. The method ran and returned its own error: an I2C address wasn't acknowledged, a pin is in use. This is the E of a method returning Result<T, E>, a normal shrink_wrap value.
  • The device can't do this at all. There is no implementation: the handler answered Unimplemented, or the device left an optional item out.
  • The call didn't go through. The link dropped, the request timed out, the device was disconnected.

This page explains how to declare errors in an API, how a device returns them, what a client gets, and how errors stay readable when the device and the host are built from different versions.

items.title: Declaring errors in an API
items.text:
A method that can fail returns Result<T, E>, where E is the error enum of its crate:

#[ww_trait]
pub trait I2c {
    /// Writes `data` to the device at `addr`.
    #[errors(Common, Nack, Arbitration, Timeout, BufferTooBig)]
    fn i2c_write(addr: u8, data: MaxLen<RefVec<'i, u8>, MAX_WRITE_LEN>) -> Result<(), I2cError<'i>>;
}

#[derive_shrink_wrap(owned(feature = "std"), derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq, Clone), display, ww_repr = unib32)]
pub enum I2cError<'i> {
    #[common]
    Common(CommonError<'i>),
    /// The address or a data byte was not acknowledged.
    Nack,
    /// Arbitration lost to another master.
    Arbitration,
    /// The bus stayed busy longer than the timeout.
    Timeout,
    /// The transfer is longer than the device can buffer ({max} bytes).
    BufferTooBig { max: u16 },
}

Use one error enum per crate (or per group of traits, when a crate's traits really fail for unrelated reasons). The same type is used on the wire, in the device's handlers and in the client, so device code can share helpers and ? them anywhere, and a driver crate converts it into its own error with a single #[from].

items.title: Which errors a method returns
items.text:
#[errors(..)] lists the variants a method can actually return. For a variant holding one enum, such as Common(CommonError), the entry names the variants of that one: Common(InUse, Refused); Common alone means any CommonError. The list is checked when the trait is parsed, so an unknown or repeated name is a compile error on that name.

The list doesn't change the type or the wire; it goes into the API model, and from there:

  • into the docs, as an # Errors section with each variant's doc line, both in the generated client and on the trait's rustdoc;
  • into introspection, so ww api tree and Python's help() show it;
  • into the evolution checker: a changed list is reported as a compatible change;
  • into a check on the client: when a device returns a variant outside the method's list, the generated and the dynamic client log a tracing warning, so a device that doesn't keep its contract is noticed early. wire_weaver_client::set_strict_error_lists(true) makes it a panic instead; the test harness (tests_common) turns that on.

A method without #[errors] may return any variant of its error enum.

Stream functions and properties take the same list, with the same outputs. On a stream function (#[stream(..)] fn, API-31) it is about the Err of its Result, which opening the stream answers; the client checks the open's result. Above a property! with an error type (property!(rw mode: Mode, ModeError)) it is about that type: a property has one error type for reading and writing, so one list covers both. The generated client checks writes (its reads return the error as raw bytes), the dynamic client reads and writes.

#[ww_trait]
pub trait I2cMonitor {
    #[errors(Common(InUse, Unsupported))]
    #[stream(I2cRecord<'i>, counted)]
    fn records(io_level: Option<Volt>) -> Result<(), I2cError<'i>>;

    #[errors(Common(Unsupported, Busy))]
    property!(rw speed_hz: u32, I2cError<'i>);
}

ww_error walks through the Common(..) nesting and real examples from ww_stdlib.

items.title: Messages from doc comments
items.text: With the display directive, the derive writes Display and std::error::Error (core::error::Error on no_std) from the first doc line of each variant, filling in {field} placeholders: BufferTooBig { max: 64 } reads "The transfer is longer than the device can buffer (64 bytes)": the trailing period of the doc line is left out, as Rust error messages go. Use #[display("...")] on a variant when the message should differ from its doc. On a device the code is unused and the linker drops it; hosts need no hand-written Display for any API error.

items.title: Common errors
items.text:
Some situations come up in almost every crate: the device doesn't support a mode, a resource is in use by something else, the device is busy. These are ww_error::CommonError (also in wire_weaver::prelude), nested as the first variant of a crate's error enum and marked #[common]:

Variant Meaning Unsupported the device knows this call but can't do what was asked (a mode, a range, a feature) InvalidArgument { arg, reason } argument number arg is invalid InUse { by } the resource is in use, by names the user Busy busy with another operation, try again later WrongState { reason } not possible in the current state NoPower { rail } the rail the operation needs has no power Refused { reason } refused, e.g. by a safety rule Timeout timed out Fault { code } a hardware fault

Strings are bounded and may be empty, so a device short on flash sends "".

On the device, #[common] gives the crate error a From<CommonError>, so a helper returning CommonError can be ?-ed into any crate's error:

fn check_level(&self) -> Result<(), CommonError<'static>> {
    if self.io_level.is_none() {
        return Err(CommonError::NoPower { rail: MaxLen::new_unchecked("VIO") });
    }
    Ok(())
}

fn write(&mut self, addr: u8, data: &[u8]) -> Result<(), I2cError<'static>> {
    self.check_level()?; // CommonError becomes I2cError::Common
    // ...
    Ok(())
}

async fn i2c_write(
    &mut self,
    _cx: &mut Context<'_, impl EventOut>,
    addr: u8,
    data: MaxLen<RefVec<'_, u8>, MAX_WRITE_LEN>,
) -> RpcResult<Result<(), I2cError<'_>>> {
    Ready(self.write(addr, data.as_slice()))
}

On the host, e.common() (trait HasCommon, in the prelude) works on any crate's error, for example on call_error.device(), so generic code (a GUI, a _hl crate) handles the common cases without knowing the crate. Tools recognise CommonError by its type in the API model: ww api tree -t marks it, and in Python RemoteError.common holds the variant and its fields next to .value.

Keep a crate-specific variant when a caller should act on exactly that case: Nack for I2C, an UnsupportedSpeed that carries the supported range.

items.title: On the client: one ? per call
items.text:
For a method returning Result<T, E>, call(), blocking_call() and promises return Result<T, CallError<E>>:

pub enum CallError<E> {
    /// The device answered with its error: the `Err(e)` of the method.
    Device(E),
    /// The device has no implementation of this item.
    Unimplemented { resource: String },
    /// The call didn't go through: link, timeout, disconnect or another framework error.
    Client(wire_weaver_client::Error),
}

CallError<E> implements std::error::Error when E does, and its Display is the inner error's, so it fits anyhow and thiserror as is:

// a script
async fn script(dev: &Board) -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    dev.i2c().i2c_write(0x50, data).call().await?;
    Ok(())
}

// a driver crate with its own error
#[derive(Debug, thiserror::Error)]
enum SensorError {
    #[error(transparent)]
    I2c(#[from] CallError<I2cErrorOwned>),
    #[error("unexpected chip id {0:#x}")]
    ChipId(u8),
}

// handling one case: retry while an EEPROM is busy with a page write
loop {
    match dev.i2c().i2c_write(0x50, data.clone()).call().await {
        Err(CallError::Device(I2cErrorOwned::Nack)) => continue,
        other => break other?,
    }
}

Methods without a Result return Result<T, wire_weaver_client::Error>; is_unimplemented() on it answers the same "can the device do this at all" question. Python already flattens all of this: a call returns T or raises.

items.title: Unsupported is not Unimplemented
items.text:
Two answers look alike and mean different things:

  • CommonError::Unsupported comes from code that ran on the device: it knows the call, and this case isn't possible.
  • Unimplemented means there is no code for the item at all: the handler returned RpcResult::Unimplemented (GetResult / SetResult for properties), or the item is an optional one the device left out.

RpcResult, GetResult and SetResult let a handler leave an implementation out without todo!(), or answer later (Deferred), and the framework reports it properly. ww api scaffold generates every handler answering Unimplemented, so a new device builds and answers sensibly before anything is written. On the client this is CallError::Unimplemented, never confused with an error of the device.

items.title: Devices and hosts of different versions
items.text:
An error enum grows: a later firmware may return a variant an older host has never heard of. Every Unsized enum (the default kind) therefore gets one more variant from the derive, Unknown(u32), which catches any discriminant the reader doesn't know instead of failing to decode the whole reply:

match e {
    CallError::Device(I2cErrorOwned::Nack) => { /* ... */ }
    CallError::Device(I2cErrorOwned::Unknown(n)) => warn!("device error {n} from a newer firmware"),
    // ...
}

The variant takes no number on the wire and isn't part of the API model, so adding it changes neither the bytes nor snapshots. The dynamic decoder and Python show such a value as <unknown N>.

Enum Gets Unknown(u32) Unsized with a free discriminant in its ww_repr yes, automatically final_structure, self_describing, sized only when written by hand every discriminant of the ww_repr already taken no marked no_future_version no, for sets that are complete by nature

When a variant of the enum is already called Unknown, name the catch-all with future_version = Other.

items.title: Optional items
items.text:
Not every device can do everything a trait describes. An API author marks such items #[optional], and a device that lacks them leaves them out at code generation, paying neither a dispatch entry nor a handler:

#[ww_trait]
pub trait I2c {
    fn i2c_configure(config: I2cConfig) -> Result<I2cConfig, I2cError<'i>>;
    /// Clocks SCL until SDA is released, then a stop.
    #[optional]
    fn i2c_wiggle_clock(count: u8) -> Result<I2cLinesState, I2cError<'i>>;
    /// Switchable pull-ups: both items or neither.
    #[optional(pullups)]
    fn i2c_set_pullups(enabled: bool) -> Result<(), I2cError<'i>>;
    #[optional(pullups)]
    property!(ro i2c_pullups: bool);
}

// a device without them
ww_codegen!(board_api::Board for Server, server = true, omit = ["i2c.i2c_wiggle_clock", "i2c.pullups"]);
  • Only items marked #[optional] can be left out; #[optional(group)] names items that go together. Paths start at the API root and skip array indices.
  • omit_if(not(feature = "pullups")) = ["i2c.pullups"] ties optional items to the device crate's cargo features.
  • An omitted item keeps its index. Called anyway, it answers Unimplemented.
  • The device's introspection lists what it left out, so clients fail such calls locally without a round trip, and the ww CLI and Python mark them "left out by this device".
  • ww api scaffold --omit .. generates the server without those stubs.

Leaving an item out saves its dispatch arm, argument decoding and handler, about 100 bytes of code each on a Cortex-M. Optional items has the details: paths, omit_if and introspection, measured code size.

Optional item or a trait of its own? Make an item optional when it is one of a few things within the trait's subject that some hardware lacks: a clock wiggle, switchable pull-ups, a hardware CRC. Make it a trait when it has state, configuration or streams of its own (a bus monitor, ADC capture), when a different set of devices implements it, or when it would be four optional items or more.

items.title: Folder structure
items.text:
Intended crate organisation is as follows:

  • my_device_api crate - contains user-defined types and resources, common to firmware, and it's driver (server and client). This crate must support no_std and optionally std.
  • MCU firmware depends on the API crate, uses common data types and implements a server. WireWeaver generates serdes and dispatch code, while user provides actual implementation.
  • Rust driver also depends on the API crate (optionally with std feature). WireWeaver generates serdes and client side code, user can optionally provide a higher-level client implementation on top of the generated one.
  • CLI, GUI and other applications depend on the Rust driver crate in order to communicate with the device.
  • TODO: Python wrapper is also automatically generated and uses Rust driver code.

Name of the API crate (from Cargo.toml) is assumed to be a globally unique identifier (see ww_version::FullVersion), hence it is advised to eventually publish it to crates.io if you are working on an open-source project or ensure to use unique enough name for internal use.

Version of the API crate is used for compatibility checks upon connection to the device. You can use it in your code as well, to show proper messages to user when interacting with an older or newer firmware from the perspective of the driver. Normal SemVer rules apply.

items.title: Methods
items.text:
Methods can be defined as follows:

#[ww_trait]
trait MyDevice {
    fn led_on();
    fn set_brightness(value: f32);
    fn temperature() -> f32;
    fn user_type(state: State);
    fn user_ret_type() -> UserType<'i>;
}

#[derive_shrink_wrap]
#[ww_repr(unib32)]
pub enum State {
    Off,
    On,
}

#[derive_shrink_wrap]
#[owned = "std"]
pub struct UserType<'i> {
    a: u8,
    b: RefVec<'i, u8>,
    c: SomeOtherType<'i>
}

Any number of arguments are supported, and they can be of any type supported by ShrinkWrap.

items.title: Server side
items.text:
Server side is responsible for deserializing requests from clients and dispatching them to user-provided functions. On a high level, this is the process that takes place:

  1. Incoming byte array is deserialized into ww_client_server::Request.
  2. Resource path contained in the Request is used to reach appropriate resource (or BadPath error is sent back).
  3. Depending on the resource kind, appropriate actions are handled (Call, Read, Write, etc.).
  4. User defined request types are deserialized (method arguments, sink data, property set values).
  5. User provided action is called.
  6. User defined types are serialized (method return types, stream data, property get values).
  7. Response is serialized and sent back to client.

Generated code can be of two flavors - async and sync. The only difference is that each user action is await'ed in the async version.

Additionally, there is deferred mode that can be turned on for user-selected methods. It works with both sync and async versions and allows to immediately return from the user handler and send an answer later. For example move_motor(x: f32) -> Result<(), Error> method can take a long time to finish, without deferred, it would block all other API resources.

items.title: async
items.text:
On the server side, this is how generated server code is tied with user provided implementation:

use api::{State, UserType};

struct ServerState {
    // any user data required for the server to function (e.g, peripherals, channels)
}

impl ServerState {
    async fn led_on(&mut self, _cx: &mut Context<'_, impl EventOut>) -> RpcResult<()> {
        /* do things */
        Ready(())
    }
    async fn temperature(&mut self, _cx: &mut Context<'_, impl EventOut>) -> RpcResult<f32> {
        Ready(20.0)
    }
    async fn user_type(&mut self, _cx: &mut Context<'_, impl EventOut>, state: State) -> RpcResult<()> {
        Ready(())
    }
}

mod server_impl {
    wire_weaver::ww_codegen!(
        api :: MyDevice for super::ServerState,
        server = true, no_alloc = true, use_async = true,
    );
}

ww_codegen! implements async fn process_request_bytes(bytes, scratch, out, medium) -> Result<..> on ServerState, which deserializes a request, calls one of the handlers and serializes the reply into scratch. ww api scaffold <api_crate> prints all the handlers a server is expected to implement, with exact signatures.

items.title: sync
items.text: By setting use_async = false, a blocking implementation is generated: handlers are plain fns and take cx: &mut Context<'_, impl BlockingEventOut>. A sync server also runs on the async ww_device::Server: events sent by its handlers are queued and sent out after it returns (EventWriter::queued()), so they are limited by the event scratch buffer size.

items.title: Handler context
items.text:
Every handler (methods, get_/set_/changed_ of properties, sideband_/write_ of streams) gets cx: &mut wire_weaver::Context as the first argument:

  • cx.seq() - sequence number of the request, 0 if the client does not expect a reply.
  • cx.medium() - the medium the request came from. The type is set with ww_codegen!(.., medium = "crate::Medium") (() by default) and the value with Server::with_medium(..). A device with USB and CAN runs one server per medium, all handling requests with the same server state.
  • cx.reply_to() - medium and seq to answer a deferred call later, None if no reply is expected.
  • cx sends events: stream updates and property updates with the generated stream_data_ser().<name>_send(&value, cx).await (_send_blocking for sync servers), or any event with send_event(). Events sent from a handler go out before its reply.
#[derive(Copy, Clone, PartialEq)]
enum Medium { Usb, Can }

impl ServerState {
    async fn start_adc(&mut self, cx: &mut Context<'_, impl EventOut, Medium>, rate: u32) -> RpcResult<()> {
        if cx.medium() == Medium::Can {
            self.adc_rate = rate.min(100);
        }
        // first sample right away, the rest from the event loop through server.sink()
        _ = server_impl::stream_data_ser().adc_send(&self.sample(), cx).await;
        Ready(())
    }
}

cx only reaches the medium the request came from. Events for other media are sent from the event loop through their servers' sink().

items.title: deferred
items.text: method_model = "move_motor=deferred, _=immediate" lets a method return Deferred and answer later. The handler keeps cx.reply_to(), and the reply is sent with the generated ServerState::move_motor_send_return(out, seq, output) (_send_return_blocking for sync), where out is another handler's cx or server.sink() of reply_to.medium. A deferred call that is never answered times out on the client.

items.title: Resource names mapping
items.text: In order to avoid complex shared data structures and allocation on no_std, all API levels are squished into one.

items.title: Client side
items.text:
client = "..." in ww_codegen! generates a client struct with one function per method. It returns a PreparedCall, which is executed with call().await, blocking_call(), call_forget() (no reply) or call_promise(marker) (polled from immediate mode UI code).

A method without Result gives Result<T, wire_weaver_client::Error>. A method returning Result<T, E> gives Result<T, CallError<E>>, so one ? is enough:

pub enum CallError<E> {
    /// The device answered with its error: the `Err(e)` of the method.
    Device(E),
    /// The device has no implementation: its handler returned `Unimplemented`, or the device's API doesn't have
    /// the method (known locally from introspection, no round trip).
    Unimplemented { resource: String },
    /// The call didn't go through: link, timeout, disconnect, another framework error.
    Client(wire_weaver_client::Error),
}

// trait: fn move_motor(x: f32) -> Result<(), MotorError>;
client.move_motor(1.0).call().await?; // with anyhow, or a thiserror enum with #[from] CallError<MotorError>

match client.move_motor(1.0).call().await {
    Ok(()) => {}
    Err(CallError::Device(MotorError::EndStop)) => { /* the device said no */ }
    Err(CallError::Unimplemented { .. }) => { /* this device can't move motors */ }
    Err(e) => return Err(e.into()), // CallError::Client: link, timeout, ...
}

Display and source() of CallError are the inner error's, and it is std::error::Error when E is. Methods without Result tell an unimplemented method apart with wire_weaver_client::Error::is_unimplemented(). A property with a user error type (property!(rw mode: u8, ModeError)) gives the same CallError<ModeError> from write(). See Errors for declaring errors, common errors and errors of newer firmware.

items.title: Several calls in one request
items.text: When the server is generated with multi_req = true (a server without it refuses the request), several methods can be called in one request/response pair, each answered on its own (Result<T, ErrorOwned> per item, in order): (client.inc(), client.dec()).multi_call().await, implemented for tuples of 2 to 8 of PreparedCall, at any depth (any methods that share a common path prefix and diverge at exactly one element). To call the same method across a whole array, use call_array(multi_idx, |i| client.pin(i).double()) (multi_idx is a Range/List/Mask32 selector) — see Properties for the full set of multi-request helpers, which is shared with methods and properties alike (multi_read/multi_call/multi_write, read_array/call_array/write_array, and the dynamic-client equivalents). A method with a custom #[errors(..)] result (CallError<E>) can't go into a tuple multi-call; call it on its own instead.

items.title: Error lists
items.text:
#[errors(..)] on a method names the variants of its error enum it returns (API-32), Common(InUse, Refused) the variants of the enum a Common(CommonError) variant holds, Common all of them:

#[ww_trait]
trait Sensor {
    /// Reads one sample.
    #[errors(Common(Busy, InUse), Nack)]
    fn read() -> Result<u16, SensorError<'i>>;
}

The list is checked when the trait is parsed (an unknown or repeated name is a compile error on that name), goes into the API model and from there into the generated client's docs (# Errors, each entry with its variant's doc line), ww api tree, Python's help() and ww api check (a changed list is a compatible change). The device and the wire don't see it: a device may still return any variant, the client logs a tracing warning when one is outside the list, and tests_common makes that a test failure (wire_weaver_client::set_strict_error_lists). Without #[errors] a method may return every variant. Stream functions and properties take the same list. More in Errors.

items.title: Optional items
items.text:
A method, property or stream of a trait can be marked optional. A device's server may then leave it out when it is built: no dispatch arm, no handler to write, no stub answering "not implemented". A client calling it gets Unimplemented, and a client with the device's introspection data knows it without asking. tests/traits has a worked example; Errors tells Unimplemented apart from a device's own errors.

#[ww_trait]
pub trait I2c {
    fn i2c_configure(config: I2cConfig) -> Result<I2cConfig, I2cError<'i>>;
    // ...
    /// Clocks SCL until SDA is released, then a stop.
    #[optional]
    fn i2c_wiggle_clock(count: u8) -> Result<I2cLinesState, I2cError<'i>>;
    /// Switchable pull-ups: both items or neither.
    #[optional(pullups)]
    fn i2c_set_pullups(enabled: bool) -> Result<(), I2cError<'i>>;
    #[optional(pullups)]
    property!(ro i2c_pullups: bool);
}

// a device without these: no handlers to write
ww_codegen!(nucleo_api::Nucleo for Server, server = true, omit = ["i2c.i2c_wiggle_clock", "i2c.pullups"]);

items.title: Marking items optional
items.text:
• #[optional] on a method, property or stream lets a device leave it out. #[optional(group)] names a set of items that go together: leaving the group out leaves out all of them.
  • Only marked items can be left out: the API author decides what is optional, the rest of the trait stays a contract every device keeps. Leaving out a required item is a compile error that lists the trait's optional items and groups.
  • An item keeps its resource index whether a device has it or not, so clients address it the same way everywhere.
  • The marker is part of the trait's signature: marking an item optional later changes the API model, and its snapshot has to be saved again.
  • #[optional] on ww_impl! (a whole trait) is rejected; mark the trait's items instead.

items.title: Leaving items out
items.text:
ww_codegen!(.., server = true, omit = [..]) takes paths "<trait item>.<..>.<item or group>" from the API root, without array indices: "periph.channel.run" leaves run out of every periph[i].channel[j]. Items of the API root itself are named directly (omit = ["reset"]). An item and a group of the same name: the item wins. Naming an item twice (by name and through its group, or in omit and omit_if) is a compile error, as is an unknown name.

omit_if(<cfg>) = [..] ties optional items to the device crate's own Cargo features:

ww_codegen!(
    nucleo_api::Nucleo for Server,
    server = true,
    omit_if(not(feature = "pullups")) = ["i2c.pullups"]
);

The dispatch arm gets #[cfg(not(<cfg>))]; the handlers are the device crate's to cfg out. The introspection data (and with it the API hash) depends on which items are left out, so it is generated for each combination of the conditions, under #[cfg(all(..))]; at most 4 different conditions per ww_codegen!.

ww api scaffold --omit i2c.pullups,reset leaves the stubs of these items out and writes the same omit = [..] into the generated ww_codegen! call; the stubs of optional items it keeps carry a comment naming their path.

items.title: What a client sees
items.text:
• A call to an omitted item is answered ErrorKind::Unimplemented, the same answer as a handler returning Unimplemented. In a generated client that is CallError::Unimplemented (see Methods).
  • The device's introspection data lists the items it leaves out (ApiItemKind::Trait { omitted }, ApiBundle::root_omitted for the API root, ApiItem::optional for the marker). A client that has it fails a call to an omitted item locally with NotImplementedByDevice, without a round trip; the compatibility check doesn't count it as a mismatch, it is the device's choice.
  • The dynamic client (DynResource::is_omitted()) and Python fail such calls locally too. Python signatures end in (optional), or (left out by this device); ww api tree and ww introspect show #[optional] and (left out by this device).
  • A device without introspection data, and no cached copy on the client: the call goes out and is answered Unimplemented.

items.title: Cost
items.text:
The fallback arm of a trait level that leaves something out answers Unimplemented for an id below the trait's item count and BadPath above it: one comparison per level, no arm per omitted item. Levels that leave nothing out are generated as before.

Measured on thumbv7em-none-eabihf (opt-level = "s", LTO, introspection off) with a Board { ww_impl!(i2c: I2c); fn other(..) } API whose I2c has one required method and three optional items (two methods and an rw property):

Server .text Stub handlers answering Unimplemented (what the scaffold generates without omit) 7496 bytes The three items left out with omit 7204 bytes The three items not in the API at all 7192 bytes

Leaving an item out saves about 100 bytes (its arm, argument decoding and the stub); the comparison costs 12 bytes per level that leaves something out.

items.title: Optional item or its own trait
items.text:
Optional items are for one to three items within the trait's subject that some hardware lacks: a clock wiggle, pull-ups, a hardware CRC. Items with their own state, configuration or streams, a subject of their own (a bus monitor, ADC capture), anything a different set of devices implements, or four items and more make a trait of their own.

Optional is for what is known when the firmware is built. A capability that depends on what is found at run time (a board variant read from EEPROM) stays a capability the device reports, or a CommonError::Unsupported answer (see ww_error).

items.title: High-level overview
items.text:
API is defined as a collections of user-defined types and resources - methods, properties, streams and traits. Multiple levels are supported. Common functionality (logging, GPIO, USART, etc.) can be extracted into external crates, see ww_stdlib. Both kind of levels can be defined as arrays (e.g., array of GpioPin's). Arbitrary user data types are supported as well, backed by ShrinkWrap.

Generated server code is completely IO-free (sans-IO), all communication with the USB or network is handled separately. On the device side, ww_device provides the link logic and event loop building blocks (the loop itself stays in user code, see link layer), and wire_weaver_usb_embassy adds USB on top of it. Generated std client code uses tokio and it's channels under the hood. Asynchronous, blocking and promise flavors are supported. Client generation for no_std is not yet implemented, but planned.

WireWeaver supports both backwards and forwards compatibility at the wire format level, but you need to ensure to follow the evolution rules for it to work properly.

items.title: Methods (RPC)
items.text:
#[ww_trait]
trait MyDevice {
    fn no_args();
    fn plain_arg(value: f32);
    fn plain_ret() -> f32;
    fn user_type(state: State);
    fn user_ret() -> UserComplex<'i>;
    fn fallible() -> Result<UserComplex<'i>, UserError>;
}

Any number of arguments are supported. Arguments can be evolved in the same way as structs (e.g., new_arg: Option<T> can be added to the end).

Return type can also be added later in a backwards+forwards -compatible way, e.g., an Option<T> or Vec<T>.

More on methods page.

items.title: Streams
items.text: More on streams page.

items.title: Properties
items.text: More on properties page.

items.title: Traits
items.text: More on traits page.

items.title: Optional items
items.text: A method, property or stream marked #[optional] (or #[optional(group)]) can be left out of a device's server with ww_codegen!(.., omit = ["i2c.pullups"]): no dispatch arm and no handler, a call answers Unimplemented, and a client knows it from the device's model. See Optional items.

items.title: Resource arrays
items.text: More on arrays page.

items.title: Properties
items.text:
A property is a value of the device the host reads, writes or both: a setting, a measured state, a mode.

#[ww_trait]
trait MyDevice {
    property!(ro button_pressed: bool);
    property!(rw speed: f32);
    property!(wo beep: u16);
    #[errors(TooBig, NotSet)]
    property!(rw mode: u8, ModeError);
    /// Known at compile time, never changes while the firmware runs.
    const LIMITS: Limits<'i>;
}
Access Declared as Read Write Observe read/write property!(rw name: T) ✓ ✓ with rw+observe read only property!(ro name: T) ✓ with ro+observe write only property!(wo name: T) ✓ const const NAME: T; ✓, once per connection

ro means read only for the host: the device changes the value whenever it likes, and may tell observers about it. +observe lets hosts observe it, see Observing changes. A const never changes while the firmware runs, see Const items.

Any type the SerDes system supports can be a property. A second type after the value's, property!(rw mode: u8, ModeError), is the property's error type: reads and writes may fail with it. #[errors(..)] above such a property lists the variants it returns, as on methods (see Errors). #[optional] / #[optional(group)] lets a device leave a property out (see Optional items), and a property can be an array, property!(rw gain[]: f32).

items.title: Device side
items.text:
A server implements each property in one of two ways, picked per property with the property_model argument of ww_codegen!: a comma separated list of regex=get_set|value_on_changed, the regex matching the property's name, _ for the rest; get_set is the default.

mod server_impl {
    wire_weaver::ww_codegen!(
        my_device_api :: MyDevice for super::Server,
        server = true, no_alloc = true, use_async = false,
        property_model = "speed=value_on_changed, _=get_set",
    );
}

ww api scaffold <api_crate> --property-model ".." prints the handlers and fields either way.

items.title: get_set: handlers
items.text:
User code provides get_<name> for reads and set_<name> for writes:

impl Server {
    fn get_button_pressed(&mut self, _cx: &mut Context<'_, impl BlockingEventOut>) -> GetResult<bool, ()> {
        Value(self.button.is_low())
    }

    fn set_beep(&mut self, _cx: &mut Context<'_, impl BlockingEventOut>, freq: u16) -> SetResult<()> {
        self.buzzer.start(freq);
        Set
    }

    fn get_mode(&mut self, _cx: &mut Context<'_, impl BlockingEventOut>) -> GetResult<u8, ModeError> {
        match self.mode {
            0 => GetError(ModeError::NotSet),
            mode => Value(mode),
        }
    }

    fn set_mode(&mut self, _cx: &mut Context<'_, impl BlockingEventOut>, mode: u8) -> SetResult<ModeError> {
        if mode > 10 {
            return SetError(ModeError::TooBig);
        }
        self.mode = mode;
        Set
    }
}
  • GetResult<T, E>: Value(v) answers the read with v; GetError(e) answers with the error; Unimplemented answers ErrorKind::Unimplemented.
  • SetResult<E>: Set acknowledges the write; SetError(e) answers with the error, the value is not applied unless the handler did so; Unimplemented answers ErrorKind::Unimplemented.
  • E is the property's error type, () without one. The error goes to the host serialized, as ErrorKind::UserBytes.

Both answer right away: a property has no deferred answer. Handlers get cx: &mut Context<'_, impl BlockingEventOut, Medium> (impl EventOut and async fn for use_async = true), properties in arrays their index chain after it.

items.title: value_on_changed: a field
items.text:
Generated code reads and writes a field of the server struct named like the property, and calls changed_<name> after a write that changed the value (the type needs PartialEq; writing the same value calls nothing):

struct Server {
    speed: f32,
}

impl Server {
    fn changed_speed(&mut self, _cx: &mut Context<'_, impl BlockingEventOut>) {
        self.motor.set_speed(self.speed);
    }
}

Reads and writes can't fail with this model: a property whose writes have to be checked uses get_set. Properties of nested traits carry the trait item chain in their names (self.motor_speed, changed_motor_speed), as every handler does.

items.title: Observing changes
items.text:
A host observes the +observe properties of a trait level (the root API, or a trait implemented with ww_impl!) with one Observe request to the level's path: per property Off, OnChange { min_us }, Periodic { every_us } or OnChangeOrBeat { min_us, max_us }, and a budget in bytes per second for the level. The device answers with what it granted and from then on sends one PropertyUpdate event per level whenever any of its observed properties is due, carrying just those: a sparse <Trait>Update with an Option per observable property, at the slot of its resource index (wire format: ww_client_server::observe, API-38).

#[ww_trait]
trait Motor {
    property!(ro+observe speed: f32);
    property!(ro+observe current: f32);
    property!(rw+observe mode: u8);
    property!(rw gain: f32); // not observable
}

For an API with +observe properties the generated server needs the ww_stream crate and three things from the user: an api_impl::ObserveState in the server struct, handed out by observe_state(), a call to the generated poll_properties in the event loop, and a mark_changed_<name>() call where the device changes a value by itself. ww api scaffold prints the field and observe_state().

struct Server {
    observe: api_impl::ObserveState,
    // ..
}

impl Server {
    fn observe_state(&mut self) -> &mut api_impl::ObserveState {
        &mut self.observe
    }

    fn on_new_measurement(&mut self, current: f32) {
        self.current = current;
        self.mark_changed_current(); // sent to hosts observing it on change
    }
}

let mut server = Server {
    // shortest period, per level and total budget (the properties' share of the link), timestamps
    observe: api_impl::ObserveState::new(ww_stream::observe::ObserveLimits::DEFAULT),
    // ..
};

// event loop, every millisecond or so, between requests
let mut buf = [0u8; 256]; // as big as the biggest update the link carries
server.poll_properties(&mut ww_server.sink(), medium, now_us, &mut buf).await?;
server.poll_streams(&mut ww_server.sink(), now_ms, &mut stream_buf, 4096).await?; // stored streams after
  • When a property is due: Periodic on a fixed grid, never early; OnChange after mark_changed_<name>() and at least min_us after its previous send; OnChangeOrBeat also once max_us passed without a send. value_on_changed properties are marked changed by the generated code after a write that changed them; get_set ones by the device. A property that starts being observed is sent once right away, so the host has a value to start from.
  • Values: get_set properties are read through their getter when they are sent (values without a size bound, such as strings, also once before that to measure them), value_on_changed ones from their field. A getter that fails skips that send.
  • Budget: each level has a token bucket at its granted bytes per second, holding a tenth of a second of it (64 bytes at least); all levels together get at most ObserveLimits::total_budget. Each poll_properties call sends at most one update per level: its due properties earliest deadline first, as many as fit the bucket and buf. The rest slips to a later call; a property left out keeps its deadline, so it goes first then, and none starves.
  • Missed: a property due and left out counts one missed send, a periodic one also every whole period it falls behind; the count goes to the host in the next update's missed.
  • Untrusted input: an Observe request is checked in full before anything changes. Entries for an unknown index, a property without +observe, an index given twice or a mode the device doesn't know are refused one by one and listed in the answer; periods are raised to ObserveLimits::min_period_us and the budget is clamped. A request that doesn't decode, or has more than 16 refused entries, fails with ArgsDesFailed / BadIndex and changes nothing. When the answer doesn't fit the reply buffer, the request fails with ResponseSerFailed and is undone too.
  • Limits: a level inside a resource array (ww_impl!(bank[]: Bank)) can't be observed yet (the bound of its indices isn't known, API-29), Observe there answers OperationNotSupported; nor can +observe properties that are in an array themselves or #[optional]. Observing stays set while the link is down; ObserveState::reset() stops it all.

Sharing the link with stored streams: properties have a reserved share of the link, the sum of the granted level budgets, at most ObserveLimits::total_budget; reliable streams get what poll_streams is given per turn. Polling properties first keeps their short deadlines, and their share bounds what they take from the streams.

items.title: Before observe requests
items.text: stream_data_ser().<name>_send(&value, out) (_send_blocking for sync servers) still sends one property's value as stream data on its own path. Generated clients receive it with observe_<name>() for properties without +observe (a plain Stream<T>, no request is sent to the device); for +observe properties observe_<name>(mode) is the observe request below. It is superseded by observe requests.

items.title: Host side
items.text:
Generated clients have read_<name>(), write_<name>(value) and observe_<name>() per property, as its access allows. Reads and writes are prepared first, then sent async, blocking or as a promise:

let speed = device.read_speed().read().await?;            // Result<f32, Error>
device.write_speed(1500.0).write().await?;                // waits for the device's acknowledgement
device.write_speed(1500.0).write_forget().await?;         // no answer asked for, nothing waited for
let pressed = device.read_button_pressed().blocking_read()?;
let mut read = device.read_speed().read_promise("speed"); // poll it from a GUI
  • A write to a property with an error type returns Result<(), CallError<E>>: CallError::Device(e) is the device's error, decoded, see Errors. Without one it returns Result<(), Error>.
  • A read returns Result<T, Error>; a device's error arrives as Error::RemoteError with ErrorKind::UserBytes, the error's bytes (E::from_ww_bytes).
  • ErrorKind::Unimplemented (CallError::Unimplemented { .. } for writes) is a handler returning Unimplemented, or a property the device left out.
  • .with_timeout(..) overrides the request timeout for one read or write.
  • Several resources in one request, when the server is generated with multi_req = true (a server without it refuses the request): each index is answered on its own (Result<T, ErrorOwned> per item, in order).
    • Different resources at the same level: (device.read_x(), device.read_y(), device.read_mode()).multi_read().await and the multi_call/multi_write equivalents, implemented for tuples of 2 to 8 of the generated PreparedRead/PreparedCall/PreparedWrite builders, at any depth (any resources that share a common path prefix and diverge at exactly one element, optionally followed by one more shared element — e.g. the same property across two array elements).
    • The same resource across a whole array: read_array/call_array/write_array (+ _blocking) take a MultiIndexOwned selector (Range/List/Mask32) and the existing generated per-index accessor, e.g. read_array(MultiIndexOwned::Range(UNib32(0)..UNib32(4)), |i| client.pin(i).read_mode()).await. The dynamic client has the same as DynResource::multi_read/multi_write/multi_call.
    • Whether each index carries the same argument/value or a different one per index (MultiArgs::Same/ Different) is chosen automatically from the serialized bytes.
  • With an #[errors(..)] list, the generated client warns when a write fails with a variant outside it (the dynamic client checks reads too).

The dynamic client and Python have the same per property: dev.speed.read(), dev.speed.write(1500) (Python).

items.title: Observing
items.text:
The host side of observing changes (CLT-28). Each trait level with +observe properties gets observe(cfg) on its client (the root client, or device.motor()), each +observe property observe_<name>(mode); both are prepared first and .subscribe() (.subscribe_blocking()) returns an Observer once the device answered:

use wire_weaver_client::observe::{on_change, on_change_or_beat, periodic};
use api_client::motor_api_motor::MotorObserve; // in the level's client module (`<api crate>_<trait>`)

let ms = Duration::from_millis(1);
let mut motor = device
    .observe(MotorObserve::default().speed(periodic(10 * ms)).current(on_change(ms)))
    .budget(20_000)                      // bytes per second, the device decides without it
    .subscribe()
    .await?;
let granted = motor.granted().unwrap();  // what the device applies: Granted { modes: MotorObserve, budget, refused }
while let Ok(u) = motor.recv().await {   // Observed { value: MotorUpdate, t, missed, received }
    if let Some(speed) = u.value.speed { /* .. */ }
}
motor.with_latest(|l| l.speed.as_ref().map(|s| (s.value, s.received)));

let mut mode = device.observe_mode(on_change(ms)).subscribe().await?; // Observer of u8 values
let m = mode.recv().await?.value;
mode.configure(MotorObserve::default().mode(periodic(100 * ms))).await?;
  • Types: per level <Trait>Update (<Trait>UpdateOwned when a property holds a String or Vec), the level's PropertyUpdate data, one Option per +observe property, the ones sent present; <Trait>Observe, one Option<ObserveMode> per property with a setter each, for asking and in Granted::modes for what was granted; <Trait>Latest, the latest Sample { value, received, t } of each property. t is the device's time, present when it sends timestamps (ObserveLimits::timestamps).
  • One subscription per level: every observer of a level asks for its own modes, the host sends the device one Observe that covers them all, per property the shortest on-change interval and the shortest period of all of them (OnChange and Periodic give OnChangeOrBeat), the biggest budget. It is sent again when an observer comes, calls configure(..) / configure_with_budget(..), or is dropped; dropping the last one turns the level Off. Each observer gets every update of its level, a property observer only the updates that carry its property. The settings are what the device applies for all observers together, so an observer may get more often than it asked for.
  • Events: recv() / recv_blocking() / try_recv() give updates, recv_event() also Disconnected, Resumed and Dropped { events } (the observer's queue on the host is bounded like a stream's, ClientConfig::stream_queue_bytes).
  • Reconnects: observers outlive disconnect().keep_streams(); resume_streams() on the next connection sends every level's subscription again (the device may still have it, ObserveState::reset is the device's choice) and the observers see Resumed. A link that goes down for good ends them (StreamError::Closed once drained).
  • Old devices: a device whose API model is ww_client_server before 0.2 can't observe, .subscribe() fails with Error::Unsupported.
  • Limits: levels inside a resource array have no observe() yet, like on the device. Absolute paths only: a trait client (client = "trait_client") observes once it has a base path (attachment()).

items.title: Const items
items.text:
A const item of a trait is a value that doesn't change while the firmware runs: a firmware name and version, a board record, chip ids, limits of an implementation.

#[ww_api_root]
trait Device {
    /// Known at compile time.
    const LIMITS: Limits<'i>;
    /// Read from the chip at boot.
    const SERIAL: &'i str;
    ww_impl!(board: ww_board_info::BoardInfo);
}

On the server, no handler is called for it. The value comes from the generated trait <RootTrait>Consts, which the server struct implements, in one of two forms, picked per item with the const_model argument of ww_codegen!:

  • const (the default): a Rust const, const LIMITS: Limits<'static> = ..;.
  • fn: a value fixed at boot or link time (OTP, a chip id register, the build id in flash), fn serial(&self) -> &str. Items in an array of traits get the index chain: fn channel_gain(&self, index_chain: [UNib32; 1]) -> u8.

Names carry the trait item chain prefix, as handler names do: BOARD of board: BoardInfo is BOARD_BOARD as a const and board_board as a fn. const_model is a comma separated list of regex=const|fn, the regex matching the whole name of the item as written in its trait (BOARD, not board_BOARD); _=fn changes the default.

impl api_impl::DeviceConsts for Server {
    const LIMITS: Limits<'static> = Limits { max_len: 64, names: RefVec::Slice { slice: &["a", "b"] } };

    fn serial(&self) -> &str {
        &self.serial
    }

    fn board_board(&self) -> BoardSummary<'_> {
        self.board.summary()
    }
}

mod api_impl {
    wire_weaver::ww_codegen!(
        device_api :: Device for super::Server,
        server = true, no_alloc = true, use_async = false,
        const_model = "SERIAL|BOARD=fn",
    );
}

ww api scaffold --const-model "SERIAL|BOARD=fn" <api_crate> prints this impl with a todo!() for every value. An #[optional] const left out with omit = [..] has no item in the trait. A trait without const items has no <RootTrait>Consts. A const can't fail, so it has no error type and no #[errors(..)].

Clients read a const from the device once per connection and keep the value: later reads of it (generated read_<NAME>(), async, blocking or as a promise, the dynamic client and Python) return it without a request. A new connection, or a disconnect() through the same Commander, reads it again; Commander::clear_const_cache() does too. Errors are not kept. ww introspect reads the consts that are not in an array of traits and shows their values in the tree (--no-values to skip them).

items.title: Stream delivery: counted and reliable streams
items.text:
A plain stream! sends each item once and forgets it: nothing tells the host that an item is missing, and nothing is kept for a host that is slow or gone. That is right for a latest-value stream (a motor controller's state at 1 kHz, where an old value is worthless), and wrong for measured data, logs and monitors, where the host must know exactly what it didn't get, or must get everything.

WireWeaver has three delivery kinds for device → host streams:

plain counted reliable Position in each event – yes yes Data the device dropped reported exactly – yes yes Link losses, duplicates, reordering detected – yes yes, and repaired Device timestamp per event – optional optional Acknowledged, resent on loss – – yes Kept while the host is slow or gone, sent when it is back – – while the device's store has room Latest values first after a reconnect, the backlog beside them – – yes Extra bytes per event 0 1-8, plus units, lost, t when present the same Device state none a few counters counters and a store

Item types carry none of this: positions, loss counts and the time of the first unit are in a small head the framework puts in front of every event, so a SampleBlock stays pure data (an item may add a time of its own, such as when a UART chunk's last byte arrived).

This page explains what counted and reliable streams guarantee and how the protocol works. How to declare them, write the device's handlers and producers, and open and resume them on the host is in Streams.
path: Stream delivery: counted and reliable streams

items.title: Where stream data gets lost
items.text:
From a producer on the device to user code on the host:

 producer ──► device buffer ──► event loop ──► framer ──► medium ──► host transport ──► event loop ──► stream queue ──► user code
 (DMA, ISR)   (user's ring)     (ww_device)               (USB..)    (nusb, socket)     (client)      (per stream)
  • The producer's buffer overflows: a producer can't wait, so it drops data. That happens on every medium, when the stream's rate is above what the link moves, while the device's event loop is busy (a flash erase, a long handler), and while no host is connected.
  • The medium loses it, depending on the transport (below).
  • The link goes down: whatever was in buffers on the way is gone, and whatever the producer makes until the host is back.
  • The host's queue is full, when user code doesn't read.
Medium The medium itself Where losses happen USB bulk / interrupt CRC and retries in hardware, flow control by NAK: no loss the producer's buffer, unplug, device reset, USB suspend, host process exit RTT RAM rings, no corruption; a chunk that doesn't fit is retried, then the link goes down the producer's buffer (a probe polls at its own pace), detach UDP datagrams lost, duplicated, reordered; a message split across datagrams is dropped whole when a piece is lost any datagram, the producer's buffer, link down WebSocket TCP: no loss while connected, backpressure blocks the device the producer's buffer, what is in flight when the connection drops In-process none the producer's buffer

Counted streams make every one of these losses visible, with its size and place. Reliable streams also repair link losses and keep data on the device while it has room.

Choose by what a missing piece costs:

  • plain: the latest value is all that matters, and counting costs more than it tells;
  • counted: measured data, telemetry over UDP: gaps are acceptable, but must be shown where they are;
  • reliable: logs, monitors whose protocol decoders can't recover from a gap, data loggers that collect while no host is connected.

The kind is part of the API, visible in introspection (ApiItemKind::StreamFn { delivery, .. }), so it is chosen in the API crate. How much a reliable stream keeps, and where, is the device's choice: one device keeps 256 KB in RAM, another days of data on an SD card, behind the same API.
path: Stream delivery: counted and reliable streams

items.title: Positions and units
items.text:
A counted or reliable stream counts units from the start of its session, as a u64. What a unit is, the stream's documentation says, and the device says how many units each item has when it sends it:

Stream Unit An item of… …has units UART receive byte 37 bytes 37 I2C monitor transaction 12 transactions 12 ADC samples sample set (one sample of every channel) 1 536 bytes, 4 channels × 12 bit 256 a status stream item one value 1

Each event carries the position of its first unit (pos) and its number of units (units). The next event starts at pos + units + lost:

  • lost: units the device dropped right before this event (producer overflow, store full, no host). It explains a jump of pos exactly and says the gap is the device's.
  • A jump of pos that lost doesn't explain is a link loss (UDP): the host knows exactly how many units are missing, though not their content. A reliable stream gets them resent.
  • An event that starts before what the host expects is a duplicate or a late one: the host drops it and counts it.

The host never counts units of an item: it only compares positions, so units are whatever the device says (an ADC block's bytes don't tell its sample sets without the sample format). Counting units rather than items keeps every position exact: a protocol decoder can say "the frame starts at byte 4711 of this capture", and a gap of 60 000 bytes says how much is missing even when the device dropped raw bytes before they ever became items.

Positions are 64-bit because a store can be big: a 32 GB SD card holds 2³⁵ bytes of a byte stream within one session. On the wire a position costs only the bytes it needs (below), and it is never truncated, so the host never has to guess its high bits.
path: Stream delivery: counted and reliable streams

items.title: Head on the wire
items.text:
A counted or reliable stream sends EventKind::StreamItem instead of StreamData:

// ww_client_server
pub enum EventKind<'i> {
    // ... Value, Written, StreamData, StreamSideband
    StreamItem { path: RefVec<'i, UNib32>, head: StreamHead, data: TailBytes<'i> },
}

// ww_client_server::stream
pub struct StreamHead {
    pub pos: u64,             // position of the event's first unit since the session started
    pub units: u64,           // units of the event's item
    pub lost: Option<u64>,    // units the device dropped right before this event; `pos` counts them
    pub t: Option<Second>,    // device time of the first unit
    pub ext: Option<HeadExt>, // rare markers: the clock epoch changed (a reboot)
}

The head is laid out by hand, so that its four flags share the first byte with the length of pos:

 byte 0:  L T X U n n n p      L, T, X, U: lost, t, ext, units follow (units only when not 1)
                               nnn: bytes of pos after this one (0..7), p: the top bit of pos
 then:    n bytes of pos (1 + 8n bits in all, big endian)
          units: UVlq64             if U
          lost:  UVlq64             if L
          t:     ww_si::Second      if T (starts on a byte, so its prefix and type tag share one byte)
          ext:   HeadExt            if X (Unsized: fields can be appended later)
pos below 2 512 128 Ki 32 Mi 8 Gi 2 Ti 512 Ti 2⁵⁷ Head bytes (one unit, no lost, t, ext) 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8

units (when not 1) and lost add 1 byte each below 128, 2 below 16 Ki, and so on; t as Second { Micro, U32 } adds 5 bytes, as U64 9. A stream of single items pays nothing for units, a byte stream 1-2 bytes. A position of 2⁵⁷ or more is a serialization error.

Example, from the tests of ww_client_server::stream: pos = 2³³, units = 3, lost = 7 and a t of Second { Micro, U32(0x12345678) } is the 13-byte head da 02 00 00 00 00 03 07 23 78 56 34 12; with the event header and a one-element path, 17 bytes come before the item's data.

A StreamData event costs 3 to 5 bytes of header and path before its data, so a long-running counted stream with a timestamp pays about 15 bytes per event: 3 % of a 512-byte item, 1 % of 1.5 KiB. Send small items in chunks (an item of type MaxLen<RefVec<'i, Record>, N>, counted in records), not one event per record.
path: Stream delivery: counted and reliable streams

items.title: Sessions, cursors and resuming
items.text:
A session is one run of a stream with one meaning of its positions, numbered by the device (session: u32, for example a boot counter combined with an open counter). A cursor names a point in it:

pub struct StreamCursor { pub session: UVlq32, pub pos: UVlq64 }
  • A session starts when the host opens the stream, or when the device starts it by itself (a logger that samples from power-on). Positions start at 0.
  • It ends when the stream is opened again (the units may mean something else now), or when the device's store is erased. It does not end when the link goes down, nor, with a store that survives reboots, on a reboot.
  • Opening can carry a cursor: a resume. The device answers with StreamOpened { session, oldest, live_from, resume_from }:
    • same session, cursor still in the store: the backlog starts at the cursor, nothing is lost;
    • same session, cursor older than the store keeps: the backlog starts at the oldest event kept, the units before it are reported lost (cause Store);
    • another session: the old one has ended, the host starts with the new one.
  • Counted streams resume too. They keep nothing, but the device keeps counting while the host is away, so after a reconnect the first event's lost says exactly what the host missed.

A host that saves data also saves the cursor with it, and resumes from it after a restart: with explicit acknowledgements (below), nothing is lost even when the host crashes between receiving data and saving it.
path: Stream delivery: counted and reliable streams

items.title: Latest values while backfilling
items.text:
A resumed reliable stream has two runs of positions, each delivered in order:

  • the live run starts at the newest event the device has (live_from), so a slow stream shows its latest value at once instead of after its next event, and goes on with everything new;
  • the backfill run goes from the resume point up to live_from.

The device sends live events first, and backfill events with whatever capacity the link has left. A data logger with six hours on its SD card shows its current readings on a dashboard as soon as the laptop connects, while the backlog arrives beside them; when the live data alone fills the link, the backlog waits in the store and nothing is lost. When the backfill run reaches live_from it ends, and the runs are one again.

Every event is sent once, and acknowledgements stay cumulative: one position per run. On the host each event says which run it belongs to, so a dashboard reads the live run, a recorder takes both and writes by position. While a backfill runs, acknowledged live events stay in the store until the backfill passes them.
path: Stream delivery: counted and reliable streams

items.title: Acknowledgements and resends
items.text:
A reliable stream's receiver (the host) tells the sender (the device) what it has. Positions are in units, grants in bytes, since what runs out on the receiving side is memory:

Sideband Direction Meaning Ack { have, backfill, grant } receiver → sender received every unit before have (live run) and before backfill (backfill run, while there is one); the sender may have up to grant bytes of events in flight beyond them ResendFrom { from, grant } receiver → sender units from from on are missing, in whichever run from falls: send again from there Query { sent, backfill } sender → receiver "I have sent up to here, where are you?", when out of credit or nothing was heard for a while; answered with Ack or ResendFrom

All three carry the whole state, so losing one is harmless: the next one replaces it.

  • The device keeps every event in its store until an Ack passes it, sends while the bytes in flight before the next event are below the grant (so a grant smaller than an item can't stall the stream), and goes back on ResendFrom (go-back-N). With no host, nothing is acknowledged: the store fills, then data is dropped and counted.
  • The host accepts events of each run in order only, drops duplicates, asks for a resend once per gap, and acknowledges every half window or 100 ms. The window is what the host queues for the stream (4 MiB by default): a host that doesn't read stops granting, the device stops sending and keeps the data in its store, so the host's memory stays bounded.
  • When data counts as received (AckMode): by default when user code takes an event; with Explicit, only when user code confirms it, for example after writing it to disk.
  • Defaults: a resend is asked again after 500 ms, the device queries after 200 ms of silence, the first grant is 4 KiB.

On USB the link doesn't lose, so ResendFrom never happens and an Ack is a few bytes every half window: a reliable stream costs almost nothing more than a counted one there, and adds backfill and bounded host memory.
path: Stream delivery: counted and reliable streams

items.title: Stores
items.text:
What a reliable stream keeps lives in a store, a ww_stream::store::StreamStore the device picks per stream: RamRing in RAM, PersistentRamRing in RAM that survives a soft reset, LogStore on an SD card or NOR flash that survives reboots and power cuts. When a store is full it drops the newest events (FullPolicy::DropNewest, the default) or the oldest (DropOldest); either way the units are counted and reported to the host as lost. See Stream stores.

Events are stored as they are sent, head included, so a resent event is bit-identical to the first send: its timestamp is the device's time when the data was made, never when it was sent. A reboot restarts the device's clock; the first event after one carries the new clock epoch in HeadExt::clock_epoch, so the host can tell the two timelines apart.
path: Stream delivery: counted and reliable streams

items.title: Sending: producers, the event loop and priorities
items.text:
A ww_stream::tx::Reliable is one state: the producer pushes events into it, whether a host is there or not, and the event loop reads the next event out of it and sends it. Shared between tasks, it sits behind the firmware's async mutex, held for a push or a store read only, never while the link is busy, so a slow link never stalls a producer.

Generated code drives it: stream_data_ser().<name>_push(..) pushes, the server's poll_streams sends and the dispatcher feeds it the host's sideband (Reliable streams). Underneath, and for a device without generated code, it is:

use ww_stream::{store::RamRing, sched::Priority, tx::{Reliable, Pushed}, Run};

let mut samples: Reliable<RamRing<{ 256 * 1024 }>> = Reliable::new(RamRing::new()).priority(Priority::Low);

// producer: units and time given here, nothing in the item type
if samples.push(&block_bytes, sets, Some(t)).await? == Pushed::Lost { /* counted, reported to the host */ }
samples.lost(dropped_sets); // the producer's own ring overflowed: goes into the next event's `lost`

// event loop: what may go out now, the host's Ack / ResendFrom, a Query when the host went silent
if let Some(ev) = samples.next_event(Run::Live, &mut buf).await? { /* send ev.head and ev.item */ }
samples.on_host_sideband(&sideband).await?;
if let Some(query) = samples.poll_query(now_ms) { /* send it */ }

ww_stream::tx::Counted is the same for counted streams, without a store: head(units, t) returns the head of the next event (None while no host has the stream open: the units count as lost), lost(units) counts drops, unsent(&head) turns an event that couldn't be sent into lost units.

With several streams, ww_stream::sched::Scheduler decides which one sends next: by priority class (High, Normal, Low, set by the device, not the API), the live run before the backfill run within a class, round-robin between streams of one class, up to a byte budget per turn so that requests are read in between. A device puts its log stream above a bulk ADC stream, a logger the other way round. Plain streams write directly and are not scheduled: data that needs a priority is counted or reliable.

On the host, ww_stream::rx::Receiver takes each event's head (on_item) and returns a Verdict: accept (with the gaps before it, each with its run, position, size and cause: Device, Link, Store or Host), duplicate, already had, late or out of order; poll(now_ms) returns the next Ack or ResendFrom to send. It runs in the client's event loop behind every PositionedStream, see Counted and reliable streams on the host.
path: Stream delivery: counted and reliable streams

items.title: Counting
items.text:
Every sending stream keeps TxStats (stats()): units sent and resent, lost by cause (producer, store full, no host), bytes acknowledged, resend requests, overruns. With the cnt feature it also counts into typed cnt instance counters, one set per stream, named by the firmware, so cnt tui shows per stream where data went:

use ww_stream::counters::StreamCnt;

static ADC_SAMPLES_CNT: cnt::Counters<StreamCnt> = cnt::counters!(StreamCnt, adc_samples);
let samples = Reliable::new(RamRing::<{ 256 * 1024 }>::new()).counters(&ADC_SAMPLES_CNT);

The host's Receiver keeps RxStats with the same causes: received, lost on the device, on the link and in the store, duplicates, late, out of order.
path: Stream delivery: counted and reliable streams

items.title: Timestamps
items.text:
t in the head is the device time of the event's first unit, a ww_si::Second in the storage the device's timer gives cheaply: Second { Micro, U32 } (5 bytes, wraps every 71.6 minutes, the host unwraps it) on most MCUs. A device uses one clock for every stream, so items of different streams line up. Three ways to timestamp, chosen per stream:
