Granularity How Cost For Per anchor t in every N-th event (e.g. every 50 ms); the host interpolates by position and the configured rate ~5 B per anchor fixed-rate streams: ADC, logic analyzer Per event t in every event 5 B per event UART chunks (a chunk ends when the line goes idle, so t is its first byte), sensor readings Per item t per event, and each item's offset from it inside the item, in the head's unit, as a DeltaOfDelta about 1.2 B per item for jittered ~100 µs gaps, 1.9 B for random 20-2020 µs gaps, 0.23 B for a regular rate monitors: I2C transactions, GPIO edges

Two examples:

  • An ADC at 500 kS/s, 12-bit packed, one channel (750 KB/s): in blocks of 1 024 samples (1.5 KiB), event header and head take 0.7 %, a t in every event 0.3 % more. Per-sample timestamps would take 15 % and tell nothing, the rate is fixed: use blocks of about 1 KiB and an anchor every 50 ms.
  • An I2C monitor at 1 MHz with about 20 000 transactions per second, in chunks of 32: 625 events per second of about 15 bytes of header, head and t (9.4 KB/s), plus per-transaction time at ~1.5 B each (30 KB/s), against ~10 bytes of data per transaction (200 KB/s).

items.title: With each transport
items.text:
Medium Counted Reliable USB, RTT, WebSocket, in-process device drops and link-down gaps exact nothing lost while the store has room; backfill after a reconnect, live first; bounded host memory UDP link losses, duplicates and reordering detected too go-back-N repairs them; acknowledgements carry the whole state, so losing one is harmless CAN, UART (planned transports) as UDP as UDP; keep events small, a message split across frames is lost whole

Resending is per stream, not in the link layer: a link that resends would hold latest-value streams back behind a lost datagram, couldn't keep data across a reconnect or a reboot, and wouldn't know about data the device dropped.
path: Stream delivery: counted and reliable streams

items.title: The ww_stream crate
items.text:
no_std, sans-IO: generated code (or a test) feeds the state machines what arrived and sends what they return, and passes the time in milliseconds where timing matters. The wire types live in ww_client_server::stream.

Module What Used by tx Counted, Reliable: sender state machines (runs, credit, go-back-N, sessions) device rx Receiver: in order per run, gaps by cause, duplicates, Ack timing host store StreamStore, RamRing device sched Scheduler: which stream sends next, by priority device counters StreamCnt (cnt instance counters with the cnt feature), TxStats device

The protocol is tested with a seeded simulation of a lossy, duplicating and reordering link with reconnects and resumes (ww_stream/src/tests/sim.rs, more seeds with SIM_SEEDS=20000).
path: Stream delivery: counted and reliable streams

items.title: Stream stores
items.text:
A reliable stream (Stream delivery) keeps every event it sends until the host acknowledges it, so it can send it again after a loss and send the backlog after a reconnect. Where these events are kept is a store, a ww_stream::store::StreamStore the device picks for each stream: it is the S of the stream's ww_stream::tx::Reliable<S> state (Reliable streams). The API doesn't change with the store: the same stream can keep 256 KB in RAM on one device and 32 GB on an SD card on another.

Store Where Survives Feature RamRing<N> N bytes of RAM host reconnects always there PersistentRamRing<N> N bytes of .uninit RAM soft resets (fault → reset), not power cuts persistent-ram LogStore<M, BUF> SD card, NOR flash reboots and power cuts log-store (+ sdmmc / nor-flash)

All keep events as they go on the wire, head included, so a resent event is bit-identical: its timestamp is the device's time when the data was made, not when it was sent.

When a store is full, it does what its FullPolicy says:

  • DropNewest (default): the new event is refused (PushError::Full), the sender counts its units as lost and reports them in the next event's lost. What is kept stays contiguous.
  • DropOldest: the oldest events are forgotten to make room, a ring of the most recent data. Their units are counted in StoreState::dropped_units.

Either way the host learns exactly how much is missing and where.

items.title: RAM: RamRing
items.text:
use ww_stream::store::{FullPolicy, RamRing};

static SAMPLES: StaticCell<RamRing<{ 256 * 1024 }>> = StaticCell::new();
let store = SAMPLES.init(RamRing::new().with_policy(FullPolicy::DropOldest));

Each event takes its item, its encoded head and 21 bytes (RECORD_OVERHEAD).

items.title: RAM across a soft reset: PersistentRamRing
items.text:
A RamRing whose bytes sit in RAM the startup code leaves alone, so they are still there after a soft reset: a HardFault or panic handler that resets the chip (SCB::sys_reset) doesn't take the last logs before the crash with it. The next boot takes the events up again and the host gets them when it connects. A power cut loses them; RAM after a power-on holds garbage, which is never taken for events.

ww_stream = { version = "0.5", features = ["persistent-ram"] }

use core::mem::MaybeUninit;
use ww_stream::store::{FullPolicy, PersistentRamRing, RamArea};
use ww_stream::tx::Reliable;

// cortex-m-rt leaves `.uninit.*` alone at boot
#[unsafe(link_section = ".uninit.ww_logs")]
static mut LOG_AREA: MaybeUninit<RamArea<4096>> = MaybeUninit::uninit();

// once, at boot
let area = unsafe { RamArea::from_uninit(&mut *core::ptr::addr_of_mut!(LOG_AREA)) };
let store = PersistentRamRing::attach(area).with_policy(FullPolicy::DropOldest);
// `store.recovery().formatted`: nothing was kept (a power-on), a new ring was started
let mut logs = Reliable::new(store);
// the ring from before the reset: continue its session and positions
logs.continue_stored_session();

Where the area goes is the firmware's business, and differs per chip: it must be RAM the startup code neither zeroes nor copies into (.bss, .data), nor a firmware's own RAM init (a loop zeroing a whole SRAM bank at boot takes the area with it). With cortex-m-rt, a .uninit.* section is enough. The same area must not be used for anything else, and only one store may be attached to it.

items.title: What it keeps
items.text: The same as a LogStore across a reboot: session, positions, the released position, dropped_units, and a new clock epoch per boot (clock_epoch(), 0 for a new ring), which the first event pushed after it carries in HeadExt::clock_epoch unless the sender set it already. state().persistent is true.

items.title: How it checks the RAM
items.text:
The area holds two 64-byte header slots and the ring. After every change (push, release, reset) the ring's header is written to the slot not written last, with a magic, the layout version, N, a sequence number and a CRC-32C; at boot, the good slot with the higher sequence number wins. A record goes into free room first, and old records a push drops to make room are forgotten by a slot written before the new record goes over them, so a reset at any byte leaves the state before or after the change, never a mix. Every record has its own CRC-32C, checked at boot too: if something wrote over the area before the reset, the ring is cut before the first bad record (recovery().truncated_bytes) and the stream continues after it.

The host tests (ww_stream/src/tests/persistent_ram.rs) carry the area's image over a simulated reset (RamArea::image(), load_image()), fault a push, release and reset after every byte written, and attach to random garbage, flipped header bits and records written over.

items.title: Sizing
items.text: Each event takes its item, its encoded head and 25 bytes (PERSISTENT_RECORD_OVERHEAD); the area is N bytes and 128 for the slots (RamArea::<N>::SIZE). Every change also writes a 64-byte slot; a push computes two CRCs (over the slot and over the record).

items.title: SD card or flash: LogStore
items.text:
LogStore is a log on a block device that keeps a stream's data across reboots and power cuts: a field logger keeps sampling to its SD card while no host is there, reboots, and the host still gets everything when it connects.

ww_stream = { version = "0.5", features = ["sdmmc"] }      # or "nor-flash"

use ww_stream::store::log::{LogConfig, LogStore, SdMedium};
use ww_stream::store::FullPolicy;
use ww_stream::tx::Reliable;

// blocks 2048.. of the card are the log's, the rest is free for a FAT partition
let medium = SdMedium::new(sd_card, 2048, num_blocks - 2048);
let config = LogConfig { segment_size: 64 * 1024, policy: FullPolicy::DropNewest };
// session 1 is used only when the card holds no log yet
let store: LogStore<_, 512> = LogStore::mount(medium, config, 1).await?;
let mut samples = Reliable::new(store);
// a log from before the reboot: continue its session and positions
samples.continue_stored_session();

On NOR flash, wrap an embedded-storage-async NorFlash (a QSPI chip, or a partition of the MCU's own flash) in NorMedium(flash); segments are then a multiple of the flash's erase size. Any other storage can implement LogMedium: its write and erase unit sizes, whether it needs erasing before a write, read, write and erase.

items.title: What it keeps
items.text:
• Positions and session: after a reboot state() gives back the session and next, the position the stream continues from, so the host sees one session across the reboot, not a new stream.
  • Released position: what the host acknowledged is freed. It is saved now and then, so after a reboot a few acknowledged events may be sent again; the host drops them as duplicates. Events not acknowledged are never lost.
  • Clock epochs: the device's clock restarts with a reboot, so each mount starts a new clock epoch (clock_epoch()), and the first event pushed after a mount carries it in HeadExt::clock_epoch, unless the sender set it already. The host maps each epoch to real time, or shows "before reboot N".

items.title: Power cuts
items.text:
A push writes its record before it returns. If the power fails during a push, at most that record is lost: on the next mount the store finds the end of the log and counts a record it finds cut short in recovery().torn_records. Positions continue after the last whole record; the cut one was never sent, so the host never saw it.

This holds for a power cut at any write or erase, which the tests check one by one on a simulated SD card and NOR flash (ww_stream/src/tests/log_store.rs). On an SD card it relies on a 512-byte block write either happening or not, as SD cards do; on NOR flash nothing is assumed about a cut write.

items.title: Sizing
items.text:
The log is a ring of segments of segment_size bytes, after two small superblock slots at the start:

  • A segment is the unit of room: it is freed once every event in it is acknowledged (or dropped), and the rest of a segment stays empty when the next event doesn't fit, and on every reboot (a new segment starts the new epoch). Make segments several times the biggest event.
  • Use many segments: a mount reads the superblock, at most a few segment headers and the last segment, and a read finds its segment by a binary search over the headers, so a big card mounts as fast as a small one. 64 KiB segments on a 32 GB card give half a million.
  • BUF is the size of the two buffers the store keeps, a multiple of the medium's write size: 512 for an SD card.

Each event takes its item, its encoded head (see StreamHead) and a 12-byte record header, rounded up to 4 bytes on an SD card or to the write size on NOR flash.

LogStore::mount returns LogError::Geometry when the medium holds a log with another segment size or medium size; LogStore::format starts a new, empty log on it.

items.title: Testing with a simulated medium
items.text: With the std feature, SimSd and SimNor are an SD card and a NOR flash in RAM. cut_power_at(n) makes the n-th write or erase the one the power fails in (it is torn, every later call fails), and image() / from_image() carry the content over a reboot, so a device's own power-cut tests run on the host.

items.title: Other stores
items.text:
Any storage can hold a reliable stream by implementing StreamStore (for a block device, implementing LogMedium for LogStore is usually less work):

pub trait StreamStore {
    type Error;
    /// Append an event, head and item bytes as they go on the wire.
    async fn push(&mut self, head: &StreamHead, item: &[u8]) -> Result<(), PushError<Self::Error>>;
    /// Copy the event at `pos`, or the first one after it, into `buf`.
    async fn read<'b>(&mut self, pos: u64, buf: &'b mut [u8]) -> Result<Option<StoredEvent<'b>>, Self::Error>;
    /// Events before `pos` are acknowledged and may go.
    async fn release(&mut self, pos: u64) -> Result<(), Self::Error>;
    /// Session, oldest and newest kept positions, next position, bytes used and capacity, persistent or not.
    fn state(&self) -> StoreState;
    /// A new session: drop everything, positions from 0.
    async fn reset(&mut self, session: u32) -> Result<(), Self::Error>;
}

A full store either refuses the push with PushError::Full (drop newest) or forgets its oldest events and moves state().oldest on, counting their units in dropped_units (drop oldest).

items.title: Streams
items.text:
A stream carries a sequence of values in one direction. Naming is from the device's point of view: a stream goes out of the device to the host (stream!), a sink goes into the device from the host (sink!).

#[ww_trait]
trait MyDevice {
    stream!(button: ButtonEvent);
    stream!(uart_rx: [u8]);
    sink!(uart_tx: [u8]);
    sink!(leds: Vec<LedState>);
}

Any type the SerDes system supports works as a stream item. Items keep their boundaries: each value sent arrives as one value, in order, even when several are packed into one packet on the way. Sending [1, 2, 3], [4], [5, 6] on uart_rx gives the same three slices on the other end. A byte item ([u8], Vec<u8>, or MaxLen<RefVec<'i, u8>, N> to bound it) is sent as is, without a length prefix.

Streams and sinks come in kinds that differ in what they promise about delivery:

Kind Declared as What is guaranteed plain stream stream!(name: T) nothing: items go out once, a lost one is gone unnoticed; the latest value wins counted stream #[counted] stream!(..), #[stream(T, counted)] fn .. every item has a position: the host learns exactly how much was lost, where and why reliable stream #[reliable] stream!(..), #[stream(T, reliable)] fn .. counted, acknowledged and resent; kept in a store on the device while the host is slow or gone plain sink sink!(name: T) nothing: writes are not acknowledged, the device keeps up or drops credit sink #[credit] sink!(name: T) flow control: the host never sends more than the device has room for, lost writes are resent

The kind is part of the API and visible in introspection, so it is chosen in the API crate. What a counted or reliable stream guarantees, and how, is the subject of Stream delivery; this page shows how to declare, implement and use every kind.

items.title: Stream functions
items.text:
A stream is opened by calling it, like a method: the host sends its arguments, the device decides whether to start, and answers with a result. A stream that takes arguments or returns a result is declared as a stream function, a trait fn with a #[stream(ItemType)] or #[stream(ItemType, counted | reliable)] attribute:

#[ww_trait]
trait Adc {
    /// Sample sets at `config.rate`; unit: sample set
    #[errors(BadRate, Common(InUse))]
    #[stream(SampleBlock<'i>, reliable)]
    fn samples(config: StreamConfig) -> Result<StreamActual, AdcError<'i>>;

    /// Bytes as they arrive on the line; unit: byte
    #[counted]
    stream!(rx: [u8]);
}

stream!(name: T) is the short form of a stream function without arguments and result, #[counted] / #[reliable] above it choose its kind. The return type is either nothing or a Result<A, E>: Ok opens the stream and gives the host A (e.g. the rate the device actually picked), Err answers with the error and leaves the stream as it was. Calling an open stream again opens it again, a new session, e.g. with another configuration.

#[errors(..)] above a stream function lists the variants of E opening it returns, as on methods (see Errors); a stream! has no result, so no list. #[optional] / #[optional(group)] lets a device leave a stream or sink out (see Optional items). Counted streams document their unit (byte, sample set, transaction), the doc comments above do so with unit: ...

On the wire, opening is a RequestKind::StreamOpen { resume, args } request, answered with a ww_client_server::stream::StreamOpened (the session and positions, empty for a plain stream) followed by the function's result. Closing is a StreamSideband::Close request from the host, or a Close event from the device when the stream ends on its own.

items.title: Device side
items.text:
ww api scaffold <api_crate> prints every handler and state field a server needs, with the right signatures for the ww_codegen! options (see ww api). For a stream named samples they are:

Handler Plain Counted Reliable Called fn samples(&mut self, cx, args..) -> RpcResult<R> ✓ ✓ ✓ the host opens the stream fn close_samples(&mut self, cx) ✓ ✓ ✓ the host closes it fn sideband_samples(&mut self, cx, sideband) -> Option<StreamSideband> ✓ other sideband from the host, see Sideband fn stream_samples(&mut self) -> &mut Counted / &mut Reliable<S> ✓ ✓ whenever generated code needs the stream's state fn new_stream_session(&mut self) -> u32 (one per server) ✓ ✓ a host opens a counted or reliable stream

All handlers get cx: &mut Context<'_, impl EventOut, Medium> (impl BlockingEventOut for use_async = false); streams in arrays get their index chain after it. The open handler answers right away: Ready(..) with the result, Unimplemented refuses it; a deferred answer is not supported for an open.

items.title: Plain streams
items.text:
The generated stream_data_ser() has, for every plain stream, <name>_send(&value, out) (async), <name>_send_blocking(&value, out), and <name>(&value, scratch) returning the serialized event. out is the cx of a handler, or server.sink() of the ww_device server anywhere in the event loop (in the snippets, server is the ww_device server and state the struct the API is implemented on):

impl ServerState {
    async fn button(&mut self, _cx: &mut Context<'_, impl EventOut>) -> RpcResult<()> {
        self.button_open = true;
        Ready(())
    }

    async fn close_button(&mut self, _cx: &mut Context<'_, impl EventOut>) {
        self.button_open = false;
    }
}

// from a handler, goes out before its reply
server_impl::stream_data_ser().button_send(&event, cx).await?;
// from the event loop
if state.button_open {
    server_impl::stream_data_ser().uart_rx_send(&chunk, &mut server.sink()).await?;
}

Nothing stops the device from sending to a plain stream no host opened: the host drops events no handle waits for. Keeping track of whether a host listens is up to the open and close handlers.

items.title: Counted streams
items.text:
A counted stream's state is a ww_stream::tx::Counted, usually a field of the server, handed to generated code by stream_<name>(). Generated code opens it (a new session, numbered by new_stream_session()), resumes it, closes it and answers a read on the stream with its StreamStatus. Producers send through it, naming the units of each item and the device time of its first unit, if any:

struct ServerState {
    rx_stream: Counted,
    sessions: u32,
}

impl ServerState {
    async fn rx(&mut self, _cx: &mut Context<'_, impl EventOut>) -> RpcResult<()> {
        Ready(())
    }
    async fn close_rx(&mut self, _cx: &mut Context<'_, impl EventOut>) {}
    async fn stream_rx(&mut self) -> &mut Counted {
        &mut self.rx_stream
    }
    /// Put a boot counter into the high bits, so that a cursor from before a reboot never matches a new session.
    fn new_stream_session(&mut self) -> u32 {
        self.sessions = self.sessions.wrapping_add(1);
        self.sessions
    }
}

let ser = server_impl::stream_data_ser();
// sent right away; while no host has the stream open, the units are counted as lost instead
ser.rx_send(&mut state.rx_stream, &chunk, chunk.len() as u64, Some(t), &mut server.sink()).await?;
// the producer's own buffer overflowed: the next event reports it
state.rx_stream.lost(dropped_bytes);

stream_<name>() may return anything that dereferences to the state, e.g. a mutex guard when a producer task shares it. Counted streams work in sync servers too (<name>_send_blocking).

items.title: Reliable streams
items.text:
A reliable stream's state is a ww_stream::tx::Reliable<S> with a store S that keeps every event until the host acknowledges it: RamRing<N> in RAM, PersistentRamRing<N> across a soft reset, or LogStore on an SD card or flash (see Stream stores). Stores are async, so reliable streams need an async server (use_async = true, a compile error otherwise).

Producers push into the store and never wait for the link; the generated poll_streams sends what the stores have, called from the event loop between requests:

struct ServerState {
    samples_stream: Reliable<RamRing<{ 16 * 1024 }>>,
    sessions: u32,
}

impl ServerState {
    async fn stream_samples(&mut self) -> &mut Reliable<RamRing<{ 16 * 1024 }>> {
        &mut self.samples_stream
    }
    // samples(), close_samples() and new_stream_session() as above
}

// producer: `scratch` holds the serialized item on its way into the store
let pushed = server_impl::stream_data_ser()
    .samples_push(&mut state.samples_stream, &block, 256, Some(t), &mut scratch)
    .await?; // Pushed::Lost when the store was full: counted, reported to the host

// event loop
loop {
    if let Either::First(ready) = select(server.wait(), Timer::after_millis(5)).await
        && let Some(event) = server.handle(ready, state).await
        && matches!(event, LinkEvent::Down(_))
    {
        // stop sending, keep the data for the host's resume
        state.samples_stream.detach();
    }
    if server.is_up() {
        let now_ms = Instant::now().as_millis();
        // by priority, live before backlog, up to 2048 bytes of items; `buf` holds the biggest item
        _ = state.poll_streams(&mut server.sink(), now_ms, &mut buf, 2048).await;
    }
}

poll_streams(out, now_ms, buf, budget_bytes) is generated when the API has reliable streams. It also asks a host that went silent where it is, and the host's acknowledgements and resend requests reach the store through the dispatcher. Detaching on LinkEvent::Down is the firmware's job: a detached stream sends nothing and keeps its data for the host's resume.

A reliable stream only stores once it has a session: from the first open by a host, or from boot on when the firmware starts one itself, so that a logger keeps what it records before any host connects:

// at boot, before the event loop
let session = state.new_stream_session();
state.samples_stream.start_session(session).await?;
// or, with a store that survives reboots: continue the session it holds
state.samples_stream.continue_stored_session();

Reliable::new(store).priority(Priority::High) sets the stream's priority against other reliable streams, see Sending: producers, the event loop and priorities. examples_mcu/rp2/src/bin/usb_log.rs is a complete firmware with a reliable log stream.

items.title: Host side
items.text:
Generated clients have one function per stream. A stream function prepares the open; .call().await (or .blocking_call()) sends it and returns the stream handle, together with the function's result when it has one:

// stream!(button: ButtonEvent): a plain stream, Stream<ButtonEvent>
let mut button = device.button().call().await?;
// a counted stream, PositionedStream<TailBytesOwned>
let mut rx = device.rx().call().await?;
// a fallible stream function: Result<(StreamActual, PositionedStream<..>), AdcError> inside the call's Result
let (actual, mut samples) = device.samples(config).call().await??;

Before .call(), the prepared open takes .with_timeout(..), .queue_bytes(..) (how much the host queues before it drops, plain and counted streams), .window(..) and .ack_mode(..) (reliable streams). Only what the device sends after the open reaches the handle; events before it are not buffered.

items.title: Plain streams: Stream<T>
items.text:
• recv() returns the next value, recv_blocking() and try_recv() (None when nothing is there yet) the same without async. They skip Connected and fail on a sideband event or a disconnect.
  • recv_any() (recv_any_blocking()) returns every event: TypedStreamEvent::Data(value), Sideband(..), Connected, Disconnected, Dropped { events, bytes }.
  • A byte stream (Stream<TailBytesOwned>) has recv_all_bytes(), collecting everything until the device sends Close, with _blocking and _timeout variants.
  • close() closes the stream on the device. Dropping the handle doesn't.

The host queues at most ClientConfig::stream_queue_bytes (4 MiB by default) of a stream's items when user code doesn't read; what comes beyond is dropped, counted in dropped() and reported once as Dropped.

items.title: Counted and reliable streams: PositionedStream<T>
items.text:
while let Ok(ev) = samples.recv_event().await {
    match ev {
        StreamEvent::Item { pos, units, t, run, value, .. } => { /* run: Live or Backfill */ }
        StreamEvent::Gap { at, units, cause, .. } => { /* cause: Device, Link, Store, Host */ }
        StreamEvent::Resumed { cursor, ended, .. } => { /* ended: the old session, when the device has a new one */ }
        StreamEvent::BackfillDone | StreamEvent::Disconnected | StreamEvent::Closed => {}
    }
}
  • recv() (_blocking, try_) returns values only; gaps are logged and counted in stats() (StreamStats: received, lost by cause, duplicates, late, out of order, resend requests, queued).
  • cursor() is where to resume from: everything before it was received (counted) or acknowledged (reliable). A recorder saves it with its data. session() is the device's session number.
  • .ack_mode(AckMode::Explicit) when opening: a reliable stream's data counts as received only once ack(pos) confirms it, e.g. after writing it to disk, so a crash in between loses nothing. By default (AckMode::OnReceive) it counts when user code takes it.
  • split() gives one handle per run, each in order: a dashboard reads the live one, a recorder both.
  • close(), or dropping the last handle, closes the stream on the device.

The receiver runs in the client's event loop, so a program that doesn't read still answers the device, and its memory stays bounded: a reliable stream holds at most its window (.window(bytes), 4 MiB by default) and the device keeps the rest in its store; a counted stream drops what goes beyond its queue and reports it as Gap { cause: Host }.

items.title: Resuming
items.text:
Counted and reliable streams also get <name>_resume(cursor) and <name>_status():

// after a restart: the backlog from the saved cursor, beside live data
let mut samples = device.samples_resume(saved_cursor).call().await?;
// open or not, session, positions, store use
let status = device.samples_status().read().await?;

A resume continues the session with the arguments it was opened with on the device, so it has no arguments and no result. A cursor of an older session (the device opened the stream again or lost its store) starts with the current session, and Resumed { ended: Some(old) } says so. Across a reconnect of the same program, disconnect().keep_streams() keeps the handles open (they see Disconnected, not the end), and Commander::resume_streams() on the next connection resumes each from its cursor: the same handle goes on with Resumed and whatever the device kept meanwhile.

The dynamic client opens streams with DynResource::positioned_stream (DynPositionedStream, values as ValueOwned), Python with open() on the stream (Python).

items.title: Sinks
items.text:
A sink is written by the host, one value per write:

// host
let mut leds = device.leds().await?;            // Sink<Vec<LedState>>, `leds_blocking()` without async
leds.send(vec![LedState::On, LedState::Off]).await?;
let mut tx = device.uart_tx().await?;           // Sink<TailBytesOwned>
tx.send_bytes(b"hello").await?;

send() / send_blocking() take a borrowed value, send_owned() an owned type (FooOwned), send_bytes() the bytes of a byte sink; try_send() (try_send_owned(), try_send_bytes()) returns Ok(false) instead of waiting, for GUIs and promise-style code.

On the device, each write calls write_<name>(cx, value); a byte sink gets the bytes as &TailBytes<'_>, a byte sink with a MaxLen bound refuses a longer write before the handler sees it:

fn write_uart_tx(&mut self, _cx: &mut Context<'_, impl BlockingEventOut>, data: &TailBytes<'_>) {
    if self.tx_ring.push_slice(data.0).is_err() {
        self.tx_dropped += 1; // the device can't push back on a plain sink
    }
}

A plain sink's writes are sent without a request id: the device sends nothing back, and the host doesn't wait. A plain sink needs no opening, send() works right away; open() and close() send the Open and Close sideband, which reach the device's sideband_<name> handler, for devices that want to know.

items.title: Flow control
items.text:
What keeps a fast side from overrunning a slow one depends on the kind:

  • Plain streams: nothing. The device sends what it has, the host queues up to stream_queue_bytes per stream and drops beyond it.
  • Counted streams: nothing slows the device down either, but every loss, on the device, on the link or in the host's queue, is reported with its size and place.
  • Reliable streams: the host grants the device a window of bytes in flight and acknowledges what it received; a host that doesn't read stops granting, and the device keeps the data in its store (see Acknowledgements and resends).
  • Plain sinks: the host's writes go through the client's bounded command queue (ClientConfig::cmd_queue_size), so a program can't outrun its own link; nothing tells it whether the device keeps up. A device that can't has to drop, or tell the host with its own sideband events.
  • Credit sinks: the device grants room in bytes and the host never sends more, below.

items.title: Credit-based flow control for sinks
items.text:
A sink marked #[credit] gets flow control and acknowledgements built in, for bulk transfers into a device over slow or lossy links: a firmware update plan streamed into a single-bank MCU that stalls on every flash write, bytes for a UART bridge, frames for a CAN transmitter.

#[ww_trait]
trait Updater {
    /// Update plan: steps and data, tens to hundreds of KB, in pieces of up to 1 KiB
    #[credit]
    sink!(plan: MaxLen<RefVec<'i, u8>, 1024>);
}

The device grants the host credit in bytes: the bytes of the sink's items, one item being the serialized value of one write, as sent. The host sends an item only when all of it fits into the credit left, and never splits one. Out of credit, send() waits, send_blocking() blocks and try_send() returns Ok(false), so the host never outruns the device's receive buffer, however slow the device or fast the link.

items.title: Why bytes and not values
items.text:
What runs out on a device is RAM: the bytes of its receive buffer. Counting values (one slot per write) would make the device size every slot for the largest value, so a buffer that holds sixteen 1 KiB pieces would also hold only sixteen 20-byte ones. Counting bytes, the same buffer holds as many items as fit, however their sizes vary.

The price is one rule, since items are never split: the device must always be able to grant at least its largest item, or the host could never send it. Three things keep a transfer from getting stuck:

  • The buffer holds the largest item. The generated <SINK>_MAX_ITEM_BYTES: Option<u32> on the level's stream serializer (also stream_data_ser().<sink>_max_item_bytes(), a const fn) is the largest item, from the type's MAX_SIZE: MaxLen<RefVec<'i, u8>, N> gives N (bytes are sent as is), a type without an upper bound ([u8]) None. SinkCredit::sized_for(buffer_bytes, max_item) checks it, a compile error in a const; try_sized_for() returns an error for a size known at runtime. For an unbounded type the host checks: a value bigger than the device's buffer (the first credit of a session) fails send() with StreamError::ItemTooBig instead of waiting forever.
  • A re-grant lets the largest item in. The device re-grants once it freed threshold bytes (half the buffer by default); sized_for caps the threshold at buffer - largest item + 1, so a host waiting for room for a big item always gets it with the next grant. With an unbounded type, set the threshold that way yourself (with_threshold), or a waiting host only learns of the room from its next CreditQuery.
  • The device consumes without waiting for more. A device that collects data before writing it out (a flash page) has to write it once less room than the largest item is left: the host can't send the next item before that.

items.title: Device side
items.text:
Generated server code does the bookkeeping; user code says how many bytes it can buffer and when it frees some. A credit sink has one more handler, credit_<name>(), returning its state, a ww_client_server::credit::SinkCredit, usually a field of the server (arrays of sinks get the index chain and need one state per index):

const BUF: usize = 4096;
/// Some(1024), from the API's MaxLen bound
const LARGEST: Option<u32> = server_impl::stream_data_ser().plan_max_item_bytes();
/// a buffer smaller than the largest item would not compile
const PLAN_CREDIT: SinkCredit = SinkCredit::sized_for(BUF as u32, LARGEST);

struct Server {
    plan_credit: SinkCredit, // PLAN_CREDIT, re-granted every BUF / 2 bytes freed
    plan_buf: heapless::Vec<u8, BUF>,
}

impl Server {
    fn credit_plan(&mut self) -> &mut SinkCredit {
        &mut self.plan_credit
    }

    fn write_plan(&mut self, _cx: &mut Context<'_, impl BlockingEventOut>, data: &TailBytes<'_>) {
        // only called for writes in order, never more bytes than the credit granted
        self.plan_buf.extend_from_slice(data.0).unwrap();
        // the next item might not fit: write out now, the host can't send more before that
        if self.plan_buf.len() > BUF - LARGEST.unwrap() as usize {
            flash_write(&self.plan_buf); // stalls for a while
            self.plan_credit.free(self.plan_buf.len() as u32);
            self.plan_buf.clear();
        }
    }

    fn sideband_plan(
        &mut self,
        _cx: &mut Context<'_, impl BlockingEventOut>,
        _sideband: StreamSideband,
    ) -> Option<StreamSideband> {
        None
    }
}

A handler of a typed sink gets the value, not its bytes: SinkCredit::last_item_len() is the size of the item it was called with, what to free() once that value is consumed.

  • On Open, generated code calls SinkCredit::open() (a new session), then sideband_<name> as for any sideband (it may change the capacity there), then sends the initial credit.
  • On a write, generated code checks its position, calls write_<name> for writes in order only, and after it returns sends new credit if free() moved the limit far enough.
  • CreditQuery is answered by generated code, sideband_<name> doesn't see it.
  • Data freed outside a handler (e.g. after a flash write in the event loop): if let Some(sb) = state.plan_credit.take_credit(), send it with stream_data_ser().plan_sideband_send_blocking(sb, out) (plan_sideband_send in an async server). If that is skipped, the host's next CreditQuery picks it up after its query interval.
  • SinkCredit::overruns() counts bytes the host sent beyond its credit (should stay 0; such writes still reach the handler).

items.title: Host side
items.text:
Sink<T> of a credit sink works like any other: send() opens the session if needed and waits for credit. Besides:

  • flush() / flush_blocking() / try_flush() waits until the device accepted everything sent so far, resending what was lost; close() flushes first, then sends Close.
  • credit_progress() returns (accepted, sent) bytes of the session, e.g. for a progress bar.
  • set_credit_config(CreditConfig { query_interval, stall_timeout }) tunes it to the link: query_interval (1 s by default) longer than the link's round trip, stall_timeout (30 s by default) longer than the device's worst stall (a flash sector erase takes 1-2 s); with no progress for that long, send() fails with a timeout.

The dynamic client and Python speak the same protocol for credit sinks.

items.title: On the wire
items.text:
A credit sink is its own resource kind (ApiItemKind::FlowSink { ty, flow: FlowControl::Credit } in ww_self), so turning a plain sink into a credit sink is an API break: its writes change. Each write is a ww_client_server::CreditWrite { pos: UVlq32, data: TailBytes } inside RequestKind::Write, pos being the byte position of the item's first byte since the session's Open (1 byte for the first 128 bytes of a session, 2 up to 16 KiB, 3 up to 2 MiB, 4 up to 256 MiB). Three sideband messages carry the rest:

Sideband Direction Meaning Credit { have, grant } device → host have bytes of items accepted in order; the host may send up to byte have + grant CreditQuery { sent } host → device "I have sent up to byte sent, where are you?", answered with Credit or Resend Resend { have, grant } device → host writes after have were lost: send again from byte have (an item boundary), up to have + grant

All three carry the whole state, so losing one is harmless: the next one, or the answer to the next query, replaces it. Positions are 32 bit, a session is limited to 4 GiB.

  1. Open starts a session: the device resets its counters and answers with Credit { have: 0, grant: capacity }. Credit events left over from an earlier session are ignored by the host until this one arrives.
  2. The host sends an item while pos + its length <= have + grant, keeping a copy of everything after have for a resend (at most the device's capacity).
  3. The device counts accepted bytes (have) and bytes it freed (consumed, e.g. written to flash); its limit is freed + capacity. When the limit has moved by at least threshold since the last grant, it sends a new Credit: a large threshold means few acknowledgements over a slow link, a small one keeps the link full.
  4. When the host is out of credit and nothing arrives for query_interval, it sends CreditQuery. This recovers from a lost Credit, from a device that freed less than threshold, and finds lost data at the end of a transfer.
  5. flush() sends CreditQuery and waits until have == sent: on a reliable link with a buffer that holds the whole transfer, the one acknowledgement it needs.

On a lossy medium (UDP, LoRa, LTE-M) the device accepts a write only at pos == have: one before it is a duplicate from a resend and is dropped; one after it means something was lost, so it is dropped too and the device sends Resend { have, grant }, once per gap. A CreditQuery { sent } with sent > have means writes were lost after the last one that arrived; the device answers with Resend instead of Credit. On Resend the host goes back to have and sends everything again from its copy (go-back-N). Requests are processed in order, so when the device sees a CreditQuery, everything sent before it has arrived or is lost; a plain Credit never rewinds the host, the rest may still be in flight. An empty item takes one position, so its loss is noticed like any other.

Credit sinks are planned to move onto the positions, acknowledgements and resume of counted and reliable streams (API-34 in Features).

items.title: Sideband
items.text:
Next to its data, every stream and sink has a sideband channel in both directions, StreamSideband values sent in order with the data. Generated code uses it for the protocol, user code may use the rest:

Sideband Used for Close the host closes a stream or sink (close_<name> on a stream, sideband_<name> on a sink); the device ends a stream Open the host opens a sink (credit sinks: a new session) FrameSync, SizeHint(n), User(n) free for the API's own meaning: frame boundaries in a byte stream, the size of what follows, application events Credit, CreditQuery, Resend credit sinks, handled by generated code Ack, ResendFrom, Query counted and reliable streams, handled by generated code

From the host, plain streams and sinks pass a sideband to the device's sideband_<name>(cx, sideband): returning Some(sideband) sends it back as a sideband event on the same stream, None only acknowledges the request. Either way the host's request gets its answer. Counted and reliable streams take only Close and the protocol messages, other sideband is refused.

// host
stream.sideband(StreamSideband::User(UNib32(5))).await?;
match stream.recv_any().await? {
    TypedStreamEvent::Sideband(StreamSideband::User(n)) => { /* .. */ }
    _ => {}
}
// device
fn sideband_uart_rx(
    &mut self,
    _cx: &mut Context<'_, impl BlockingEventOut>,
    sideband: StreamSideband,
) -> Option<StreamSideband> {
    Some(sideband) // echo
}

The device sends sideband events on its own with stream_data_ser().<name>_sideband_send(sideband, out) (_sideband_send_blocking, <name>_sideband(sideband, scratch)), for streams and sinks alike; a Close this way ends a stream on the host (recv_all_bytes() returns, a PositionedStream sees Closed):

// e.g. tell the host a sink's buffer is full
server_impl::stream_data_ser().uart_tx_sideband_send(StreamSideband::User(UNib32(1)), cx).await?;

On the host, a Stream returns sideband events from recv_any(), a Sink from recv_sideband() (_blocking, try_recv_sideband()); credit events of a credit sink are used up internally.

items.title: Arrays of streams
items.text:
Streams and sinks can be arrays, and sit in arrays of traits:

#[ww_trait]
trait Board {
    #[counted]
    stream!(adc[]: [u8]);
    ww_impl!(port[]: Port);
}

#[ww_trait]
trait Port {
    stream!(event: PinEvent);
}

Each index is its own stream: the host opens device.adc(2).call() or device.port(0).event().call(), and every device handler gets the index chain after cx (index_chain: [UNib32; 1]), as does stream_adc(index_chain). valid_indices_root_adc() says which indices exist. On the device, send through the same chain: stream_data_ser().adc_send(2, &mut state.adc_streams[2], &chunk, units, t, out) for the array itself, stream_data_ser().port(0).event_send(&event, cx) inside an array of traits.

Reliable streams can't be in arrays yet: poll_streams refuses them with a compile error.

items.title: Properties as streams
items.text: An ro or rw property sends its changes as stream data on its own path: stream_data_ser().<property>_send(&value, out) on the device, observe_<property>() on the host, a plain Stream<T>. See Observing changes.

items.title: Traits
items.text:
Traits in WireWeaver are used to define API blocks, as you can see from examples above, entry point for a device API is also a trait. They carry similar meaning to Rust traits, in a sense that trait defines some functionality, that server "implements" and client code can then interact with.

But they are not implemented like Rust traits: Rust syntax is used to bypass writing a whole parser from scratch, and all the magic happens through code generation in the ww_codegen! macro, which reads the trait from its source file. What #[ww_trait] leaves in place is a Rust trait of the same name that only describes the API, so that cargo doc and docs.rs show it, see In rustdoc below.

items.title: Traits for API resources grouping
items.text:
Trait defined in the same file as the API root itself is a way to cleanly group related resources together.

#[ww_trait]
trait MyDevice {
    ww_impl!(motor_control: MotorControl);
    ww_impl!(led_control: LedControl);
}

#[ww_trait]
trait MotorControl {
    fn turn_on();
    fn turn_off();
}

#[ww_trait]
trait MotorControl {
    fn led_on();
    fn set_brightness(value: f32);
}

Note that in this case, one additional path index will be used, so in total there will be 4 valid paths here:

  1. [0, 0] - turn_on
  2. [0, 1] - turn_off
  3. [1, 0] - led_on
  4. [1, 1] - set_brightness

If preserving very small size is of big importance, try not to create too many levels. Also one can put more important functionality higher up, in order to leverage variable length encoding (e.g. numbers 0..=7 take only 4 bits on the wire).

TODO: splitting into multiple files

items.title: Traits (global)
items.text:
The idea behind global traits is to leverage crates.io to define a set of common traits used across many devices. Device can then implement all the traits it needs and on the client side, common code can be used to control similar functionality of different devices. ww_gpio (see ww_gpio std library page) is the first such trait actually implemented; more generic traits are currently planned:

  • FirmwareUpdate
  • EmbeddedLog
  • BoardInfo
  • Counters
  • DeviceUserInfo
  • RegisterAccess
  • CanBus

A device API, instead of re-implementing the same things over and over, can look like follows (ww_impl! just needs a path to the trait; the crate providing it - ww_gpio here - is a normal Cargo dependency of the API crate, see examples/all_gpio_api):

#[ww_api_root]
trait MyAwesomeDevice {
    ww_impl!(gpio[]: ww_gpio::Bank);
    // and some device specific functionality in addition to common things
}

Client code can be written in a completely agnostic way, e.g., only capable of interacting with a Bank trait, regardless of which exact device it is implemented on, at which resource path, or how it is physically connected - see Trait attachments below for how that decoupling actually works.

One can also interact with devices using trait-addressing mode, e.g., calling set_indication_mode(Mode::Night) on all devices on a CAN bus, putting all boards with LEDs into night mode. More on that on the addressing page

items.title: Trait attachments
items.text:
Every generated client struct, at every level of the API tree (the root struct itself, or the struct returned for a nested / array trait, whether it implements a global trait or a project-local one), gets a .attachment() method for free. It returns a wire_weaver_client::Attachment: a self-contained handle bundling the underlying Commander (already pointing at that exact resource path on that exact device), plus the source crate name + version and trait name of whatever trait lives there. Because it carries this identity, an Attachment can be handed to code that has never heard of the concrete device or its top-level API trait, as long as that code knows what to do with the global trait underneath.

examples/all_gpio/examples/high_level.rs is the reference for this pattern end-to-end:

let device = AllGpio::new().connect_blocking()?;

// get a global trait "attachment" point
let attachment = device.port(0).attachment();
// init a high-level, hand-written driver with better ergonomics than generated code
let mut bank = BankBlocking::new(attachment)?;

let bank_name = bank.name()?;
let mut pins = bank.all_pins()?;
for pin in &mut pins {
    println!("{}{}: {:?}", bank_name, pin.index(), pin.mode()?);
}

device.port(0) only exists because all_gpio_api::AllGpioApi happens to declare ww_impl!(port[]: ww_gpio::Bank)

  • it is all_gpio-specific generated code. .attachment() erases that specificity: BankBlocking::new never sees AllGpio or AllGpioApi, only something that claims to be a ww_gpio::Bank. It checks trait_name() and source_crate() on the attachment and returns Error::IncompatibleTrait if they don't match, so it will refuse an attachment that isn't really a ww_gpio::Bank, whatever device or resource path it actually came from - that runtime check is what makes it safe to accept an attachment from arbitrary device APIs.

The ww_gpio_hl crate (in ww_stdlib/ww_gpio_hl) is the reference for the driver side of this pattern - a higher-level API built on top of plain generated code:

  • src/ww.rs defines small wrapper structs (BankClient, GpioClient) and invokes ww_impl! against ww_gpio::Bank / ww_gpio::Pin directly, with client = "trait_client". That generated code only depends on ww_gpio, never on all_gpio_api or any other specific device API crate, so it is written and generated exactly once and reused by every device that happens to expose a compatible bank somewhere.
  • src/blocking.rs builds ergonomic, stateful types on top of that (BankBlocking, FlexBlocking, PushPullOutputBlocking, InputBlocking, OpenDrainOutputBlocking), each one constructed straight from an Attachment (BankBlocking::new, FlexBlocking::new_ignore_mode / new_get_mode). src/promise.rs does the same for immediate-mode UI use (BankPromise, FlexPromise); src/asynchronous.rs is the same idea for async, but is currently an empty stub.

Put together, a single ww_gpio_hl dependency can drive the GPIO bank of any device - regardless of what its top-level API trait is called - as long as it implements ww_gpio::Bank somewhere in its resource tree; reaching it takes exactly one .attachment() call on the device's own generated client.

items.title: Attaching without generated client code
items.text:
.attachment() is only available because the device's own API crate was run through ww_codegen!/ww_impl!, which is what generates device.port(0) (and every other accessor) in the first place. When that generated code is available, it is the convenient, recommended way to obtain an attachment.

Conceptually, an Attachment doesn't need to come from generated code at all: since it is just a Commander (already addressed to a device), a resource path, and the source crate/trait identity, the same identity information could in principle be discovered at runtime by introspecting a device's API (as ww_self is designed to do, see std library overview) and used to build an Attachment by hand, without any per-device generated code, wiring up a trait client dynamically to whatever resource path advertises a compatible global trait.

This dynamic-introspection path is not implemented yet - today, obtaining an attachment always goes through codegen-produced .attachment() methods.

items.title: In rustdoc
items.text:
#[ww_trait] and #[ww_api_root] turn the trait into a Rust trait of the same name and visibility, with every resource and its doc comment, so an API crate's documentation on docs.rs or from cargo doc shows the whole API. Methods keep their signature, the other resources become functions returning a marker from wire_weaver::api_doc:

pub trait Uart {
    fn rx<'i>() -> Stream<RxChunk<'i>>;               // stream!(rx: RxChunk<'i>);
    fn tx() -> Sink<[u8]>;                            // sink!(tx: [u8]);
    fn configure(config: UartConfig) -> Result<UartConfig, Error>;
}
pub trait Bank {
    fn pin(index: UNib32) -> impl Pin;                // ww_impl!(pin[]: Pin);
}
pub trait Pin {
    fn pull() -> Property<Pull, Error>;               // property!(rw pull: Pull, Error);
}

Access mode, array index, flow control and #[since] are added as the last paragraph of each resource's docs. reserved! doesn't show up. The trait is never implemented, handlers are generated by ww_codegen! (see server side), but it can be linked from docs ([Uart], [Uart::rx]).

Because it is a real trait, the compiler checks it in the API crate: every type must be valid Rust (RefVec<'i, &'i str>, not RefVec<'i, str>, lifetimes written out), and a trait used from another crate through ww_impl! must be pub.

items.title: Versioning
items.text: Each type and "ww_trait" version is it's crate version, same versioning rules apply. Types and "ww_trait's" are globally identified by their crate name and version. FullVersion type is provided in ww_version crate that carries crate name in addition to version numbers.

items.title: Evolution checker
items.text:
ww api check <path> compares the traits and types of a crate with the latest snapshot saved in <path>/api_snapshots/, and fails if the crate version is not bumped enough for what changed, following the evolution rules. The crate is parsed from source, same as for ww api save, so nothing has to be built.

$ ww api check ww_stdlib/ww_uart
ww_uart 0.1.0 (ww_stdlib/ww_uart/api_snapshots/ww_uart_0_1_0.ron) -> 0.1.1 (source): compatible changes
  compatible: Uart::flush added
version is bumped enough

The snapshot used is the newest one of the same crate with a version not newer than the one in Cargo.toml, so it is the snapshot of the current version if it was already saved, and of the previous version otherwise. --against <file> compares with a specific snapshot instead. Nothing is checked if there is no snapshot yet.

<path> can also be a snapshot file, which is then compared with the previous snapshot in the same directory, e.g. to check snapshots that were saved with --force.

ww api save runs the same check before saving a snapshot of a new version, and refuses to save it if the version is not bumped enough (--force saves anyway). So in a crate that has snapshots of all of its published versions, every new snapshot is checked against the previous one.

items.title: Listing all changes
items.text:
ww api diff <path> compares the same versions as ww api check (and also takes --against or a snapshot file), and lists every difference, doc comments included, followed by the verdict. It never fails, and doesn't tell why a change is breaking, ww api check does:

$ ww api diff ww_stdlib/ww_uart
ww_uart 0.1.0 (ww_stdlib/ww_uart/api_snapshots/ww_uart_0_1_0.ron) -> 0.1.0 (source)
  ~ Uart::rx: docs
      /// Receive stream
    + /// of chunks
  ~ Uart::prevent_back_feed: docs
      /// Detect RX low for more than 1 byte interval and set TX low to avoid powering device in sleep mode through it.
    - /// Optional, check [Capabilities] if supported.
    + /// Check [Capabilities] if supported.
  + Uart::flush: fn flush()
  ~ RxFlags: field `parity_error`: docs
    + /// Parity error
  + RxFlags: field `framing_error`: framing_error: bool
breaking changes, version has to be 0.2.0 or later (run `ww api check` for details)

Each line is an added (+), removed (-) or changed (~) trait, resource, type, struct field, enum variant or dependency crate version. Changes are: a resource's signature (kind, arguments, return type, property access, stream direction, array or not), a resource's or variant's name, a type's kind, size kind or repr, a field's position, type or #[default] value, #[since] of any of them, and doc comments, shown as a line diff. Items are matched as described below, enum variants by discriminant, fields by name and unnamed ones by position. A renamed type is removed and added.

evolution::diff() in wire_weaver_client returns the same list, for use from other tools.

items.title: What is checked
items.text:
Changes are sorted into four kinds, and each kind requires a bump of a version position:

Change Examples Bump None exactly the same traits and types, doc comments included none Doc comments only a doc comment on a trait, resource, type, field or variant is changed compatible position (patch before 1.0, minor after) Compatible new trait, new resource at the end of a trait, new field with #[default] at the end of an Unsized type, new field in unused padding bits of any type, new type, #[since] or #[default] value changed, max length raised or removed compatible position (patch before 1.0, minor after) Breaking see below breaking position (minor before 1.0, major after)

Doc comments are not on the wire, but a released version's snapshot never changes, so they need a new version as well (see doc comments). A bigger bump than required is always fine.

Resources are matched by their id inside each trait (their position, as the device sees them), traits and types by name. A change is breaking if:

  • a trait, resource or type is removed, or a resource moved to another id (e.g. a new one inserted before it: add new resources at the end),
  • a resource, struct field or enum variant is renamed, or struct fields change between named and unnamed: this does not change the wire, but breaks Rust code using them,
  • a resource of the old version can't be used with the new one, in either direction (old client with a new device, and new client with an old device), compared the same way as a client checks its API against a device's: resource kind, number and types of arguments, return type, property access, stream direction, array or not,
  • a type can't be written by one version and read by the other: e.g. field type changed, field added without #[default] at the end of an Unsized type, field added in between old ones outside of unused padding bits (see below), field added at the end of a final_structure, self_describing or sized type, enum variant added or removed, ww_repr or size kind changed,
  • a max length is lowered or added (T -> MaxLen<T, N>): data the old version writes may no longer be read,
  • a trait or type from another crate is replaced by one from a wire-incompatible version of that crate (e.g. ww_si 0.1 -> 0.2), or one from the same crate version with a different definition.

It also warns about additions without #[since], or with a #[since] that is not the new version.

items.title: New fields in padding bits
items.text:
Padding inside a type, before a field aligned to a nibble or a byte, is always written as zero bits and skipped when reading. A new field of any type, Unsized or not, can take such bits, anywhere between the old fields, if:

  • none of the old fields moves and the size doesn't change: the new field only takes bits that were padding,
  • all zero bits are a valid value of it, as that is what it reads from old data: bool, numbers, arrays and non-Unsized structs of them, or an enum without data that has a variant with discriminant 0,
  • it's fixed size (not UNib32, Option, an enum with data, an Unsized type, ...).

Old fields are then matched by name. Where padding is depends on the bit offset the type starts at. An Unsized type always starts at a byte boundary, so its padding is always in the same place:

#[derive_shrink_wrap]
pub struct U {
    pub f: bool,
    // 7 bits of padding before `b`
    #[since = "0.1.1"]
    pub g: u7, // added in 0.1.1, reads as 0 from old data
    pub b: u8,
    pub s: String,
}

An Unsized type can gain fields with #[default] at the end as well, in the same version. Bits after its last field are not free though: lengths of variable size fields are written there.

final_structure, self_describing and sized types are packed tightly into their parent, so they can't grow at the end, and they can start at any bit inside the parent, so the checker requires that the new field fits for every start offset:

#[derive_shrink_wrap(sized)]
pub struct S {
    pub a: u8,
    pub f: bool,
    // 7 bits of padding before `b`, wherever S starts, as `a` is byte-aligned
    #[since = "0.1.1"]
    pub g: u3, // added in 0.1.1, reads as 0 from old data
    pub b: u8,
}

Without a, the padding before b is 7 bits if S starts at a byte boundary, but none if it starts at bit offset 7, so g can't be added. Padding after the last field is never free: whatever follows the type in its parent starts right there. Enum variants with data are not padded to the same size, so there are no free bits after a shorter variant either.

All of this was checked against real bytes: old and new versions read each other's data, with the new field reading as zero from old data. The client uses the same rules when comparing its API with a device's.

items.title: Limitations
items.text:
• Snapshots of all published versions have to be kept in api_snapshots/, the checker can only see what is saved there. A crate without snapshots is not checked.
  • Only traits and types that ww api save finds are checked (see ww api).
  • Semantic changes that keep the same bytes, like changing units or the meaning of a value, can't be detected.
  • Padding bits are only reused when that works for every bit offset a type can start at, even if in all of its actual uses it's always at the same offset.

items.title: Evolution rules
items.text:
Two different things can break when a WireWeaver crate changes, and they are tracked separately:

  • Wire compatibility - whether bytes written by one side can still be read by the other. Firmware lives in the field for years, hosts are updated on their own schedule, and shrink_wrap blobs may be stored on disk. A wire break means deployed devices stop talking to new hosts (or the other way around), which no cargo update can fix.
  • Rust (SemVer) compatibility - whether code still compiles against the new crate version. A break here is annoying, but it is found by the compiler and fixed by the developer, before anything ships.

A change can break one without the other: renaming a BufWriter method breaks Rust code but not a single byte on the wire; changing a field's u8 to u16 in an API type compiles fine and silently breaks the wire. The rules below say which versions to bump for each, depending on where in the crate stack the change is.

items.title: Crate layers
items.text:
Layer Crates Versioning 1. Wire format shrink_wrap, shrink_wrap_derive own version, changes rarely 2. Shared API & types ww_stdlib/*: base types (ww_numeric, ww_si, ww_date_time, ww_version) and traits (ww_gpio, ww_i2c, ww_client_server, ...); framework base types ww_global and ww_self (repo root) own version per crate, the version is the API identity 3. Framework wire_weaver, wire_weaver_core, wire_weaver_derive, wire_weaver_client, wire_weaver_cli, ww_device, ww_link, ww_framer, ... shared [workspace.package] version, free to break Rust API 4. User API my_device_api and friends (see folder structure) own version, the version is the API identity, checked on every connection

Everything above layer 1 implements shrink_wrap's traits. Base type crates depend on shrink_wrap directly, trait crates and user API crates depend on wire_weaver, which re-exports shrink_wrap. Generated code refers to shrink_wrap::... through that re-export, so a single shrink_wrap version must be shared by the whole dependency graph of an application.

items.title: Layer 1: shrink_wrap
items.text:
shrink_wrap is the foundation that every other crate and every user type is built on, so it is kept stable and changes to it are rare and deliberate.

Wire format changes - anything that changes the bytes produced for an existing type (alignment, length encoding, discriminant or flag layout, the meaning of an existing derive_shrink_wrap directive) breaks every device, every host and every stored blob at once, regardless of any API version. Post 1.0 this is not allowed at all. Before 1.0 it is allowed only with a strong reason, batched with other such changes, and listed under ### ⚠️ Breaking in the changelog starting with Wire format:, so that it can't be mistaken for a Rust-only break. The byte-level claims in shrink_wrap, derive and showcase must be re-verified in the same change.

Rust API breaks (0.2 -> 0.3) do not touch the wire, but they still ripple through the whole ecosystem: to Cargo, shrink_wrap 0.2 and 0.3 are unrelated crates with unrelated SerializeShrinkWrap traits. A type from a ww_stdlib crate still built on 0.2 does not implement 0.3 traits, and can't be used inside a type or an API built on 0.3. So every ww_stdlib crate, the framework and every user API crate has to be re-released together. Therefore:

  • Prefer additive changes (new types, new methods, new directives, new features). They do not break anything and are released as a patch version (0.2.0 -> 0.2.1), so the rest of the ecosystem picks them up without re-releasing. This is the one exception to the "every change bumps minor" rule.
  • Collect breaking Rust API changes and release them together, rarely. When it happens, bump all ww_stdlib crates in the same release cycle.
  • shrink_wrap_derive is versioned together with shrink_wrap, as the generated code is tightly coupled to it.

items.title: Layer 2: ww_stdlib
items.text:
ww_stdlib crates are meant to be shared between unrelated projects, so their types end up inside many different APIs. Their versions travel on the wire (as FullVersion / CompactVersion with a ww_global id) for trait-based requests and introspection, so the version is not just Cargo metadata, it's a compatibility statement, same as for user API crates (layer 4):

  • Wire-compatible change (following the data type and API rules below) -> bump the compatible position: patch before 1.0 (0.1.0 -> 0.1.1), minor after.
  • Wire-incompatible change -> bump the breaking position: minor before 1.0 (0.1.0 -> 0.2.0), major after. Every crate and user API that exposes the changed type or trait over the wire is then wire-incompatible too, and has to bump its own breaking position when it upgrades.
  • A Rust-only break (e.g. renaming a helper method, changing a std convenience impl) is still a Cargo breaking change and bumps the breaking position, even though the wire is unaffected. Avoid mixing such changes with releases that are supposed to be wire-compatible additions; prefer deprecating and adding.

Base type crates (ww_numeric, ww_si, ...) are used by other ww_stdlib crates as well, so their breaking changes cascade the same way shrink_wrap ones do, just over a smaller set of crates - check reverse dependencies in the root Cargo.toml before breaking one. ww_version and ww_global are special: FullVersion, CompactVersion and ApiHashPair are exchanged during link setup, before any version could be checked, so they are final_structure and must not change on the wire at all.

ww_client_server is the API model: it defines the request/event encoding that every generated server and client speaks. Its version is sent to the host in DeviceInfo::api_model_version, and a wire break there is a wire break for every user API, so it is treated with almost the same care as shrink_wrap - see API model.

items.title: Layer 3: framework
items.text:
The framework crates share one version and are free to break their Rust API: bump the minor version once per release cycle and describe what users must change in the changelog. A user API crate built against wire_weaver 0.5 keeps working with a host or firmware built against wire_weaver 0.6, as long as both still use the same shrink_wrap major version and the same wire protocol.

The exception is code that defines what goes on the wire:

  • ww_framer (frame layout, heads, checksums) and ww_link (message kinds, DeviceInfo, LinkSetup) - changing these breaks every device from every host. The link version is sent in DeviceInfo::dev_link_version but it is not checked yet, so a break there is not even detected cleanly. Only add new message kinds that old peers ignore; never change existing ones.
  • Server and client codegen in wire_weaver_core - how resources are indexed, how arguments and return values are wrapped. Changing it changes the wire for every user API without any user version changing, so it must stay byte-identical for the same API definition.

These are wire changes even though they live in "free to break" crates, so they follow the layer 1 rules: avoid, batch, and mark as Wire format: in the changelog.

items.title: Layer 4: user API
items.text:
Name and version of the user API crate are sent during link setup, and both device and host refuse to connect if they are not compatible (ww_version::Version::is_protocol_compatible):

  • Before 1.0: major and minor must match, so 0.2.0 and 0.2.7 connect, 0.2.0 and 0.3.0 don't.
  • After 1.0: major must match.

So the compatible position (patch before 1.0, minor after) is for wire-compatible additions: new methods, properties, streams, new fields with defaults, etc. Mark them with #[since = "0.2.3"], so that a newer host can report a clean error when calling a resource that an older device doesn't have (see examples/blinky_api_evolved). Everything else bumps the breaking position.

items.title: Doc comments
items.text:
Doc comments on traits, resources and types are not part of the wire format, but they are shipped in introspection data and in crate snapshots, so a GUI or CLI can show them. A released version's snapshot never changes, so a doc-only change is still a new version: bump the compatible position (patch before 1.0, minor after), same as for a wire-compatible addition. Devices with the old version keep connecting, and tools can tell that improved docs are available. ww api save refuses to overwrite a snapshot with changed docs, and the evolution checker requires the compatible bump.

The API crate's dependencies are part of this contract: upgrading a ww_stdlib crate or shrink_wrap to a wire-incompatible version, or the API model, is a breaking change of the user API too.

items.title: Checklist before breaking something
items.text:
1. Is it a wire change or only a Rust change? If unsure, serialize a few values before and after and compare the bytes (to_ww_bytes()), and run the evolution checker.
  2. Which layer is it in? Wire changes in shrink_wrap, ww_framer, ww_link, ww_client_server or server/client codegen affect every device - avoid them, and if unavoidable, batch them and mark them Wire format: in the changelog.
  3. For shrink_wrap (and base ww_stdlib types), list the reverse dependencies that need to be re-released.
  4. Bump the right position: patch for compatible additions in shrink_wrap and API crates before 1.0, minor for everything else before 1.0.
  5. Write the changelog entry, saying what users must change and whether deployed devices are affected.

items.title: Data types
items.text: WireWeaver considers two root types for evolution and evolution rule checks - struct and enum (plain and with data variants). Size of a type is marked as one of: Unsized, FinalStructure, SelfDescribing or Sized.

items.title: Unsized types
items.text:
By default, user defined struct or enum is Unsized. Both can contain variable-size types - vectors, strings or other structs and enums. Unsized types support all the evolution options. It is recommended to stick with unsized types, unless extreme space-saving is required.

A TailSize<N> field (see wire format) is part of the layout like a Sized field: adding, removing or moving it, or changing N, breaks compatibility; fields after it evolve as usual, and old readers skip what newer writers append.

A Delta<T>, DeltaOfDelta<T> or XorFloat<T> field (see wire format) is like a Vec<T> field: it can be appended with #[default = Default::default()] (old data reads as an empty sequence), but swapping it for a Vec<T> or another of the three, or changing T, changes the bits and breaks compatibility.

When serializing, size of such objects is calculated and written to the resulting byte array. Which is the only overhead, giving all the nice backwards and forwards compatibility benefits.

  • New fields with #[default = ..] can be added to the end of structs and enum struct variants. Old data reads as the default (see derive), T can be anything:
    • Option<T> - #[default = None],
    • Vec<T>, String - #[default = Vec::new()], #[default = String::new()],
    • a bit-sized field (bool, nibble, Option / Result flag) can land in padding bits of the old data's last byte, which read as 0: give it its zero value as the default.
  • New enum variants can be added at the end. Readers of older versions fail on them unless the enum has a #[future_version] variant; with one, they get its discriminant. Every Unsized enum has one unless it says no_future_version (SW-47). In an Unsized enum new variants may carry data, in a sized or self_describing one only new unit variants can be read past by older readers. Adding or removing no_future_version changes the Rust type, not the wire: a Rust API break only.
  • New fixed size fields can be added in between old ones, into previously unused padding bits, without moving any other field (see the checker for exact conditions).
  • TODO: clarify: T -> struct containing T
  • Struct fields and enum variants can be renamed (but their position must NOT change).

items.title: Maximum lengths: MaxLen<T, N>
items.text:
A MaxLen<T, N> has the same bytes as T, so a bound never changes the wire, only which values the reader accepts (a longer one is an error, never truncated). Whether a change is compatible depends on what the old version writes:

  • Raising a bound or removing it (MaxLen<T, 64> -> MaxLen<T, 256> or T): compatible. Everything the old version writes is still read. The checker lists it as max length raised, because values the new version writes beyond the old bound are rejected by the old version (with an error): a new client sending a long piece to an old device gets an error reply, the same as any argument the device refuses.
  • Lowering a bound or adding one (T -> MaxLen<T, 64>, MaxLen<T, 256> -> MaxLen<T, 64>): breaking. Values the old version is allowed to write no longer fit, and nothing on the wire tells the old version so.
  • Changing T inside the bound follows the usual rules for T.

At connect time the client does not refuse a device whose bounds differ from its own: a longer value is rejected when it is sent, by whichever side has the smaller bound.

items.title: Compressed sequences: Delta, DeltaOfDelta, XorFloat
items.text: Each has bytes of its own, so Vec<T> -> Delta<T>, Delta<T> -> DeltaOfDelta<T> or Delta<u32> -> Delta<u64> is breaking (ww api check reports it), unlike the borrowed / owned form (Delta<'i, T> / DeltaOwned<T>), which is the same type.

items.title: Sparse structs
items.text:
A sparse struct (DER-13) has a slot per field, all of them Option<T>:

  • New fields can be appended after the last slot, without #[default]: older data reads them as None, older readers ignore them.
  • A field can't be inserted before the last slot, also not into a gap left by #[slot = N]: a reader that doesn't know the slot can't step over a present value in it and fails with Error::OptionAnyVecUnknownSlot. Removing a field breaks too: data from an older writer can still have it present.
  • A field's slot and its T can't change (T evolves by its own rules); fields can be renamed.
  • Turning an ordinary struct into a sparse one or back changes every byte: breaking.

items.title: FinalStructure, SelfDescribing and Sized types
items.text:
• Sized can become SelfDescribing and back (sized <-> self_describing): neither gets a size slot from its parent, the bytes are the same, and the checker reports it as compatible. A sized enum must have variants of one size (see derive).
  • New fixed size fields can be added in between old ones, into previously unused padding bits, without moving any other field (see the checker for exact conditions).
  • Struct fields and enum variants can be renamed (but their position must NOT change).

items.title: API
items.text:
Data types used in API are a part of SemVer guarantee and are subject to the rules above. Meaning that it's not allowed to break compatibility on any of the data types used directly or indirectly without also bumping the breaking position of the API version as well (minor before 1.0, major after, see layer 4).

  • Adding argument
  • T to struct of T in return position
  • T to Vec<T> in return position?

Streams (API-30, API-31, stream reliability): the delivery kind of a stream is part of the API. Turning a plain stream! into a #[counted] or #[reliable] one (or back, or one into the other), or giving a stream arguments or a result (#[stream(T)] fn name(args) -> Result<A, E>), changes its events and how it is opened, so it is a break of the API crate: bump its breaking version position, as for a plain sink becoming a #[credit] one. A plain #[stream(T)] fn name() without arguments and result is the same as stream!(name: T), the same bytes in introspection.

items.title: API model
items.text:
API model (like ww_client_server) is part of the compatibility equation, it is not allowed to update the model version without breaking compatibility.

E.g., if user_device_api v0.1.0 depends on ww_client_server v0.4.0 and a new major version of ww_client_server comes out (v0.5.0), then user_device_api must be bumped to v0.2.0 to use the newer API model. This should only happen to add new features though, and if previous version is doing all that it is supposed to, there might not be a need to upgrade.

items.title: Examples and Templates
items.text: To start a new project, use the wire_weaver_template repository. The examples in this repository follow the same shape: an <name>_api crate with the trait and types (no_std), and a <name> crate with the host client using it (see folder structure).

items.title: Host side (examples/)
items.text: Example What it shows minimal_shrink_wrap Using the shrink_wrap wire format directly compare_wire_formats Wire size of shrink_wrap compared with other formats blinky_api, blinky Smallest API with two methods, and its client blinky_api_evolved, blinky_evolved The same API evolved with a new method, used with old firmware blinky_py Python wheel wrapping the blinky client all_gpio_api, all_gpio Arrays of traits from the standard library uart_api, uart USB/Ethernet/CAN to UART bridge

items.title: Firmware (examples_mcu/)
items.text:
Firmware implementing the APIs above for real boards, using embassy. Each board is a separate project, excluded from the repository's Cargo workspace, and built from its own directory.

Board MCU nucleo_g0b1re STM32G0B1RE, Nucleo board nucleo_h743zi2 STM32H743ZI, Nucleo board usb_stm32h725ig STM32H725IG with a USB ULPI PHY (480 Mbit/s) rp2 Raspberry Pi RP2350 mcu_qemu Cortex-M3 emulated in QEMU (all_gpio_api)

A firmware short of flash or RAM for code: linker relaxation on RISC-V saves about 10 %, and on very small targets a byte-wise memcpy about 320 bytes, with downsides, see code size on small CPUs.

A connected device can be inspected with the command line tool: ww list, then ww introspect.

items.title: Code size on small CPUs
items.text:
How much code shrink_wrap costs on a CPU with a few kilobytes of memory, where the bytes go, what was changed because of it and what is left. Measured in October 2026 for a softcore firmware with 8 KB of RAM for code, data and stack (the QERV RISC-V of fpga_tools' busgen). Its request/reply codec was hand-written because the derived one did not fit; since fpga_tools 0.9.0 (BUS-12) the firmware runs on head_tail views and variant writers (SW-52, SW-53, SW-54), and no hand-written codec is left.

Summary:

  • The derived codec of that firmware went from 11.3 KB to 9.0 KB on RV32IC (15.1 → 12.5 KB on RV32I, 9.3 → 7.3 KB on Cortex-M0) with five changes that keep the wire format as it is. With sized / final_structure types and linker relaxation it is 7.3 KB. The same codec written by hand is 5.2 to 5.8 KB.
  • Half of what was saved came from one thing: plain fields are no longer checked for an error one by one.
  • An encoder whose types have no lists, strings or nested evolvable types does not link the code for lengths at all: a struct of eight fields is 964 bytes on RV32IC instead of 1476 (1934 before any of this).
  • No cargo feature was needed, and none is proposed: what a firmware does not call is not linked, and a feature that changes the wire format would be a trap (see Feature flags).
  • A build setting found on the way is worth more than any of the code changes on RISC-V: linker relaxation was off, -C target-feature=+relax saves 9 to 11 % for any firmware, hand-written ones too.

items.title: The bench
items.text:
just size-bench (the size_bench crate in shrink_wrap/size_bench) builds one bare firmware image per test case from shrink_wrap/size_bench/fw and prints .text + .rodata in bytes. just size-bench -c busgen -t rv32ic -s 30 prints the 30 largest symbols of an image instead.
