The build profile is the one of the softcore firmware: nightly, build-std = ["core"], panic = "immediate-abort", opt-level = "z", fat LTO, one codegen unit, -Zlocation-detail=none -Zfmt-debug=none. Targets:

name target flags rv32i riscv32i-unknown-none-elf rv32ic riscv32i-unknown-none-elf -C target-feature=+c (what the softcore runs) rv32ic-relax riscv32i-unknown-none-elf -C target-feature=+c,+relax thumbv6m thumbv6m-none-eabi Cortex-M0, for comparison thumbv7em thumbv7em-none-eabihf Cortex-M4F / M7 (Thumb-2), for comparison with larger MCUs

Every case is a run(rx, tx) that decodes from one buffer and encodes into another. Inputs and outputs go through core::hint::black_box, so nothing is computed at compile time and every decoded field counts as used. The images are measured, not run.

case what it holds empty no shrink_wrap code: 38 bytes on RV32IC, the floor of every other case rw_de, rw_ser BufReader / BufWriter alone: a u8, a bool, a u16, a u32 (rw_ser ends with finish_no_lens() since step 4) struct_de, struct_ser a struct of eight integers and flags (Wave) enum_de, enum_ser an enum of five small variants vec_de, vec_ser a struct with a u16 and a RefVec<u16>, the list walked after decoding bits_de, bits_ser a bit-packed struct: U3, bool, U4, U12, I10, U20, U5, u8 (Sample, since SW-38) option_de, option_ser a struct of ten fields, two of them Option busgen_de the softcore firmware's receive side: Request (18 variants, lists of structs and of u16, nested structs, an Option<Wave>) decoded and acted on busgen_ser its transmit side: one of the nine Reply variants encoded busgen both: a request decoded, acted on, its reply encoded busgen_hand the same as busgen with a hand-written codec: bytes, little endian, a list is a count and its items, reading past the end gives zeros reply a method's reply as ww_codegen! server code encodes it: a Wave return value alone, then the ww_client_server::Event around its bytes, and the error event when that fails

The cases with derived types are built twice: evolvable (the default, every type Unsized) and final (sized where the fields allow it, else final_structure). The two differ only where a type is nested in another, so the small cases give the same number for both.

busgen_hand is the yardstick, not empty: the handler that acts on a request, the enum values it builds and the bench's own black_box calls are in both busgen and busgen_hand. What the two differ by is the codec.

Read as: on RV32IC the derived codec is now 1.55 times the hand-written one with evolvable types and 1.4 times with final ones (it was 1.95 and 1.8 times), and Cortex-M0 code is about 20 % smaller than RV32IC for the same source.

The encoders, before and after steps 4 and 5 alone (the length FIFO, SW-36; the decoders did not change):

case types rv32i rv32ic rv32ic-relax thumbv6m rw_ser 1456 → 688 996 → 462 920 → 428 794 → 384 struct_ser 2092 → 1348 1476 → 964 1336 → 872 1240 → 830 enum_ser 2160 → 1420 1536 → 1012 1396 → 920 1298 → 864 option_ser 2220 → 1452 1572 → 1048 1412 → 936 1286 → 888 vec_ser 1958 → 1634 1378 → 1142 1286 → 1074 1180 → 1030 busgen_ser evolvable 5496 → 5284 3820 → 3650 3424 → 3256 3344 → 3224 busgen_ser final 4708 → 4464 3356 → 3180 2972 → 2820 2944 → 2796 busgen evolvable 12744 → 12532 9170 → 9000 8260 → 8114 7400 → 7320 busgen final 11364 → 11148 8232 → 8062 7446 → 7296 6660 → 6512

rw_ser, struct_ser, enum_ser and option_ser have no lengths and lose the FIFO code (step 4). vec_ser and the busgen cases have lists and keep it, smaller (step 5).

items.title: Where the bytes went
items.text:
The largest symbols of busgen (evolvable) on RV32IC before the changes, 11100 bytes of .text:

bytes symbol what 6958 _start everything inlined into the caller: Request decode, the handler, Reply encode 506 BufWriter::encode_len_fifo the lengths at the end of the buffer, u16 slots turned into nibbles 338 compiler_builtins::mem::memcpy moves of the request and reply values, and every write_u16 / write_u32 326 BufReader::read::<Wave> a nested evolvable struct of 8 fields 270 BufReader::read::<UartFormat> 6 fields 238 BufWriter::write::<RxFrame> 2 fields, with the size slot of an Unsized type 156 BufReader::read_rev_len 138 + 132 BufReader::read::<RefVec<Wave>>, <RefVec<u16>> one pass over the list to find its end 138 BufWriter::write_nib 132 + 32 + 8 u32_div_rem, u32_normalization_shift, __udivsi3 one division by 3, see below 124 + 76 RefVecIter<Wave>::next, RefVecIter<u16>::next 122 BufWriter::write_rev_len 118, 118, 114 BufReader::split, read_bool, read_raw_slice 108, 98 BufWriter::write_bool, write_raw_slice 92, 88, 78 BufReader::read_u32, read_u8, read_u16 three copies of the same bounds checks 82, 64 BufWriter::align_nibble, align_byte

By kind:

part bytes notes BufReader primitives 810 BufWriter primitives 1260 850 of them only for the length FIFO compiler builtins 560 memcpy 346, division 180, multiplication 32 generic code per type, not inlined 1300 read::<T>, write::<T>, RefVec<T>, RefVecIter<T> _start 6960 the hand-written codec has 4400 here

So 2.6 KB did not depend on the types at all, where the hand-written codec has 1.15 KB outside _start (memcpy included). The code that does depend on the types, the generic instances and _start, was 8.3 KB against 4.4 KB by hand.

Per field. A derived des_shrink_wrap is a run of let x = rd.read_u32()?;. On RV32IC that was 22 to 26 bytes per field: Result<u32, Error> came back through memory, because Error had variants with a payload, so every call passed a pointer to a stack slot, loaded the tag, compared it, loaded the value, and had an error exit of its own (store the error, jump). The hand-written reader returns the value in a register and has no error exits: 6 to 10 bytes per field. Request has about 80 fields and Reply about 40.

The length FIFO. Lengths of lists, strings and nested Unsized values are collected as u16 slots at the end of the buffer and turned into nibbles by finish(). encode_len_fifo, write_nib, align_nibble, write_rev_len and the nibble counting are 850 bytes on the encode side, read_rev_len 156 on the decode side. finish() was always called, so an encoder paid for this even when its types had no lengths: rw_ser (four integer writes) was 1806 bytes. Steps 4 and 5 below are about this.

A division. UNib32::len_nibbles was (32 - leading_zeros).div_ceil(3). RV32I has neither a divider nor a count-leading-zeros instruction, so this one line linked 172 bytes of division and a software clz: 430 bytes in every image that encodes (rw_ser 1806 → 1378 with a three line loop instead).

Evolvable nesting. Every use of an Unsized type inside another is a size slot, a split() and an encode of the slots the value used. busgen has ten such uses (three types, used in lists, in an Option and directly): final is 0.9 to 1.0 KB smaller, and the messages are shorter too. This is the only saving that changes the wire format, and it is chosen per type, as before.

Lists. RefVec<T> is decoded twice: once when its parent is decoded, to find where the list ends, and again when it is walked. Each T costs a read::<RefVec<T>> (130 to 140 bytes) and a RefVecIter<T>::next (75 to 125 bytes). Encoding a RefVec<T> also contains the decoder of T, for its Buf variant (a list taken from another buffer); the optimizer removes it only when it can prove the list is a slice.

Decode only, encode only. Nothing to switch off: the linker keeps what is called. busgen_de is 6.0 KB, busgen_ser 3.7 KB, and neither contains the other's primitives.

Bounds checks and panics. With panic = "immediate-abort" no panic code or message is left, a failed check is one unimp. The checks themselves stay: BufReader and BufWriter compare against their own limits and then index a slice, which checks again. It is 4 to 8 bytes per access and was three times in three functions for read_u8 / read_u16 / read_u32.

Cortex-M0. The same picture with smaller numbers: _start 4864 of 7292 bytes after the changes, memcpy 316, encode_len_fifo 174. Thumb has no linker relaxation to forget, and a call is 4 bytes.

items.title: What was changed
items.text:
All five keep the wire format: every byte-level test of the workspace passes unchanged.

step busgen evolvable busgen final rw_ser struct_de before 11308 10320 1806 638 1. no division in UNib32::len_nibbles 10872 9870 1378 638 2. Error without payloads, shared integer read / write 10184 9076 984 532 3. latched errors for plain fields 9170 8232 996 554 4. no FIFO code for types without lengths 9170 8232 466 554 5. smaller length FIFO 9000 8062 462 554

(RV32IC, bytes. The other targets move the same way, see Results.)

  1. UNib32::len_nibbles is a shift loop. No division routine, no software clz.
  2. Error has no payloads and is #[repr(u32)], and read_u8 / read_u16 / read_u32 / read_i16 / read_i32 / read_f32 are one function taking a length (write_* likewise, read_bool through one bit reader). Result<u32, Error> is now two registers, Result<(), Error> one with Ok as zero, and the bounds checks exist once. Writing an integer no longer calls memcpy. Breaking: Error::OutOfBoundsWriteUN, OutOfBoundsReadUN and OutOfBoundsSplit lost their UNib32 payload (the bit count or length asked for). An Error of one byte was tried first and gained nothing: Result<u32, Error> stays in memory then.
  3. Latched errors. BufReader and BufWriter have read_*_latch / write_*_latch methods for bool and the integers up to 32 bits: no Result, an error is kept in the reader or writer and the read gives 0. rd.latched() / wr.latched() return the first error and clear it; BufWriter::finish() returns it too. #[derive_shrink_wrap] uses them for plain fields, Option / Result flags and u8 / u16 / u32 discriminants, and checks once per struct or enum (and before a TailSize slot). A field is then a call and a move: 12 to 14 bytes on RV32IC, 6 to 8 with relaxation. Fields with #[default = ..], lists, strings and nested types are read as before, so evolution is untouched. The price: BufReader is 24 bytes instead of 20 (so is every RefVec), and the smallest cases grow by 10 to 30 bytes.

The rule for hand-written code that uses the _latch methods: don't use a value before latched() returned Ok, in particular not as a loop bound. 4. No FIFO code for types without lengths (SW-36). SerializeShrinkWrap has an associated constant PUSHES_LEN: whether ser_shrink_wrap can leave a length for finish() to encode. to_ww_bytes ends with wr.finish_for::<Self>(), which is finish() when it is true and finish_no_lens() (latched error, align to a byte, done) when it is false. The choice is made at compile time, so encode_len_fifo, write_nib and the rest are not linked: 510 to 530 bytes less on RV32IC for rw_ser, struct_ser, enum_ser and option_ser, about 750 on RV32I, 400 to 440 on Cortex-M0.

The default is true for everything that is not Sized, so a hand-written impl stays correct without knowing about it. #[derive_shrink_wrap] computes it from the fields: false only when no field is a string, a list, a RefBox, a nested Unsized type (its size slot is a length) or a user type that pushes one itself (asked through its own constant, also inside Option, Result, arrays and tuples). Evolvable (Unsized) root types made of plain fields qualify, they need no sized. A type that says false and pushes a length anyway panics in a debug build and gets Error::LenFifoNotEmpty in a release one, never a message without its lengths.

Code that calls ser_shrink_wrap and finish() itself gets the same with wr.finish_for::<T>(), where T is the type of everything written into that writer. 5. A smaller length FIFO (SW-36), for the types that do have lengths. write_nib aligns and writes in one step (140 → 130 bytes on RV32IC) and encode_len_fifo no longer needs align_nibble (82 bytes, not linked any more); the nibbles are counted in one pass over a slice, as a parity, and written by a loop that does not ask for the length of each number first (276 → 214 bytes; 216 → 174 on Cortex-M0). vec_ser 1378 → 1142, busgen 9170 → 9000.

Fixed on the way: aligning to a nibble from the last three bits of a byte (align_nibble(), write_nib(), a length after 5 to 7 bits) left those bits as they were in the buffer instead of zero. A reader skips them, so nothing on the other end changes, but the bytes depended on what the buffer held before.

items.title: Lists of plain numbers: time for bytes
items.text:
Done after the five steps (SW-37), and the one change here that makes the code larger. Decoding a RefVec<T> reads every element once just to find where the list ends. For u8..u128, i8..i128, f32 and f64 that is now one bounds check: reading such a value is "align to a byte, take N bytes" and nothing else, so count reads succeed exactly when one read of count * N bytes does. A list that is too short, or a count whose size overflows, still goes through the pass, so the error and the reader state are the ones it always gave. The wire format does not change.

RefVec<u8> of 16 of 256 of 4096 decode pass 43 ns 631 ns 10254 ns one bounds check 5 ns 5 ns 6 ns

(from_ww_bytes on an x86-64 host, for the proportion. On a small CPU the pass is a call of read_le32, about 30 instructions, per element; on a bit-serial softcore each of them takes 32 clock cycles or more.)

It was expected to save code as well, and does not. Since step 2 the pass over a list of integers is a loop of about 22 bytes around the shared read_le32, nothing like the 130 byte read::<RefVec<u16>> of the first profile. The check comes on top of it (the pass stays for the error case), and read_raw_slice is no longer inlined into its only caller:

case types rv32i rv32ic rv32ic-relax thumbv6m vec_de 908 → 1004 592 → 652 548 → 596 536 → 582 busgen_de evolvable 8468 → 8604 6040 → 6126 5442 → 5504 5044 → 5112 busgen_de final 7588 → 7708 5452 → 5524 4920 → 4982 4496 → 4556 busgen evolvable 12532 → 12664 9000 → 9086 8114 → 8180 7320 → 7384 busgen final 11148 → 11268 8062 → 8134 7296 → 7356 6512 → 6576

Every other case is unchanged, to the byte: the choice is a constant per element type (DeserializeShrinkWrap::PLAIN_BYTES, hidden, None by default), so a list of anything else compiles to the pass alone. Two other shapes were measured and were larger: one shared function that computes the end and the reader state after a failure (vec_de 714, busgen 9082 on RV32IC), and the same on top of read_raw_slice (670, 9114).

Only these twelve types, on purpose. ElementSize::Sized { size_bits } is not used to skip other elements:

  • It is the size of the value without alignment padding, so it is not the stride of an element: struct { a: bool, b: u8 } is 9 bits and takes 2 bytes. bool, u1..uN and Nibble are bit-packed, their elements share bytes with each other and the last one with the lengths read from the back.
  • The pass is also where an element is validated: an enum's discriminant, a string's UTF-8, a nested length. Without it those errors would move from decode time to the iteration, where code written against today's behaviour does not expect them.

shrink_wrap/tests/ref_vec_skip.rs holds the two against each other, result and whole reader state: every type, empty to long lists, every truncation, counts up to u32::MAX, lists that start in the middle of a byte or end where the lengths begin, inside a struct with every byte damaged in turn, and 40 000 random buffers read from random reader states. just fuzz-shrink-wrap-ref-vec does the same under libFuzzer.

items.title: Latched bit fields
items.text:
Done after SW-37 (SW-38). U1..U64 and I2..I64 fields are read like the integers of step 3: no error check each, one rd.latched()? per type. The derive cannot tell U4 from a nested struct by its name, so the type says so itself: their DeserializeShrinkWrap::des_shrink_wrap_latch (hidden, read by default) calls BufReader::read_un32_latch / read_un64_latch, which are read_un32 / read_un64 with the error kept, and the derive reads every field of a user type through it. The wire format does not change.

case types rv32i rv32ic rv32ic-relax thumbv6m bits_de 1364 → 1276 886 → 846 786 → 746 700 → 666

Every other case is unchanged, to the byte: none of them has such a field.

As first landed, this was limited to types whose every field is latched: since step 3 a type that mixed latched fields with lists or nested types could report a later error instead of the first one, and the U/I fields were not to join that. The mixed types were fixed right after (SW-41, Fixed on the way), and the limit went with it.

Not latched: Nibble, u64 / i64 / f64, u128 / i128, the varints. Tried, and one field of a kind costs more than it saves: the read is a function of its own then, where with ? it was inlined into its only caller. A struct of five U/I fields, a bool, a Nibble, a UNib32 and a u64 (every field latched, before the rule above):

latched rv32i rv32ic thumbv6m nothing (before) 1628 1086 900 U/I 1580 1060 872 U/I, Nibble, u64, UNib32 1628 1090 908 the same with three more Nibble, UNib32 and u64: nothing 2232 1452 1204 U/I 2172 1424 1180 U/I, Nibble, u64, UNib32 2036 1358 1100

From about two fields of a kind it would pay.

Discriminants other than u8 / u16 / u32 (Nibble, u1..u31, UNib32) and TailSize slots are read with ? as before: the code decides with them before latched() is checked. (u8 / u16 / u32 discriminants and Option / Result flags have been latched since step 3: a failed one reads as 0 / false, i.e. variant 0 or None / Err, and since SW-41 the kept error is what the type returns in every case.)

shrink_wrap/tests/latched_reads.rs holds each of the 126 types against its read with a Result (value, error, whole reader state, from every bit offset and from 20 000 random reader states, an earlier kept error stays first) and derived structs and enums against the same fields read one by one with ?; six hand-made mutants (a wrong value after an error, an overwritten, lost or wrong error, a wrong value, no sign extension) each fail it. just fuzz-shrink-wrap-latched does the same under libFuzzer.

items.title: Fixed on the way
items.text:
Bit reads and the lengths in the last byte (SW-40). The last byte of a message can hold forward data in its high nibble and the first length nibble in its low one. read_un32 / read_un64 read to the end of that byte (with 4 bits left, read_un8(6) returned 2 bits of the length), and a length was read from a nibble the forward side had read past. Both are errors now, for malformed input only. In bytes: the bit loop is shorter, the reverse read has one check more:

case types rv32i rv32ic rv32ic-relax thumbv6m vec_de 1004 → 1040 652 → 664 596 → 608 582 → 622 bits_de 1276 → 1168 846 → 774 746 → 686 666 → 622 busgen_de evolvable 8604 → 8696 6126 → 6182 5504 → 5564 5112 → 5168 busgen_ser evolvable 5284 → 5296 3650 → 3676 3256 → 3282 3224 → 3228 busgen evolvable 12664 → 12756 9086 → 9142 8180 → 8244 7384 → 7440 busgen final 11268 → 11360 8134 → 8190 7356 → 7416 6576 → 6632

(busgen_ser grows because encoding a RefVec<RxFrame> contains its decoder, see Lists.)

The first error in types that mix latched and other fields (SW-41). Since step 3, a type with latched plain fields and fields read with ? (a list, a string, a nested evolvable type, an Option of one) could return a later error instead of the first: in a u32 followed by a RefVec<u8>, decoded from 0 to 5 bytes, 11 of 24 cases gave OutOfBoundsRev or OutOfBoundsReadU8 where reading field by field gives OutOfBoundsReadRawSlice. It was an error in every case, but not the one it was before step 3. Now an error kept in the reader stops it: every read with a Result returns that error, a _latch read gives 0, and no read moves; an enum without a variant 0 checks latched() before it reports an unknown discriminant (a discriminant read after an error is 0). So every error exit of a derived decoder reports the first error, and nothing read after it decides anything.

Four forms were measured, RV32IC, bytes over the code before the fix:

form struct_de vec_de busgen evolvable busgen final map the error that leaves a derived decoder to the kept one (latch.take().unwrap_or(e), per type) +26 +124 the check at the start of every read +16 +48 +68 +116 the same, the reads with a Result only, the _latch ones go on 0 +34 +30 +90 the check at the start of every read, the byte reads sharing one bounds check (chosen) +48 +28 +20 +20

The last one is the cheapest for a real decoder; the small cases pay for a function call the first one inlines. All targets, with the chosen form:

case types rv32i rv32ic rv32ic-relax thumbv6m rw_de 648 → 732 444 → 492 404 → 446 364 → 402 struct_de 840 → 924 554 → 602 478 → 520 440 → 478 enum_de 1004 → 1088 678 → 726 586 → 628 512 → 550 vec_de 1040 → 1060 664 → 692 608 → 628 622 → 632 bits_de 1168 → 1256 774 → 822 686 → 728 622 → 652 option_de 980 → 1064 658 → 706 554 → 596 520 → 558 busgen_de evolvable 8696 → 8736 6182 → 6202 5564 → 5596 5168 → 5196 busgen_ser evolvable 5296 → 5348 3676 → 3718 3282 → 3324 3228 → 3296 busgen evolvable 12756 → 12800 9142 → 9162 8244 → 8276 7440 → 7468 busgen final 11360 → 11388 8190 → 8210 7416 → 7438 6632 → 6652

shrink_wrap/tests/latched_errors.rs holds a request enum with each of these shapes against the same fields read one by one with ?: the result (error included) and the reader of every truncation, every byte damaged in turn and 20 000 random buffers; an enum without a variant 0 after a failed field. Removing any one of the checks makes a test fail.

items.title: Fixed-layout fast path
items.text:
A type whose encoding is a fixed byte layout (SW-44, derive) does not need BufReader or BufWriter at all: each field is a load or store at a constant offset. The cases header_de / header_ser read and write Header (a [u8; 4], two u8, a u16, four u32 and a u64) through the reader and writer, fixed_de / fixed_ser the same type with from_fixed / to_fixed. bits_fixed_* is the bit-packed Sample of bits_* (SW-45: shifts and masks at constant bit offsets instead of the bit loop of the reader and writer):

case rv32i rv32ic rv32ic-relax thumbv6m thumbv7em header_de 884 566 484 484 410 fixed_de 580 406 354 228 120 header_ser 1408 1022 918 888 856 fixed_ser 788 612 548 462 452 bits_de 1256 822 728 652 650 bits_fixed_de 464 308 292 276 268 bits_ser 1740 1204 1098 1034 716 bits_fixed_ser 616 458 430 278 310

A third to a half less, and the gap grows with the number of types: the fast path has no shared runtime, each type is its own straight-line code. The bytes left in fixed_ser are mostly memcpy (see Build settings).

Since SW-53 every multi-byte number goes through fixed_layout::Le at the bytes of its field: on RISC-V (no unaligned loads, so a u32 is four byte loads and three shifts and ors, some 28 bytes) ld and st are one function per type and a field is a call with a pointer, elsewhere they are inlined. That costs a type read or written once: fixed_de / fixed_ser above grew from 378 / 498 bytes on RV32IC (the two functions per type are more than the eight fields save). It pays as soon as fields are read and written in many places, as in a firmware: busgen_ht 6004 → 5658 on RV32IC, busgen's own firmware 8.1 KB → 7.7 KB before its views. On a Cortex-M0, which has no unaligned loads either, the inlined byte loads of 2-byte instructions take less than the calls (busgen_view 3894 inlined, 4196 out of line), so it stays inline there. The bit fields' bytes are now cleared once per head or struct instead of per field (bits_fixed_ser 698 → 458 on RV32IC, 560 → 278 on Cortex-M0). On a real format, chunky_mcu_updater's plan reader (header, signed descriptor, steps) takes 892 bytes on Cortex-M0 with the fast path, 840 with its hand-written parser and 1854 through BufReader (its just size-bench). Since chunky 0.9.0 its steps are a head_tail enum read through Step::view (a WRITE's data is a List<u8>, the same wire bytes), and the reader is 734 bytes on Cortex-M0 and 912 on RV32IMC: below format 1's hand-written 840 / 1252 and below the fast path's 892 / 1086 (chunky_mcu_updater FEATURES.md, PROTO-3).

items.title: Head and tail
items.text:
busgen_ht is busgen with head_tail types (SW-46, derive): the plain structs fixed_layout, Utx, I2c, I2cSlave, Request and Reply head_tail, lists as head_tail::List, the same handler. Every fixed field is a load at a constant offset, the lists, the string and the Option<Wave> are taken from the tail by lengths already read from the head:

case types rv32i rv32ic rv32ic-relax thumbv6m thumbv7em busgen final 11388 8210 7438 6652 6816 busgen_hand 7824 5762 5152 4408 4318 busgen_ht 7752 5658 5234 4590 3992 busgen_view 6572 4988 4546 3894 3496

busgen_view is the same types and handler through views and the variant writers (SW-52): Request::view(rx) checks the lengths and walks the tail, the handler reads each field at its offset when it uses it, and each reply is written by Reply::write_<variant>(tx, fields..), without making a Request or a Reply first. It is the smallest of all: 13 % below the hand-written codec on RV32IC, 12 % on Cortex-M0, 19 % on Thumb-2. In busgen's real firmware (fpga_tools BUS-12), where the handler also drives the engines, the views take 5608 bytes of .text for the UART image and 5090 for the I2C one on RV32IC, against 4552 / 4716 hand-written: the hand-written firmware reads a field as one small call and checks no length, the views check every length before the first field is used.

busgen_ht (values: from_head_tail, to_head_tail) is 2 % below the hand-written codec on RV32IC and 4 % above on Cortex-M0, 31 % below the derived one; on Thumb-2 it is smaller. Unlike the hand-written one it checks every length (a short message is an error, not zeros) and the UTF-8 of the string. Linker relaxation helps it less than the others: its calls are fewer, the code is mostly inline loads. Two things were worth taking out of the runtime on the way: a checked multiplication for the length of a list (on a Cortex-M0 its overflow check links a 200-byte division routine) and chunks_exact_mut (divides by the chunk length); the list iterator walks a cursor instead of computing i * len. On the wire it is a little smaller than busgen's own format too, since the bools of the head are bits.

items.title: Replies of generated servers
items.text:
Measured after SW-41, not changed. The code ww_codegen! generates for a server ends every message with finish(): the request's reply, a stream's data, a deferred return, an error. All but one of them write a ww_client_server::Event, and Event pushes lengths whatever it holds (PUSHES_LEN is true: its ErrorKind is evolvable and has a size slot, StreamData has a RefVec path), so for them finish_for is finish. The one that is not is the return value of a method, serialized alone into a scratch buffer before it goes into the event as TailBytes. reply is that code, and with --fw-features finish_for the same with finish_for::<Wave>() for the return value:

return value ends with rv32i rv32ic rv32ic-relax thumbv6m finish() (as generated) 5120 3632 3236 3144 finish_for::<Wave>() 5144 (+24) 3646 (+14) 3250 (+14) 3160 (+16)

The same for both flavors (a root Wave pushes no length either way). Event::ser_shrink_wrap is one function for every variant of the event, so encode_len_fifo, write_rev_len and write_nib are linked in any firmware with a generated server, even one whose methods all return plain values; finish_for at the return value only adds finish_no_lens next to finish. The generated code keeps finish(). For the length FIFO to drop out of a server, Event itself would have to lose its lengths: a final_structure/sized event, which is a wire change of ww_client_server.

items.title: Larger MCUs: Cortex-M4F / M7
items.text:
The thumbv7em column is there to see whether Thumb-2 changes the picture. It does not: with the same profile the images are about as large as on Cortex-M0, and the changes above saved about as much. Before them (925a29b1) and now:

case types thumbv6m before thumbv6m now thumbv7em before thumbv7em now rw_ser 1460 384 1224 412 struct_ser evolvable 1596 830 916 516 enum_ser evolvable 1606 864 1374 572 vec_ser evolvable 1472 1030 844 684 option_ser evolvable 1710 888 1414 608 busgen_de evolvable 6316 5196 6356 4836 busgen_ser evolvable 4054 3296 3902 3386 busgen evolvable 9302 7468 9058 7612 busgen final 8370 6652 8426 6816 busgen_hand 4408 4408 4318 4318

The small serializers are 30 to 40 % smaller on Thumb-2 than on Cortex-M0, the whole codec is not (7.6 against 7.5 KB): 16 % smaller than before on Thumb-2, 20 % on Cortex-M0. In a real firmware the share is what makes the difference small: examples_mcu/usb_stm32h725ig's all_gpio (embassy, USB, defmt; 66 KB of flash) went from 67412 to 66172 bytes, 1.8 %.

items.title: Build settings
items.text:
Not shrink_wrap's to fix, but worth more than each code change:

  • Linker relaxation on RISC-V. riscv32i-unknown-none-elf builds without it, so every call that is not inlined is auipc + jalr, 8 bytes. With -C target-feature=+relax the linker turns them into jal (4 bytes) or c.jal (2 bytes): busgen 9000 → 8114, busgen_hand 5762 → 5152. Add it to the rustflags of any RISC-V firmware that is short of space.

  • A byte-wise memcpy, for very small targets only (SW-39): a measurement and advice, nothing in shrink_wrap depends on it or asks for it. The memcpy of compiler_builtins is 338 bytes on RV32IC (316 on Cortex-M0), word-wise with alignment handling. It is linked as soon as a value of more than a few words is moved, which a request or reply enum is, and an encoder's value is; -Zbuild-std-features=optimize_for_size does not change it. A firmware can define its own, a byte at a time: 22 bytes on RV32IC and Cortex-M0, 36 on RV32I. Its symbol wins over the weak one of compiler_builtins. Only worth it where 300 bytes decide whether the firmware fits (the 8 KB softcore above), and only with the downsides in mind:

    • Speed: one byte per iteration instead of a word, about four times slower for long copies. Fine for moves of a few dozen bytes, not for a firmware that copies buffers.
    • It replaces memcpy for the whole firmware, every crate in it: HAL, drivers, buffer copies of the transport, not only shrink_wrap's moves.
    • The loop can be turned back into a call of memcpy: LLVM recognizes a byte copy loop and replaces it with memcpy, which here is the function itself, an endless recursion. compiler_builtins is built with #![no_builtins] against this; the code below uses a volatile store. With the nightly of October 2026 LLVM leaves the loop alone without it as well, in memcpy and in __aeabi_memcpy, but nothing promises that. Check the disassembly when changing it.
    • memmove, memset, memcmp are separate and stay those of compiler_builtins (none of them is linked in the bench images).
    • On Arm, code calls __aeabi_memcpy, whose compiler_builtins version calls its own memcpy directly, so that symbol has to be defined too (and __aeabi_memcpy4 / __aeabi_memcpy8 if the code uses them).
mod byte_memcpy {
    use core::ffi::c_void;

    #[inline(always)]
    unsafe fn copy(dest: *mut c_void, src: *const c_void, n: usize) {
        let (dest, src) = (dest.cast::<u8>(), src.cast::<u8>());
        let mut i = 0;
        while i < n {
            // volatile: LLVM must not turn the loop back into a call of `memcpy`, i.e. of itself
            unsafe { dest.add(i).write_volatile(*src.add(i)) };
            i += 1;
        }
    }

    #[unsafe(no_mangle)]
    pub unsafe extern "C" fn memcpy(dest: *mut c_void, src: *const c_void, n: usize) -> *mut c_void {
        unsafe { copy(dest, src, n) };
        dest
    }

    #[cfg(target_arch = "arm")]
    #[unsafe(no_mangle)]
    pub unsafe extern "C" fn __aeabi_memcpy(dest: *mut c_void, src: *const c_void, n: usize) {
        unsafe { copy(dest, src, n) };
    }
}

just size-bench --fw-features byte_memcpy builds the bench with it (shrink_wrap/size_bench/fw/src/main.rs, off by default, the tables above are without it); every image that copies a value is 300 to 410 bytes smaller, the others do not change:

case types rv32i rv32ic rv32ic-relax thumbv6m struct_ser 1348 → 936 964 → 640 872 → 554 830 → 526 vec_ser 1634 → 1222 1142 → 818 1074 → 756 1030 → 726 busgen_de evolvable 8604 → 8192 6126 → 5802 5504 → 5182 5112 → 4806 busgen_ser evolvable 5284 → 4872 3650 → 3326 3256 → 2938 3224 → 2922 busgen evolvable 12664 → 12252 9086 → 8762 8180 → 7848 7384 → 7082 busgen final 11268 → 10856 8134 → 7810 7356 → 7030 6576 → 6270 busgen_hand 7824 → 7412 5762 → 5438 5152 → 4834 4408 → 4104 rw_de, struct_de, vec_de, bits_de, .. unchanged

The other _ser cases lose the same 412 / 324 / 318 / 304 bytes. With both settings the derived busgen codec is 7848 bytes on RV32IC (evolvable) and 7030 (final), the hand-written one 4834.

items.title: Feature flags
items.text:
The options that were on the table, and why none became a cargo feature:

idea verdict decode-only / encode-only nothing to do: unused code is not linked (6.0 KB and 3.7 KB of the 9.0 KB) no u4 / nibble / varint support nothing to do for the types (UNib32, UVlq32, Nibble are linked only when used); the nibble code of the length FIFO is linked only for types with lengths (step 4) no evolution support exists per type as sized / final_structure (0.9 to 1.0 KB here). As a cargo feature it would change the wire format of every type at once, and cargo unifies features across a build: one crate in the tree turning it on would silently change the bytes of all the others fixed-size-only mode, no length FIFO done without a flag (step 4): decided per type at compile time cheaper errors done (step 2), for everybody #[inline(never)] shared helpers, non-generic paths done for the integer reads and writes (steps 2 and 3)

items.title: What is left
items.text:
With views and writers (SW-52, Head and tail) the derived codec fits the 8 KB softcore: busgen's firmware is 5608 bytes (UART) and 5090 (I2C) on RV32IC, against 4552 / 4716 hand-written, with a ceiling of about 6.3 KB. What is left below is for the value path (BufReader, from_ww_bytes) and evolvable types, which the views do not use; the sizes quoted in the list are of busgen through that path, still 3.0 to 3.3 KB above the hand-written codec on RV32IC. In order of what they would bring:

  1. RefVec<T> of Sized structs and enums without a decode pass: not planned. It was done for plain numbers only (SW-37, above), where it is provably the same as the pass, and there it costs code instead of saving it. For other Sized types it would also change behaviour: the stride of an element is not its size_bits (alignment padding: struct { a: bool, b: u8 } is 9 bits, 2 bytes per element), and an invalid element (an enum discriminant) would be reported when the list is walked instead of when it is decoded.
  2. Latched reads for the rest: done for U1..U64 / I2..I64 (SW-38, above): 40 bytes less for a bit-packed struct on RV32IC, nothing for the busgen types. Not done: Nibble, u64 and the varints pay only from about two fields of a kind. Fixed on the way: mixed types report the first error again (SW-41, 20 bytes on busgen).
  3. A firmware-side memcpy: measured and documented as advice for very small targets, not a code change (SW-39, Build settings): 324 bytes less on RV32IC for a firmware that moves a value, at the price of speed and of replacing memcpy for the whole firmware.
  4. finish_for in generated server and client code: measured, not done (Replies of generated servers): every server message is a ww_client_server::Event, which always pushes lengths, so the FIFO stays; finish_for for a return value costs 14 bytes on RV32IC instead of saving any. The client side runs on std only. What would remove it is a size-assumed Event, a wire change.
  5. The rest of the length FIFO for types with lengths: encode_len_fifo 214, write_nib 130, write_rev_len 126 bytes on RV32IC. Most of what is left is byte loads and stores, which have no compressed form there, and two checks against the end of the buffer.

For a softcore with 8 KB in all the derived codec is the right choice now, through views: the firmware it was measured for is 4.55 KB (UART image) with the hand-written codec and 5.6 KB with views. The value path alone (derived BufReader codec, 7.3 KB at best) would not fit, and nothing in the list above changes that. With 16 KB, or on a Cortex-M0 with 32 KB of flash, either fits with room to spare.

Where the views' last kilobyte goes. In the real UART image the views are about 1 KB above the hand-written codec (symbol diff of fpga_tools v0.8.0 and v0.9.0, 14 October 2026, RV32IC):

  • main is 802 bytes larger: the handler reads each field inline, so the byte loads and stores of u8 fields, tags and headers (lbu 33 → 50, sb 47 → 58) are in the dispatch itself, where the hand-written one calls a small function. The reply buffers are built with a few memcpy and memset calls (4 and 2).
  • A few __mulsi3 calls: this RISC-V has no multiplier, so every multiplication by a non-constant is a call. They do not come from walking a list (ListIter advances a cursor and divides nothing). The remaining places are List::get(i), which multiplies the index by the item length, and take_items, a count times an item length (a constant per list type, so mostly shifts). Which of them produced the four calls was not looked at.
  • ListIter<Wave> and ListIter<u16> together are 244 bytes; Wave::from_fixed is 150 against 92 for the BufReader read of the same struct, since every multi-byte field goes through Le (SW-53).

Ideas to win some of it back (fewer inline byte accesses, an index without the multiplication, replies written straight into the output buffer) are tracked in the project's task list, estimated at 300 to 500 bytes; the firmware fits without them.

items.title: A small UART transport
items.text:
The softcore talks over a UART with its own framing: COBS(seq, message, crc16) 0x00, CRC-16/XMODEM a nibble at a time from a 16-entry table, streaming on both sides (no second buffer), a reply carries the seq of its request. That module of busgen_proto, built alone with the same profile:

rv32i rv32ic thumbv6m encoder 472 326 242 decoder 376 254 226 both 724 500 418

plus 32 bytes of CRC table in .rodata, 8 bytes of decoder state and the receive buffer.

As a crate of its own (ww_uart_lite or similar: a framing layer below ww_link, with the host side as a Transport in wire_weaver_client) it would cost about that, 0.5 KB on RV32IC. Not built, and not measured: what ww_link's link setup and ww_client_server's request/response types add on top on such a CPU. The bench has a place for that case when the transport is built.

items.title: Derive
items.text:
Writing out serializing and deserializing code by hand would be very tedious and error-prone. So a procedural macro attribute, #[derive_shrink_wrap(..)], is provided that generates all of it from a struct or enum definition.

Besides SerializeShrinkWrap and DeserializeShrinkWrap (and their ..Owned counterparts), the same attribute can:

  • Generate a borrowed (zero-copy) representation, an owned (alloc/std-based) representation, or both, from a single field/variant definition (&str becomes String, RefVec<'i, T> becomes Vec<T>, etc).
  • Support #[default = ..] field attributes so newer and older versions of a type stay wire-compatible.
  • Let you trade away some forward compatibility for a smaller wire size, via final_structure / self_describing / sized.

This page goes through every argument the attribute accepts. All examples were checked against the current macro implementation, so they compile and run as shown.

items.title: Prerequisites
items.text: All examples below assume that wire_weaver dependency is added in Cargo.toml: wire_weaver = "0.5.0".

items.title: Quick start
items.text:
use wire_weaver::prelude::*;

#[derive_shrink_wrap(borrowed, derive(Debug, PartialEq))]
struct CoordV1 {
    x: u8,
    y: u8,
}

fn derive_on_struct() {
    let mut buf = [0u8; 64];
    let coord = CoordV1 { x: 0xAA, y: 0xCC };
    let bytes = coord.to_ww_bytes(&mut buf).unwrap();
    assert_eq!(bytes, &[0xAA, 0xCC]);

    let des = CoordV1::from_ww_bytes(bytes).unwrap();
    assert_eq!(des, coord);
}

Two things to notice, both explained in detail below:

  • Regular derives (Debug, PartialEq, ...) are requested with a derive(..) argument to derive_shrink_wrap, not with a separate #[derive(..)] attribute. That's because derive_shrink_wrap can emit more than one item (a borrowed struct and an owned struct) from one definition; a plain #[derive(..)] attribute would only ever decorate whichever single item follows it in the source, not each generated type.
  • CoordV1 has no lifetime and no alloc fields, so the macro cannot tell whether you meant a borrowed or an owned type - that's why borrowed is spelled out explicitly here. See Borrowed, owned, or both? below.

items.title: Evolving types
items.text:
#[default = ..] on a field marks it as added in a later version: newer and older versions of the type read each other's data. Fields with a default go after all the others.

#[derive_shrink_wrap(borrowed, derive(Debug, PartialEq))]
struct CoordV1 {
    x: u8,
    y: u8,
}

#[derive_shrink_wrap(borrowed, derive(Debug, PartialEq))]
struct CoordV1_1 {
    x: u8,
    y: u8,
    #[default = None]
    z: Option<u8>,
}

fn evolved_struct() {
    let mut buf = [0u8; 64];
    let coord = CoordV1_1 { x: 0xAA, y: 0xCC, z: Some(0xFF) };
    let bytes = coord.to_ww_bytes(&mut buf).unwrap();
    assert_eq!(bytes, &[0xAA, 0xCC, 0x80, 0xFF]);

    // newer type from older data
    let coord: CoordV1_1 = CoordV1_1::from_ww_bytes(&[0xAA, 0xCC]).unwrap();
    assert_eq!(coord, CoordV1_1 { x: 0xAA, y: 0xCC, z: None });

    // older type from newer data
    let old_coord: CoordV1 = CoordV1::from_ww_bytes(bytes).unwrap();
    assert_eq!(old_coord, CoordV1 { x: 0xAA, y: 0xCC });
}

This works for as long as the type stays Unsized (the default - see Size assumptions below).

A field with a default reads as its default only when it starts at the end of the data and its read runs out of data. A field that starts with data left is read as usual: a truncated or malformed value is an error, never replaced with the default. The default can be any expression of the field's type (#[default = 7], #[default = Vec::new()], #[default = Default::default()]).

Padding bits read as 0

The last byte of older data can have unused bits (the rest of a byte after a bool, or the nibble next to a size at the back of the buffer). A new bit-sized field there (bool, nibble, the flag of an Option or Result) is read from them as 0, newer data packs it the same way. So give such fields their zero value as the default: false, None. An Option with #[default = Some(..)] reads as None or the default depending on where the old data ends.

items.title: Enum variants from a newer version
items.text:
A reader that gets a discriminant it doesn't know fails with Error::EnumFutureVersionOrMalformedData. An enum that will grow (errors, modes) ends with a #[future_version] variant instead: it holds any discriminant this version doesn't know, so an older host reports a newer device's error instead of failing to decode the reply, and can pass the value on. How this fits with the rest of an API's errors: Errors.

Every Unsized enum (the default) gets it without writing it (SW-47): the derive adds Unknown(u32) as if it were written last. So this

#[derive_shrink_wrap(borrowed, derive(Debug, PartialEq), ww_repr = unib32)]
enum IoError {
    InUse,
    Refused,
}

is the same type as

#[derive_shrink_wrap(borrowed, derive(Debug, PartialEq), ww_repr = unib32)]
enum IoError {
    InUse,
    Refused,
    /// A variant from a newer version of this type, with its discriminant.
    #[future_version]
    Unknown(u32),
}
Enum Gets the variant Unsized with a free discriminant in its ww_repr yes, as Unknown(u32) no_future_version no: complete by nature (Level, Parity), or its readers must fail on a newer value future_version = Newer yes, as Newer(u32): needed when Unknown is a variant of its own every discriminant of the repr taken (ww_repr = u1 with two variants) no final_structure, self_describing, sized only when written: they can't skip a newer variant's fields written #[future_version] X(u32) as written
  • The variant is last, has one u32 field (the discriminant), no discriminant of its own and no #[cfg]. It takes no number on the wire: the next version adds NoIoLevel as 2 before it, and an older reader gets Unknown(2).
  • The enum's bytes, ELEMENT_SIZE and MAX_SIZE are the same as without it, so it can be added in any version.
  • New variants may carry data only in an Unsized enum (the default): its size slot skips their fields. A sized or self_describing enum has no size slot, there only new unit variants can be read past.
  • Writing Unknown(d) writes the discriminant d without fields, so a newer reader gets the variant back if it has no fields. A d that doesn't fit ww_repr or is a known variant's gives Error::SubtypeOutOfRange.
  • discriminant() returns the wire discriminant, also for Unknown(d). See evolution rules for the full picture, and the evolution checker tool for automatically verifying compatibility across versions.

items.title: Borrowed, owned, or both?
items.text:
Before looking at the individual arguments, it helps to know how derive_shrink_wrap decides what to generate, since several arguments (borrowed, owned, derive_borrowed, cfg_attr_owned, ...) only make sense in that context.

The macro looks at the fields/variants of the type it's attached to and classifies it into one of three kinds:

Kind Detected when What gets generated Implied borrowed Any field has a lifetime (&'i str, RefVec<'i, T>, UserType<'i>, ...) and no alloc type (String, Vec, Box) is used The type itself, as written, is the borrowed type. If owned is also requested, {Name}Owned is generated by mapping borrowed types to their owned equivalents (see table below). Explicit owned The type's name ends in Owned and no field has a lifetime The type itself, as written, is the owned type. If borrowed is also requested, {Name} (with the Owned suffix stripped) is generated by mapping owned types back to borrowed ones. Ambiguous Every field is a plain type (u8, bool, another plain type, ...) - no lifetimes, no alloc types Exactly one type is emitted (no renaming). You must say whether it should implement the borrowed or the owned traits (or both) via the borrowed/owned arguments.

Mixing the two styles (a lifetime and an alloc type, or an Owned-suffixed name that still has a lifetime) is a compile error asking you to pick one, since it would otherwise be ambiguous which type is "the" borrowed/owned one.

// Implied borrowed: has a lifetime, no `owned` requested -> only `Coords<'i>` is generated.
#[derive_shrink_wrap]
struct Coords<'i> {
    points: RefVec<'i, u8>,
}

// Ambiguous: no lifetime, no alloc type -> must say which trait(s) to derive.
#[derive_shrink_wrap(borrowed, derive(Debug, PartialEq))]
struct CoordV1 {
    x: u8,
    y: u8,
}

The zero-copy and owned types section below has a full example of the borrowed+owned case.

items.title: Attribute arguments
items.text:
#[derive_shrink_wrap(directive, directive, ..)] accepts a comma separated list of directives. Order doesn't matter to the parser, but the codebase consistently writes them in this order (and so do the examples below):

borrowed, owned, cfg_attr*, derive*, non_exhaustive, final_structure|self_describing|sized|sparse, ww_repr,
discriminants, display, no_future_version|future_version

items.title: borrowed, borrowed(<cfg predicate>)
items.text:
Requests generation of the borrowed type. Only needed for an Ambiguous type (where it's otherwise not generated at all), or to gate an implied-borrowed type's generation behind a cfg predicate:

// Ambiguous type - `borrowed` is what makes generation happen at all.
#[derive_shrink_wrap(borrowed)]
struct Flags {
    a: bool,
    b: bool,
}

// Implied borrowed type - already generated unconditionally; `borrowed(..)` restricts *when*.
#[derive_shrink_wrap(borrowed(feature = "defmt"), owned(feature = "std"))]
struct Name<'i> {
    value: &'i str,
}

items.title: owned, owned(<cfg predicate>)
items.text:
Enables generation of the owned type, converting borrowed fields to their owned equivalents (see the type mapping table). Bare owned generates it unconditionally; owned(<cfg predicate>) gates it behind an arbitrary cfg predicate, most commonly a feature flag:

#[derive_shrink_wrap(owned(feature = "std"), derive(Debug))]
pub struct FullVersion<'i> {
    pub crate_id: &'i str,
}

behind feature = "std", this additionally generates:

#[cfg(feature = "std")]
#[derive(Debug)]
pub struct FullVersionOwned {
    pub crate_id: String,
}

along with matching SerializeShrinkWrapOwned/DeserializeShrinkWrapOwned impls that produce/consume the exact same bytes as the borrowed side.

items.title: cfg_attr(..), cfg_attr_owned(..), cfg_attr_borrowed(..)
items.text:
Splice a #[cfg_attr(condition, attr, ..)] verbatim onto the generated type(s) - the base one, the owned one only, or the borrowed one only, respectively. Can be repeated. The contents are captured as-is and not interpreted by derive_shrink_wrap itself, so any valid cfg_attr body works, e.g. for optional trait impls:

#[derive_shrink_wrap(
    borrowed,
    owned(feature = "std"),
    derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq),
    cfg_attr_borrowed(feature = "defmt", derive(defmt::Format)),
    cfg_attr_owned(feature = "serde", derive(serde::Serialize, serde::Deserialize)),
    ww_repr = nib,
    sized
)]
pub enum Level {
    Low,
    High,
}

defmt::Format only ends up on Level (and only when the defmt feature is on), serde's traits only on LevelOwned (and only behind feature = "serde").

items.title: derive(..), derive_owned(..), derive_borrowed(..)
items.text:
Extra derives (paths, so core::fmt::Debug works too) added to the base / owned-only / borrowed-only generated type, exactly like Rust's own #[derive(..)]. derive(..) applies to whichever type(s) are actually generated; use derive_owned/derive_borrowed when a trait only makes sense (or only compiles) on one side - e.g. Copy, which a String/Vec-carrying owned type could never implement:

#[derive_shrink_wrap(
    owned(feature = "std"),
    derive(Debug, PartialEq),
    derive_borrowed(Copy, Clone),
    final_structure
)]
struct Version<'i> {
    pub major: u8,
    pub minor: u8,
    pub patch: u8,
    pub label: Option<&'i str>,
}

fn borrowed_is_copy() {
    let v = Version { major: 1, minor: 2, patch: 3, label: None };
    let v2 = v; // fine, `Version` is `Copy` (via `derive_borrowed`)
    let _ = v; // still usable
    let _ = v2;
}

items.title: Size assumptions: final_structure, self_describing, sized
items.text:
By default, every generated type is Unsized: its serialized size isn't known up front, so when it's nested inside another struct/enum, the parent stores a reverse-length for it (nibble-based, similar to UNib32, but in reverse order). This is what makes the evolution example above work - fields can be added or removed later without breaking anyone.

The three directives below (mutually exclusive - specifying more than one is a compile error) opt a type out of that flexibility in exchange for a smaller wire size. They map directly onto shrink_wrap's ElementSize:

Directive ElementSize Meaning Trade-off (none) Unsized Size unknown, stored as a reverse length in the parent. Fully evolvable. final_structure UnsizedFinalStructure Size still unknown, but the type is flattened onto its parent - no reverse length is stored for it at all; parent and this type share the same size-marker "budget". Cannot be evolved, only the very first evolution can be marked final_structure, and it cannot be removed later. self_describing SelfDescribing No size is stored; a reader can tell where the value ends from the encoding itself (e.g. UNib32's own variable-length encoding). No overhead, but only applicable to types whose encoding is inherently self-delimiting. sized Sized { size_bits } Size is fixed and known at compile time (computed automatically from the fields - you don't specify a bit count). Nothing is stored for it, ever. Cannot evolve at all: adding/removing/resizing a field changes the layout for every existing reader. Most compact option.

Tip

Even though a type can be fnial_structure or sized, it can still be evolved. But only by reusing previously unused gaps, which by default are set to 0. For example if bool is followed by u8, 7 bits are left unused and skipped by readers, which can later be reclaimed.

For an enum, only one variant is on the wire, so its size is the discriminant (see ww_repr below) plus the fields of one variant, not of all of them:

  • sized needs every variant to take the same number of bits (unit variants take 0), and a fixed size discriminant (anything but unib32). ELEMENT_SIZE is then Sized { size_bits: discriminant + variant }.

  • Variants of different sizes make the enum self_describing: the discriminant tells how long the value is. Asking for sized is a compile error that names the variants and their sizes:

    sized enum Reading: variants differ in size (Short: 8 bits, Long: 32 bits); use self_describing instead of
sized, or pad the variants to one size

sized and self_describing produce the same bytes, for the type and for whatever contains it, so switching between the two is not a wire change. Note that pairing an enum with ww_repr alone does not make it compact - without one of these three directives it stays Unsized, exactly like a struct:

#[derive_shrink_wrap(borrowed, derive(Debug, PartialEq), ww_repr = u2)]
enum SpeedUnsized { Slow, Medium, Fast, Turbo }

#[derive_shrink_wrap(borrowed, derive(Debug, PartialEq), ww_repr = u2, sized)]
enum SpeedSized { Slow, Medium, Fast, Turbo }

// Wraps a `Sized` field - its 2 bits are known up front, so a field placed right after it
// can carry on packing into the very same byte.
#[derive_shrink_wrap(borrowed, derive(Debug, PartialEq))]
struct PayloadWithSized {
    speed: SpeedSized,
    after: bool,
}

// Wraps an `Unsized` field - its size isn't known up front, so the struct reserves a
// reverse-length marker for it, and everything that follows starts fresh on the next byte.
#[derive_shrink_wrap(borrowed, derive(Debug, PartialEq))]
struct PayloadWithUnsized {
    speed: SpeedUnsized,
    after: bool,
}

fn compact_vs_not() {
    let mut buf = [0u8; 4];
    // Sized, so (Slow, Turbo) packs into 2+2 = 4 bits of a single byte:
    let bytes = (SpeedSized::Slow, SpeedSized::Turbo).to_ww_bytes(&mut buf).unwrap();
    assert_eq!(bytes, &[0x30]);

    // Unsized, standalone, needs no reverse length here since nothing follows it -
    // but as soon as it's nested next to another field, an extra size marker appears.
    let mut buf2 = [0u8; 4];
    let bytes2 = SpeedUnsized::Turbo.to_ww_bytes(&mut buf2).unwrap();
    assert_eq!(bytes2, &[0xC0]);

    // `SpeedSized` is 2 bits wide, so `after`'s bit packs right in after it, same byte:
    // 0b11_1_00000 - Turbo (11), then `after` (1), then unused padding.
    let mut buf3 = [0u8; 4];
    let sized_payload = PayloadWithSized { speed: SpeedSized::Turbo, after: true };
    let bytes3 = sized_payload.to_ww_bytes(&mut buf3).unwrap();
    assert_eq!(bytes3, &[0xE0]);

    // `SpeedUnsized` gives no such guarantee, so its byte gets padded on its own, and `after`
    // starts a new byte (with a reverse-length marker for `speed` sharing its low bits):
    let mut buf4 = [0u8; 4];
    let unsized_payload = PayloadWithUnsized { speed: SpeedUnsized::Turbo, after: true };
    let bytes4 = unsized_payload.to_ww_bytes(&mut buf4).unwrap();
    assert_eq!(bytes4, &[0xC0, 0x81]);
    // bool and reverse length end up in the same byte, and there are even 3 bits left, neat!
}

Whichever assumption you pick, the macro inserts a compile-time assertion checking that the type's actual generated ELEMENT_SIZE matches the one you asked for - if a field turns out to make the type Unsized after all, the build fails instead of silently producing an incompatible layout. User types are counted wherever they are in a field (Point, [Point; 3], (Point, u8), Option<Point>, Range<Point>): the macro can't see their size, so it emits a const expression over their ELEMENT_SIZE and the compiler folds it.

size_bits is the sum of the fields' own bits. Alignment padding between fields depends on where the value starts in the buffer and is not part of it: struct { a: bool, b: u8 } is Sized { size_bits: 9 } and takes 2 bytes on its own.

items.title: fixed_layout: fields at fixed offsets, and the fast path
items.text:
shrink_wrap writes a value field after field. When no field's size depends on its value, every field starts at the same place in every value: a header, a record in flash, a descriptor that is signed as bytes. Reading a field is then a load at a constant offset, and the macro generates that next to the usual serdes code (SW-44, SW-45):

  • ENCODED_LEN: the longest encoding, the buffer to have ready. MIN_LEN: the shortest. fixed_len(): the length of this value. All three are the same unless the last field has a variable length (see below);
  • an offset const per field: COUNT_OFFSET in bytes, or for a bit field URGENT_BIT_OFFSET and URGENT_BITS, counted from the most significant bit of the first byte; for an enum TAG_LEN, and per variant <VARIANT>_TAG, <VARIANT>_LEN and <VARIANT>_<FIELD>_.. (unnamed fields by their index); an Option's flag is <FIELD>_FLAG;
  • from_fixed(&[u8]) and to_fixed(&mut [u8]): loads and stores (shifts and masks for bit fields) at those offsets, without a BufReader or BufWriter. The bytes are those of ser_shrink_wrap. A short buffer is an error, never a panic;
  • the FixedLayout trait, whose write_c prints the C reader of the type: a define per offset and a static inline reader per field (shrink_wrap::fixed_layout::write_c_header writes a whole header).

What has a fixed offset:

field rule u8..u64, i8..i64, f32, f64, arrays of them start on a byte, little-endian, as BufWriter writes them bool, U1..U32, I2..I32, Nibble packed most significant bit first; a Nibble starts on a 4-bit boundary; the next byte-aligned field starts a fresh byte another fixed_layout type starts on a byte; it cannot share a byte with bit fields of the parent (a compile error asks for a byte-aligned field between them) Option<T>, Result<T, E>, an enum whose variants differ in length only as the last field: the fields before it keep their offsets, nothing after it could. The payload starts on a byte; the flag is an ordinary bit field, also where #[flag] moves it

Not: lists, strings, MaxLen, varints (UNib32 and friends), RefBox, TailSize, tuples, ranges, 128-bit numbers, bit fields wider than 32 bits, #[default] fields. A struct must be sized, final_structure or self_describing; an evolvable struct may grow, so it has no fixed layout. An enum must be sized or self_describing with a byte-aligned tag (ww_repr = u8, u16 or u32).

The rule for variable length is the same everywhere: an Option, a Result and an enum of unequal variants are each a value whose length depends on what it holds. As a whole type, or as the last field of one, that is fine: fixed_len() says how long this value is. Before another field it is not, because that field would move.

Types that qualify get the fast path without asking. The fixed_layout directive makes it a requirement: a field that breaks it is a compile error that says why and what to use instead, for example "field count: a variable-length number takes more bytes for larger values, so the fields after it have no fixed offset. Use u32 / u64, or U1..U32 for fewer bits". Only with the directive may a field be another fixed-layout type (the macro cannot look inside a type it does not see; the compiler checks that it implements FixedLayout). On a struct the directive also picks the size assumption when none is given: sized, or self_describing when the last field is an Option or Result. A struct whose last field is an enum of unequal variants says self_describing itself.

#[derive_shrink_wrap(borrowed, fixed_layout)]
struct Header {
    magic: [u8; 4],
    urgent: bool,
    retries: U3,
    count: u32,
    inner: Inner,         // another fixed_layout type
    extra: Option<Extra>, // last: present when its flag bit is set
}

let header = Header::from_fixed(&bytes)?; // what a tiny bootloader links: loads at constant offsets
let header = Header::from_ww_bytes(&bytes)?; // the same value through BufReader

On a Cortex-M0, decoding a header of eight integers takes 276 bytes of code this way and 484 through BufReader; a bit-packed sample 276 instead of 652 (code size).

items.title: head_tail: a fixed head and a sequential tail
items.text:
For types with lists, strings or options in the middle, where no fixed layout exists, head_tail picks a wire format of its own (SW-46), made for the smallest reader on a microcontroller:

  • the head has a length known at compile time and holds every fixed-width field at a constant offset, as fixed_layout places them, and for each variable field what is fixed about it: a u16 count for a list or string, the flag bit of an Option or Result, the head of a nested head_tail or fixed_layout type;
  • the tail follows the head and holds the variable parts in field order: list items, string bytes, option payloads, the tails of nested types.

An enum is its tag (ww_repr = u8, u16 or u32), then the head and tail of its variant. Reading the head is loads at constant offsets; the tail is read front to back by a cursor that only takes lengths it already knows (Tail). There are no lengths at the back, no BufReader, no per-type generic reader.

use shrink_wrap::head_tail::List;

#[derive_shrink_wrap(head_tail)]
struct Utx<'i> {
    ch: u8,
    fmt: UartFormat,        // a fixed_layout type: in the head
    glitch: Option<Wave>,   // flag bit in the head, the Wave in the tail
    perr: List<'i, u16>,    // count in the head, the items in the tail
    name: &'i str,          // the same
    defer: bool,            // a bit in the head, after all of them
}

let utx = Utx::from_head_tail(&bytes)?;
let n = utx.to_head_tail(&mut buf)?;

A list is a shrink_wrap::head_tail::List<'i, T>: List::new(&items) to write, and read from the wire it keeps the bytes and reads an item when its iterator reaches it. Its items are numbers or fixed_layout types of one length. Option / Result payloads are numbers, arrays of them, or head_tail / fixed_layout types. Every fixed_layout type implements HeadTail (all head when it has one length, else all tail), so the types of a protocol mix freely.

It is one type with one format: a head_tail type has no SerializeShrinkWrap / DeserializeShrinkWrap (and no owned version), so it cannot be a field of an ordinary shrink_wrap type or a ww API argument. write_c_ht prints the C reader: head defines and readers as for fixed_layout, and per type a <name>_tail_t and a <name>_tail() that walks the tail and points at each variable part (shrink_wrap::head_tail::write_c_header writes a whole header).

Views and writers (SW-52), for firmware that should not make the whole value first. Utx::view(&bytes)? checks the lengths and walks the tail once (counts and flags are the only fields it reads) and gives a UtxView<'_>: a reference to the head whose accessors (v.ch(), v.defer()) read each field at its offset when called, and the variable parts found on the way (v.perr() a List, v.glitch() an &Option<Wave>, a nested head_tail type its own view). An enum's view is an enum of its variants' views: RequestView::Stop(v) with v.mask(), a tuple variant of one nested type holds that type's view (RequestView::Utx(UtxView)). Each enum variant also gets a writer, Reply::write_run(&mut tx, run, started, mark, lead, mark_line)?, which writes the same bytes as to_head_tail of that variant without making the value. Both come from the code of from_head_tail / to_head_tail and are tested against it byte for byte. View types are always pub (the View of the public HeadTail trait).

Enum variants may have a #[cfg] (SW-54): a variant compiled out keeps its tag, and a build without it reads that tag as an unknown one. One protocol enum can then serve firmware images that each handle a part of it.

On busgen's request and reply enums the codec takes 4590 bytes on a Cortex-M0 through values and 3894 through views and writers, a hand-written one 4408 and the derived shrink_wrap one 6652 (code size).

items.title: sparse: a struct of optional fields
items.text:
sparse (DER-13) encodes a struct whose fields are all Option<T> as an OptionAnyVec: a presence header, then only the present values. Each field is one slot, in declaration order, and #[slot = N] places a field at slot N instead (slots increase, gaps are allowed). It is made for updates that carry any subset of many values, as the per trait level <Level>Update of an observe request, whose slots are the level's resource indices with methods and streams in between:

#[derive_shrink_wrap(owned, derive(Debug, PartialEq, Default), sparse)]
struct MotorUpdate<'i> {
    speed: Option<u16>,    // slot 0
    name: Option<&'i str>, // slot 1
    #[slot = 5]
    current: Option<f32>,  // slot 5, slots 2..=4 are never present
    on: Option<bool>,      // slot 6
}

let update = MotorUpdate { speed: Some(1500), on: Some(true), ..Default::default() };
assert_eq!(update.to_ww_bytes(&mut buf)?, [0x17, 0x82, 0xdc, 0x05, 0x80]);

1 7: the dense header mode, 7 slots, then a bit per slot, 1000001 and a padding bit (82); dc 05 is speed, the 80 bit on. With all four fields present it is 17 c6 dc 05 4c 00 00 c0 3f 81: the bits 1100011, speed, "L", 1.5f32, the on bit, and the length of "L" in the last nibble. One field present is three bytes (MotorUpdate { speed: Some(1500), .. } is 01 dc 05: the all mode, one slot), none is no bytes at all. The writer picks the header mode with the fewest bits for the present set (dense, all, two-level or an index list, see the wire format).

A field may be any type, including another sparse struct: a child level is then one slot holding its own sparse struct, so one message carries any subset of a tree of levels. The borrowed and the owned type write the same bytes.

Rules, checked at compile time:

  • every field is an Option<T>; #[flag] and #[default = ..] don't apply (any field can be absent, a field added later reads as None from older data);
  • sparse is an encoding of its own: no final_structure, self_describing, sized, fixed_layout or head_tail with it, and no enums. The struct is Unsized;
  • #[slot = N] is an integer literal past the previous field's slot, below u32::MAX, and only on sparse fields.

Evolution: fields are only appended, after the last slot (see the rules). An older reader reads the fields it knows and ignores the rest, a newer reader reads the new fields as None. A reader whose struct has a gap where the data has a present value fails with Error::OptionAnyVecUnknownSlot: a gap is never filled later.

items.title: ww_repr = <repr> (enums only)
items.text:
Sets the wire representation of an enum's discriminant. Required for every enum - structs must not set it. Accepted values: u1..u32 (or ub<N> for arbitrary bit widths), nib (4-bit nibble), unib32 (UNib32, variable-length, 1 or more nibbles), and the byte-aligned u8/u16/u32. Pick the smallest one that fits the number of variants you expect to ever need - it directly determines the discriminant's on-wire size (and, combined with sized, the whole enum's size):

// Fits in 2 bits (up to 4 variants) - future variants beyond 4 would be a breaking change.
#[derive_shrink_wrap(borrowed, derive(Debug), ww_repr = u2, sized)]
enum Pull { None, Up, Down, UpDown }

// Variable-length - room to grow past the initial variant count without repr changes.
#[derive_shrink_wrap(borrowed, derive(Debug), ww_repr = unib32, self_describing)]
enum ErrorCode { NotFound, Timeout, /* ... */ }

Every generated enum also gets an inherent fn discriminant(&self) -> <repr's native type> method regardless of whether discriminants is used.

items.title: #[cfg(..)] on enum variants
items.text:
A variant can be compiled out, typically behind a cargo feature, when only some targets need it: firmware enables the few it uses, a host enables all of them.

#[derive_shrink_wrap(borrowed, non_exhaustive, self_describing, ww_repr = unib32)]
pub enum Number {
    U8(u8),
    #[cfg(feature = "f32")]
    F32(f32),
    #[cfg(feature = "u128")]
    U128(u128),
}
  • The wire format does not depend on it. Discriminants are numbered over all variants, U128 is 2 with or without f32, so two builds with different features agree on every variant they share.
  • The variant, its serializing and deserializing code and its part of the size exist only where the predicate holds: without u128 the enum above is 8 bytes in memory instead of 32, and no 128-bit code is linked.
  • Reading a variant that is compiled out gives Error::EnumVariantDisabled (an unknown number is still EnumFutureVersionOrMalformedData).
  • A sized enum needs at least one variant without #[cfg], so its size cannot change with features.
  • Cargo features are unified across a build: a crate that matches such an enum without a _ arm stops compiling when another crate enables one more variant. The non_exhaustive argument puts #[non_exhaustive] on the generated types and makes the _ arm mandatory outside the defining crate.

ww_numeric::NumericValue is built this way. #[cfg] on fields is not supported: it would change the bytes.

items.title: crate_path(<path>)
items.text:
Generated code refers to shrink_wrap items by path, so neither use shrink_wrap::prelude::* nor any other import is needed for the macro, and the names it uses (BufReader, Error, ElementSize, ...) never clash with the module's own. The macro finds the crate in Cargo.toml: ::shrink_wrap (or whatever it is renamed to), or ::wire_weaver::shrink_wrap when only wire_weaver is a dependency. crate_path(..) overrides that, for a crate that reaches shrink_wrap through some other re-export:

#[derive_shrink_wrap(borrowed, crate_path(my_framework::shrink_wrap))]
struct Point { x: u8, y: u8 }

When neither crate is a dependency and nothing is given, the names are left unqualified and the prelude import is needed, as it was before.

items.title: no_future_version, future_version = <Name> (enums only)
items.text:
An Unsized enum gets Unknown(u32) for discriminants from a newer version (see Enum variants from a newer version). no_future_version leaves it out, for an enum that is complete by nature or whose readers must fail on a value they don't know (a request kind a device can't act on). future_version = <Name> names the variant, when Unknown is taken:

#[derive_shrink_wrap(borrowed, derive(Debug, PartialEq), ww_repr = u2, no_future_version)]
enum Parity {
    None,
    Even,
    Odd,
}

#[derive_shrink_wrap(borrowed, derive(Debug, PartialEq), ww_repr = u8, future_version = Newer)]
enum Reason {
    Unknown,
    User,
    // Newer(u32) is added
}

Either is an error next to a written #[future_version] variant, and future_version = <Name> on an enum that can't get one (not Unsized, or every discriminant taken).

items.title: discriminants (enums only)
items.text:
Additionally generates a fieldless {Name}Discriminants enum, carrying only the variants (no payloads) plus its own .discriminant() method. It's for the case where you need to commit to which variant you're writing before you've built that variant's payload - e.g. a streaming/builder API that reserves space for the discriminant, keeps writing, and only decides the final variant afterward:

#[derive_shrink_wrap(borrowed, derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq), ww_repr = nib, discriminants)]
enum EventKind<'i> {
    Value { data: RefVec<'i, u8> },
    Written,
}

fn discriminant_ahead_of_time() {
    // `EventKindDiscriminants` can be produced (and its wire discriminant read) without ever
    // constructing an `EventKind::Value`'s `data` field.
    let placeholder = EventKindDiscriminants::Value;
    let full = EventKind::Value { data: RefVec::new_bytes(&[1, 2, 3]) };
    assert_eq!(placeholder.discriminant(), full.discriminant());
}

This is exactly how ww_client_server's response builder writes a placeholder discriminant up front, then goes back and patches it in once the actual variant being sent is known.

items.title: display (DER-12)
items.text:
Generates core::fmt::Display and core::error::Error (a bare impl, no source()) for the borrowed side, the owned side, or both, whichever owned/borrowed generate. The message is the first doc line: a struct's own, or each variant's own for an enum, without its trailing period (Rust's convention for error messages, so it reads well inside a longer one; ... is kept, #[display("..")] is used as written). {field} is filled in from the type's own field of that name, format specs work too ({field:#x}); a tuple variant's fields are {0}, {1}, ... #[display("..")] overrides the doc line, for a tuple variant's fields or when the doc line should say more than the message (error enums in APIs: Errors):

#[derive_shrink_wrap(owned(feature = "std"), derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq, Clone), display, ww_repr = unib32)]
pub enum IoError<'i> {
    /// Not supported by this device.
    Unsupported,
    /// In use by {by}.
    InUse { by: &'i str },
    /// Hardware fault {code:#x}.
    Fault { code: u32 },
    #[display("wrapping: {0}")]
    Wrapped(u8),
}

fn display_message() {
    assert_eq!(IoError::Unsupported.to_string(), "Not supported by this device");
    assert_eq!(IoError::InUse { by: "USART2" }.to_string(), "In use by USART2");
    assert_eq!(IoError::Fault { code: 0xBEEF }.to_string(), "Hardware fault 0xbeef");
    assert_eq!(IoError::Wrapped(7).to_string(), "wrapping: 7");
    // the owned side gets it too
    assert_eq!(IoErrorOwned::Unsupported.to_string(), "Not supported by this device");
}

A variant with neither a doc comment nor #[display("..")] is a compile error naming it, so a message is never silently missing; the #[future_version] variant (SW-47) always has one, written or not. A field not mentioned by the message is simply unused, not an error. display is unused on the device if nothing calls it (no Display or Error method is ever invoked there), so the linker drops it - there is no no_std downside to turning it on for an API's error types.

items.title: Zero-copy and owned types
items.text:
Often there is a need to serialize an owned type into a buffer and deserialize it as a borrowed type on no_std without allocation, or vice versa. Typing out two definitions by hand - one using borrowed data (RefVec<'i, T>, &'i str, etc.) and one owned - would be very error-prone. owned(<cfg predicate>) (see above) generates the owned definition and its serdes code automatically.

Pseudo-code usage example:

fn round_trip() {
    // on no_std, no allocator
    let v = FullVersion { .. };
    let bytes = v.to_ww_bytes(&mut buf).unwrap();

    // on host, with allocator
    let v_owned = FullVersionOwned::from_ww_bytes_owned(bytes).unwrap();
    assert_eq!(v.to_owned(), v_owned);

    let bytes_from_owned = v_owned.to_ww_bytes_owned().unwrap();
    assert_eq!(bytes, bytes_from_owned);

    // again on no_std
    let v_ref = FullVersion::from_ww_bytes(bytes_from_owned).unwrap();
    assert_eq!(v, v_ref);
}

items.title: Type mapping
items.text:
Borrowed type Owned equivalent RefVec<'i, u8> Vec<u8> &'i str String RefBox<'i, T> Box<T> MaxLen<RefVec<'i, T>, N> MaxLen<Vec<T>, N> MaxLen<&'i str, N> MaxLen<String, N> UserType<'i> UserTypeOwned UserType<'i, T> UserTypeOwned<T>

Generic arguments of a user type are emitted as written (Twice<u8> stays Twice<u8> on both sides); only a leading lifetime is replaced by the generated type's and dropped in the owned variant. The borrowed/owned pairs of shrink_wrap itself follow this scheme too (Delta<'i, T> / DeltaOwned<T>, XorFloat<'i, T> / XorFloatOwned<T>).

Array lengths can be any const expression ([f32; MAX_SERIES], [u8; N * 2]), not only literals; a sized type's ELEMENT_SIZE carries them symbolically.

MaxLen<T, N> (a list or string of at most N elements, N any const expression) has the same bytes as T and is checked on serialize and deserialize, see bounded lists and strings. The borrowed type gets a MAX_SIZE (worst-case serialized size, Some when every field is bounded) next to ELEMENT_SIZE; the owned one does not have it yet.

TailSize<N> is the same on both sides: a slot the macro fills in with the size of the rest of the value, see the wire format page. It is only allowed in types without a size assumption.

items.text: Check out API overview.

items.title: Showcase
items.text:
A tour of shrink_wrap tricks, from plain bit-packing to self-referential types, illustrated with real code from wire_weaver itself and from the ww_stdlib crates (ww_version, ww_date_time, ww_client_server, ww_self). Every byte sequence shown below was produced by actually running the snippet - none of it is hand-waved.

Read wire format and derive first if you haven't; this page assumes you know what Unsized/final_structure/self_describing/sized mean and how #[derive_shrink_wrap(..)] decides between borrowed and owned types.

items.title: Sub-byte packing
items.text:
bool is 1-bit aligned, nib (the Nibble type) is 4-bit aligned, and u1..u64/i2..i64 (U1, U2, ..., I2, ...) are 1-bit aligned regardless of width - they just cost exactly as many bits as you ask for, packed back-to-back with no padding in between:

let mut buf = [0u8; 8];
let mut wr = BufWriter::new(&mut buf);
wr.write_bool(true).unwrap();          // 1 bit
wr.write(&U2::new(3).unwrap()).unwrap(); // 2 bits
wr.write(&U1::new(1).unwrap()).unwrap(); // 1 bit
let bytes = wr.finish().unwrap();
assert_eq!(bytes, &[0b1111_0000]); // 1 + 11 + 1 = 4 bits used, rest padded with zeros

A whole tuple of 8 bools packs into a single byte, no framing at all:

let bytes = (true, false, true, false, true, true, false, false)
    .to_ww_bytes(&mut buf).unwrap();
assert_eq!(bytes, &[0b1010_1100]);

This is what the ElementSize::Sized { size_bits } case (see derive.md) is built on: a sized struct/enum's fields are just laid out bit after bit, so putting a bool field or a small enum next to another Sized field is free - they share the same byte instead of each getting its own.

items.title: Bit-sized fields and variant payloads: a 7- or 10-bit I2C address
items.text:
The same U1..U64 / I2..I64 types work as struct fields, enum variant payloads and #[ww_trait] method arguments, returns and properties. Next to a 1-bit discriminant they share its byte:

#[derive_shrink_wrap(borrowed, derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq, Copy, Clone), ww_repr = u1, self_describing)]
enum I2cAddress {
    Seven(U7),
    Ten(U10),
}

let seven = I2cAddress::Seven(U7::new(0x50).unwrap());
assert_eq!(seven.to_ww_bytes(&mut buf).unwrap(), &[0x50]);       // 0 1010000: 8 bits
let ten = I2cAddress::Ten(U10::new(0x3ff).unwrap());
assert_eq!(ten.to_ww_bytes(&mut buf).unwrap(), &[0xff, 0xe0]);   // 1 1111111111 00000: 11 bits

With Seven(u8) instead, the byte-aligned u8 pads the discriminant to a byte and the same address takes [0x00, 0x50]. The variants are 7 and 10 bits, so the enum is self_describing, not sized (a sized enum needs variants of one size, see derive.md). Same-sized payloads can be sized and then nest without any size information, e.g. a 32-bit frame (shrink_wrap/tests/sub_byte.rs):

#[derive_shrink_wrap(borrowed, derive(..), ww_repr = u1, sized)]
enum Offset { Up(U7), Signed(I7) }                                  // 1 + 7 bits

#[derive_shrink_wrap(borrowed, derive(..), ww_repr = u2, sized)]
enum Reg {                                                          // 2 + 14 bits
    Wide { addr: U10, write: bool, len: U3 },
