items.title: 1L-UPD-STEP: Pit-stop Shuttle
items.text:
One app slot; the app reboots into an updater (a bootloader with a transport, or a recovery app), which receives the plan one call per step and applies it in place as it arrives.

Setup. One app slot, no extra flash. The updater is either the bootloader with its own transport (USB, CAN) or a small write-protected recovery app at its own address; it must come back up after any cut and finish the job.

| bootloader + transport = updater | APP slot: rewritten in place |
| bootloader | recovery app (updater, write-protected) | APP slot: rewritten in place |

The app implements UpdateNode and BootControl only (often just reboot(BootTarget::Updater) matters). The updater implements UpdateNode, BootControl, Inventory and Stage (NodeInfo::role is Bootloader or Recovery).

Choose it when the flash has no room for a second image or a plan area, and the bootloader (or a recovery app) can have a transport. It is the fastest end to end and needs no extra flash, but the device does nothing else from the reboot into the updater until the new app starts.

Flow.

  1. To the app: UpdateNode::node: offers has no stage, so the host calls BootControl::reboot(BootTarget::Updater).
  2. The host reconnects to the same device; the updater answers, with a different API.
  3. UpdateNode::node, Stage::limits: an updater usually has a small buffer, chunks come in pieces of max_piece.
  4. Stage::begin(Target::Live, header): from here on the app slot is not bootable until the session finishes (BootState::Updating); the updater records the session in flash.
  5. Stage::erase / copy / write applied in place as they arrive; the planner never copies from a chunk an earlier step has overwritten.
  6. Stage::finish: the new image is checked against the descriptor and marked bootable (Confirmed).
  7. BootControl::reboot(BootTarget::App): the new app runs.

Failures and power cuts. A cut leaves no bootable app: the bootloader sees that and starts the updater again (BootState::Updating, app_version: None), and the host continues. A lost link the same. The updater must be able to resume any session it started, which is why it keeps its session record (header and next step) in flash.

Resume. begin with the same header: resumed: true, resume_from the step after the last one that finished; the step in flight is redone from its first piece (Stage::progress shows the piece offset while the link is up).

What the device checks: the header (format, geometry, floor, signature) before erasing anything, every index against the app slot, COPY source hashes, WRITE chunk hashes after the last piece, the image against the descriptor.

items.title: 1L-UPD-BULK: Pit-stop Freight
items.text:
One app slot; the app reboots into an updater, which receives the whole plan as one stream and applies it in place as the steps complete.

Setup. One app slot, no extra flash; the updater is the bootloader with a transport or a recovery app.

| bootloader + transport = updater | APP slot: rewritten in place |
| bootloader | recovery app (updater, write-protected) | APP slot: rewritten in place |

The app implements UpdateNode and BootControl. The updater implements UpdateNode, BootControl, Stage and StageBulk.

Choose it when there is no room for a second image or a plan area, the updater has a transport, and round trips are long, or the link is fast and the host just wants to stream the plan without waiting on every step.

Flow.

  1. To the app: UpdateNode::node, then BootControl::reboot(BootTarget::Updater).
  2. The host reconnects; the updater answers. UpdateNode::node, Stage::limits.
  3. StageBulk::begin_bulk(Target::Live, header, total_len, ack_every: 0): the app slot stops being bootable.
  4. The plan after its header on the plan credit sink, in segments of at most max_piece; the updater parses the steps from the stream and applies each in place as soon as it is complete.
  5. PlanAck { status: Complete } on plan_ack, then Stage::finish: checked, Confirmed.
  6. BootControl::reboot(BootTarget::App): the new app runs.

Failures and power cuts. A cut leaves no bootable app; the bootloader starts the updater again and the host resumes. A step that fails ends the session with PlanAck { status: Failed(error) }; the device stays in the updater until a session finishes.

Resume. begin_bulk with the same header answers the byte after the last applied step (the updater keeps it in its session record); bytes of a step that was not complete are sent again.

What the device checks: segment offsets, the header before erasing anything, each completed step (ranges, COPY source hash, WRITE hash), the image against the descriptor.

items.title: About the transcripts and their tests
items.text:
Every transcript on this page is recorded by its test in tests/dfu_scenarios (src/scenarios.rs) and checked against the file included here: a test fails when the exchange changes, until just dfu-transcripts writes the new one and the change is looked at. So the bytes here are the bytes the current code sends.

  • Two views. The readable one decodes each ww_link message with the API model of the firmware that runs: method, arguments, result, sink writes (⇐) and stream items (⇒), credit and sideband events, with each message's size and first bytes. The wire view shows every unit of the medium: USB packets, UDP datagrams or WebSocket frames. Both are taken on the device side.
  • Left out: link setup (Nop, GetDeviceInfo, LinkSetup, LinkReady, the WebSocket upgrade), which is the same on every connection and carries crate versions that change with every release, and pings. WebSocket frames from the host are masked with a random key; they are shown unmasked with the key zeroed.
  • The device is a simulation with real firmware logic on a simulated flash: two banks with NOR semantics (programming only clears bits), 8 chunks of 64 bytes, erase blocks of 128 bytes, a plan area, an apply journal, and power cuts injected at a given step. A reset restarts the device thread on the same link endpoint, running the bootloader logic first; the host reconnects as it would to a real device. The firmwares are generated ww_dfu servers (tests/dfu_app_api, tests/dfu_lean_app_api, tests/dfu_updater_api).
  • The plan format is a small stand-in for chunky's (a 35-byte header with a toy signature; steps 01 block, 02 dst src hash, 03 dst hash len data), so the step bytes in the transcripts are readable. Hashes are SHA-256 truncated to 8 bytes, as in chunky's format 2. The real records are in The other side: chunky.
  • The links are the real ones from ww_device up: WebSocket and UDP on localhost through wire_weaver_client's ws and udp transports; USB is simulated by wire_weaver_client::in_process::usb_device, which runs the real USB framing on both ends with full-speed (64 B) or high-speed (512 B) packets, but not USB itself (enumeration, data toggles, NAKs). RTT is not used: with a debug probe attached a device is flashed directly, without a bootloader.
  • Changing a scenario's link is one line, const LINK: Link = ... in its test (UART and CAN will join Link).

items.title: The other side: chunky
items.text:
ww_dfu is the transport half of an update. What it carries, and the code that checks and applies it on the device, is chunky (chunky_mcu_updater, public).

  • SPEC.md is the protocol in octets (a draft): the records, the receiver's checks in order, delivery modes, resume and segmentation, with annotated vectors. Its §10 describes this carrier.
  • chunky_format/src/lib.rs defines the records. They are shrink_wrap types with a fixed little endian layout, and the same bytes are read by Rust (with or without BufReader) and by a generated C reader:
    • Descriptor (CKY2): a 64-byte body (product, version, security counter, image length, geometry, SHA-256 of the image) and a 64-byte seal over a domain string and exactly the body's bytes. The scheme is Ed25519, or SHA-256 only for an unsigned build, which a signed device refuses.
    • Plan (CKP2): a 145-byte header (geometry, step count, body length, the descriptor), then the steps. A step is a head_tail enum read through Step::view: ERASE is 3 bytes, COPY 13, WRITE 13 plus one chunk.
    • Manifest (CKM2): a 13-byte header and one entry per chunk, a hash (8 bytes of SHA-256), blank or unreadable.
  • chunky/src/apply.rs is the apply engine: it runs an untrusted plan against the DFU slot over embedded_storage, one step per call, checking the descriptor first, then every COPY source and WRITE hash, then the whole image.

The raw octets are these records: Stage::begin and StageBulk::begin_bulk take the 145 header bytes, Stage::write carries one step's data, and the StageBulk::plan sink carries the body as segments. What a node answers with Error::BadSignature, BelowFloor, WrongGeometry or VerifyFailed is what chunky decides; WrongGeometry is what chunky and the spec call GeometryMismatch.

Status. Chunky does not implement the ww_dfu traits yet (chunky NET-1 is open): it is the device core and the record format that ww_dfu carries, and the server side that exposes them as UpdateNode, Stage and the rest is to come. Until then the exchanges on this page are recorded with the stand-in plan above.

The code of the API itself: ww_stdlib/ww_dfu/src/lib.rs.

items.title: ww_error
items.text:
Errors every API can return (STD-16): Unsupported, InUse, Busy, ... look the same in every crate, generic host code handles them without knowing the crate, and tools recognise them by their type. An API crate nests them as one #[common] Common(CommonError) variant of its own error enum (see below and Errors).

wire_weaver re-exports the crate: wire_weaver::prelude has CommonError, CommonErrorOwned (with std) and HasCommon, so an API crate needs no dependency of its own.

items.title: CommonError
items.text:
Variant Message (its doc line) When Unsupported Not supported by this device (a mode, a range, a feature of the call). The device knows the call, and can't do what was asked. InvalidArgument { arg: u8, reason } Argument number {arg} is invalid: {reason}. arg counts from 0. InUse { by } In use by {by}. A resource another function holds ("USART2"). Busy Busy with another operation, try again later. WrongState { reason } Not possible in the current state: {reason}. NoPower { rail } No power on {rail}. A missing supply or IO level ("VIO"). Refused { reason } Refused: {reason}. Possible, but the device won't (locked, a policy). Timeout Timed out. Fault { code: u32 } Hardware fault {code:#x}. Device-specific code.

Strings are bounded (reason 64 bytes, by 32, rail 16) and may be empty: a device that saves flash sends "", and the message leaves the part out (Refused). CommonError is an Unsized enum, so it ends in Unknown(u32) (SW-47): a variant added in a newer ww_error reaches an older host as Unknown(n), not as a decode error.

Unsupported is not the framework's Unimplemented: that one means the device has no implementation at all (a handler returning Unimplemented, an item left out), and stays a framework error.

Display and core::error::Error are implemented for both types, the message is the variant's doc line with its fields filled in, without the final period: In use by USART2.

items.title: In an API's error enum
items.text:
Put CommonError first, marked #[common], and keep the crate's own variants for what a tool or a caller should act on specifically (Nack, UnsupportedSpeed with the range):

use wire_weaver::prelude::*;

#[ww_trait]
trait Sensor {
    fn read() -> Result<u16, SensorError<'i>>;
    /// An error enum of its own isn't needed when only common errors can happen.
    fn calibrate() -> Result<(), CommonError<'i>>;
}

#[derive_shrink_wrap(owned(feature = "std"), derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq, Clone), ww_repr = unib32)]
pub enum SensorError<'i> {
    #[common]
    Common(CommonError<'i>),
    /// The sensor did not answer.
    Nack,
}

#[common] makes #[derive_shrink_wrap] add, for the borrowed and the owned type:

  • From<CommonError<'i>> for SensorError<'i> (From<CommonErrorOwned> for SensorErrorOwned): a helper returns CommonError and is ?-ed into the error of any crate.
  • HasCommon with fn common(&self) -> Option<&CommonError>: generic code gets the common part of any crate's error.

One variant per enum can be #[common], and it has exactly one unnamed field. On the wire a common error takes two discriminants (Common, then the CommonError variant), 4 bits more than a variant of the crate's own.

items.title: Device side
items.text:
fn claim(&mut self) -> Result<(), CommonError<'static>> {
    if self.uart_active {
        return Err(CommonError::InUse { by: MaxLen::new_unchecked("USART2") });
    }
    Ok(())
}

fn sample(&mut self) -> Result<u16, SensorError<'static>> {
    self.claim()?; // CommonError into SensorError
    Ok(self.adc.read())
}

fn read(&mut self, _cx: &mut Context<'_, impl BlockingEventOut>) -> RpcResult<Result<u16, SensorError<'_>>> {
    Ready(self.sample())
}

items.title: Host side
items.text:
fn is_retryable<E: HasCommon<Common = CommonErrorOwned>>(e: &E) -> bool {
    matches!(e.common(), Some(CommonErrorOwned::Busy | CommonErrorOwned::Timeout))
}

tests/common_error runs these through a generated server, the generated client and the dynamic client.

items.title: Which errors a method returns
items.text:
#[errors(..)] on a method lists the variants it actually returns, checked against the error enum when the trait is parsed: an unknown or repeated name is a compile error pointing at that name, not the whole attribute (see Errors for the full mechanics — the model, the client check, the evolution checker). For the #[common] variant, name just the CommonError cases that apply, or leave them out for all of them:

#[errors(Common(Busy, NoPower, Timeout), NoSuchChannel)]
fn read(channel: u8) -> Result<Reading, AdcError<'i>>;

#[errors(Common)]
fn calibrate() -> Result<(), CommonError<'i>>;
  • Common(Busy, NoPower, Timeout) — only those three CommonError variants, plus the crate's own NoSuchChannel.
  • Common alone — any CommonError variant.
  • An error enum with no #[common] case lists only its own variants: #[errors(WrongAddress, Refused)].
  • When the error type is CommonError directly (no crate enum around it, as ww_indication::Indication::identify returns Result<(), CommonError<'i>>), the list names CommonError's own variants without nesting: #[errors(Unsupported, Busy)].

items.title: What it does
items.text:
The list changes neither the type nor the wire: it is metadata in the API model, and from there:

  • a # Errors section, one line per entry with the variant's own doc comment (its first line, without the final period; any CommonError for Common alone) — on the trait's own rustdoc (wire_weaver::api_doc) and on the generated client's method;
  • introspection: ww api tree -t, ww introspect and Python's help() show the same list next to the method;
  • the evolution checker: a changed #[errors(..)] list is reported as a compatible change (nothing on the wire moves, and the device never checks it), but worded so the reviewer sees which variants a client of the old list would warn about;
  • a check on the client: a device replying with a variant outside the method's list logs a tracing warning ('<resource>' returned <value>, which is not in its #[errors(..)]). wire_weaver_client::set_strict_error_lists(true) turns it into a panic instead, for the whole process; the tests_common end-to-end harness turns it on, so a device that breaks its own contract fails in CI, not in the field.

A method without #[errors(..)] may return any variant of its error enum; nothing checks it, and clients get no # Errors section for it.

The same list goes on the two other items that return errors, with the same meaning and outputs:

  • a stream function (#[stream(..)] fn, API-31): the list is about the Err of its Result, the answer to opening the stream (ww_adc::AdcStream::samples, ww_i2c::I2cMonitor::records);
  • a property! with an error type: one list above the property!, about that type. A property has one error type for reading and writing (GetResult<T, E>, SetResult<E>), so one list covers both (ww_gpio::Pin::pull, ww_log::LogText::level, ww_user_info::UserInfo::name).
#[errors(NoSuchChannel, Common(InvalidArgument, Unsupported, Busy, InUse, NoPower))]
#[stream(SampleBlock<'i>, counted)]
fn samples(config: StreamConfig<'i>) -> Result<StreamActual, AdcError<'i>>;

#[errors(TooLong, Common(Busy, Fault))]
property!(rw name: MaxLen<&'i str, MAX_NAME_LEN>, UserInfoError<'i>);

A plain stream!, a sink!, a const and ww_impl! have no error to list, #[errors(..)] on them is a compile error.

items.title: Real examples
items.text:
ww_adc::Adc::read lists three CommonError cases plus the crate's own NoSuchChannel:

#[errors(Common(Busy, NoPower, Timeout), NoSuchChannel)]
fn read(channel: u8) -> Result<Reading, AdcError<'i>>;

ww_adc::AdcCapture::capture lists five:

#[errors(
    Common(InvalidArgument, Unsupported, Busy, InUse, NoPower),
    NoSuchChannel
)]
fn capture(config: CaptureConfig<'i>) -> Result<CaptureActual, AdcError<'i>>;

ww_memory::Memory::write_many has no Common(..) nesting, only the crate's own variants alongside one common one:

#[errors(WrongAddress, Common(Refused))]
fn write_many(addr: u8, data: RefVec<'i, u8>) -> Result<(), MemoryError<'i>>;

items.title: Tools
items.text:
Tools recognise ww_error::CommonError by its type in the API model (crate ww_error, any version), also when a device left its definition out because it is known from the snapshots (ww_self::TypeOwned::is_common_error, ValueOwned::common_error).

  • Python: RemoteError.common holds the common error ({"InUse": {"by": "USART2"}}, "Busy"), None for an error of the API's own; .value the whole error as before. The message is the doc line: read() returned an error: In use by USART2.
  • ww CLI: ww api tree -t and ww introspect -t mark the type and the variants holding it as common errors.

items.title: ww_firmware_info
items.text:
ww_firmware_info answers two questions about any device: which firmware is this (FirmwareInfo) and why did it last reset (LastReset). It is no_std by default; std adds the owned types and every architecture's fault record.

[dependencies]
ww_firmware_info = { version = "0.1", default-features = false, features = ["build-id", "cortex-m"] }

[build-dependencies]
ww_firmware_info = { version = "0.1", features = ["build"] }

items.title: FirmwareInfo
items.text:
#[ww_trait]
pub trait FirmwareInfo {
    const FIRMWARE: FirmwareSummary<'i>;
    const BUILD_ID: MaxLen<RefVec<'i, u8>, 32>;
    #[optional]
    const BUILD_RECORD: MaxLen<RefVec<'i, u8>, 512>;
}
  • FIRMWARE - name, ww_version::Version, git commit (20 bytes) and dirty flag, build time and profile. A host prints b200_usb_io 0.5.0 (a1b2c3d-dirty, built 3 Oct 2026 18:20) from it, as our CLIs print --version.
  • BUILD_ID - the GNU build id of the image. It is the firmware's identity: the linker hashes the linked output, so it changes with every byte of code, unlike a git commit (dirty builds, two profiles of one commit) or a version. A host finds the firmware's ELF by it, which defmt logs, cnt counters and crash records need. Empty when the firmware did not keep the note.
  • BUILD_RECORD - the bedrock_build_info compact record as stored in flash (crate features, dependencies, compiler, target); the full one is in the ELF only. Optional: leave it out with omit = ["firmware.BUILD_RECORD"].

All three are const items: they do not change while the firmware runs, a server provides them without handlers and a host reads each once per connection. FIRMWARE and BUILD_RECORD are Rust consts, BUILD_ID is known at link time only, so it is a fn (const_model = "BUILD_ID=fn"); ww api scaffold prints the impl with the exact names.

items.title: Producing the summary
items.text:
build.rs calls ww_firmware_info::build::emit() (feature build, std, no extra crates). It runs git rev-parse HEAD and git status --porcelain, reads the package name and version from Cargo, uses SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH as the build time when set (reproducible builds) and sets WW_FW_* variables with cargo:rustc-env. It asks Cargo to rerun when .git/HEAD or .git/index changes. firmware_summary!() builds the value at compile time, for firmware: FirmwareInfo in the API root Device:

impl api_impl::DeviceConsts for Server {
    const FIRMWARE_FIRMWARE: FirmwareSummary<'static> = ww_firmware_info::firmware_summary!();

    fn firmware_build_id(&self) -> MaxLen<RefVec<'_, u8>, BUILD_ID_MAX_LEN> {
        MaxLen::new_unchecked(RefVec::new_bytes(ww_firmware_info::build_id()))
    }

    const FIRMWARE_BUILD_RECORD: MaxLen<RefVec<'static, u8>, 512> = /* bedrock's COMPACT record */;
}

Outside git the commit is empty and git is None. Strings are cut at their bounds.

items.title: Build id
items.text:
Ask the linker for the note and keep it in flash:

# .cargo/config.toml
[target.thumbv8m.main-none-eabihf]
rustflags = ["-C", "link-arg=--build-id=sha1"]

/* memory.x */
SECTIONS {
  .note.gnu.build-id : ALIGN(4) {
    __build_id_start = .;
    KEEP(*(.note.gnu.build-id))
    __build_id_end = .;
  } > FLASH
} INSERT AFTER .rodata;

With the build-id feature, ww_firmware_info::build_id() returns the bytes of the note between the two symbols (parse_build_id_note does the parsing and is available everywhere, for hosts reading an ELF's section).

items.title: LastReset
items.text:
#[ww_trait]
pub trait LastReset {
    fn last_reset() -> ResetRecord<'i>;
    fn boot_count() -> u32;
    fn clear();
}

ResetRecord has the cause (PowerOn, Brownout, Pin, Watchdog, Software, Lockup, Fault, Panic, Updated, Undetermined), the build_id of the firmware that crashed (the record may be older than an update), uptime at the crash, the architecture's fault registers, up to 32 words of stack, a message of up to 128 bytes and boots_since_crash (0: the last reset was the crash; a crash kept across later normal resets shows a cause other than Fault / Panic and a count above 0). boot_count with the cause tells a reset loop from a single crash; clear forgets both once the host saved them. Capturing the record (a fault or panic handler writing into RAM that survives a reset) is firmware infrastructure; this trait only reports it.

Fault has one variant per architecture behind a cargo feature: CortexM(CortexMFault) (cortex-m) and RiscV(RiscVFault) (riscv); std enables all. A variant keeps its number whether it is compiled in or not (see #[cfg] on enum variants), so firmware enables the one it needs and a host all of them. At least one must be enabled for ResetRecord to be usable.

items.title: Evolution
items.text: Everything is evolvable: FirmwareSummary, ResetRecord and the enums can grow with #[default] fields and new variants. Hosts print Unknown causes as numbers.

items.title: ww_gpio
items.text:
ww_gpio is a global WireWeaver trait for controlling GPIO pins remotely: reading and setting output levels, reading input levels (one pin, or several at one instant), configuring pin mode / pull / drive strength, and observing edge events as a stream. It is no_std by default and depends only on wire_weaver and ww_si (for the Volt IO level).

Add it to a device API crate with:

[dependencies]
ww_gpio = "0.1"

items.title: Traits
items.text: GPIO pins are grouped into banks (ports), mirroring how most MCUs expose GPIO in hardware. Both levels are traits, so they compose with the rest of the API using ww_impl! and can be nested as arrays.

items.title: Bank
items.text:
One bank (port) of pins sharing the same IO level:

#[ww_trait]
trait Bank {
    ww_impl!(pin[]: Pin);

    fn read_inputs(
        pins: MaxLen<RefVec<'i, UNib32>, MAX_PORT_PINS>,
    ) -> Result<MaxLen<RefVec<'i, Level>, MAX_PORT_PINS>, GpioError<'i>>;
    fn write_outputs(levels: MaxLen<RefVec<'i, PinLevel>, MAX_PORT_PINS>) -> Result<(), GpioError<'i>>;

    reserved!(3..=7);

    fn capabilities() -> BankCapabilities<'i>;

    fn configure(config: BankConfig) -> Result<BankConfig, Error>;

    fn name() -> &'i str;
}
  • pin[] - array of individual pins in the bank, indexed 0-based; see Pin below. Indexing can either follow the natural range of a bank (e.g. an IO expander) or a list of specific indices (e.g. exposing only PB1 and PB5 of an MCU port).
  • read_inputs / write_outputs - several pins in one call, at one instant where the hardware allows, see Port access below.
  • capabilities() - static description of what the bank supports: which IO levels, modes and custom mode/pull/speed strings, see BankCapabilities under Types below.
  • configure - what the pins of the bank share, in a BankConfig: the IO level, adjustable if the hardware has level translators (io_level: None leaves it as it is). Answers with what was actually set, so configure with None reads the level in effect. Same shape as the configure of ww_uart, ww_i2c, ww_spi.
  • name() - user-friendly bank name (e.g. "PA").

items.title: Pin
items.text:
One pin of a bank. Commonly used operations (set_output_level, toggle, output_level, input_level) are defined first, to get more compact resource paths since low path indices take fewer bits on the wire (see traits):

#[ww_trait]
pub trait Pin {
    fn set_output_level(level: Level);
    fn toggle();
    fn output_level() -> Level;
    fn input_level() -> Level;

    #[stream(IoPinEvent, counted)]
    fn event(enabled: IoPinEnabledEvents<'i>) -> Result<(), Error>;

    fn set_mode(mode: Mode, initial: Option<Level>) -> Result<(), Error>;
    fn mode() -> Mode;

    property!(rw pull: Pull, Error);
    property!(rw speed: Speed, Error);

    fn capabilities() -> PinCapabilities<'i>;
}
  • set_output_level / toggle / output_level - control and read back the pin's output register. If the pin is currently an input, these still act on the output register without changing pin mode.
  • input_level - reads the input register. If the pin is configured as output and its input buffer is disabled, the current output level should be returned instead.
  • event - a counted stream function of IoPinEvents (rising/falling edge, custom sources): the host opens it with the sources to report (Common(Unsupported) for one the pin can't generate) and closes it to stop. Its unit is an event: the event head carries the device time of each edge and exactly how many edges the device dropped (stream delivery).
  • set_mode / mode - switch between push-pull, open-drain, input, high-z, analog or a custom mode, optionally setting the initial output level before the switch. Can fail with Common(Unsupported), or DifferentModes on a bank whose pins share one mode.
  • pull - pull resistor configuration, can fail with Common(Unsupported).
  • speed - drive strength/slew rate, can fail with Common(Unsupported).
  • capabilities() - what this pin supports: modes, pulls, speeds, whether event works, and its name, see PinCapabilities under Types below.

items.title: Port access
items.text:
Bank::read_inputs and Bank::write_outputs act on several pins of a bank in one call, for what per-pin calls can't do even when the client packs them into one packet: change or sample them at the same instant. A host bit-banging a parallel bus sets the data lines and the strobe in one write, or reads a data byte without a pin changing halfway through it.

  • read_inputs(pins) - the input levels of the listed pins (indices into pin[]), answered in the same order. Reads the input register like Pin::input_level, whatever mode a pin is in.
  • write_outputs(levels) - a list of PinLevel { pin, level }. Writes the output register like Pin::set_output_level: no pin changes its mode (direction), an input keeps the level for when it becomes an output. All or nothing: an index that isn't a pin of the bank, or a pin listed twice, is Common(InvalidArgument) and nothing is written; InUse, NoPower and Refused as for Pin::set_mode.

BankCapabilities::simultaneous_read / simultaneous_write say whether a call is one register access. If so, every listed pin is sampled or changes at the same instant (an STM32 port: one IDR read, one BSRR write). If not (an IO expander behind I2C, pins spread over several registers), the device goes pin by pin in list order, still in one request: list the strobe last. A bank without either answers Common(Unsupported).

Pins are addressed by index, not by a bitmask, as everywhere in the IO family: indices work the same for a bank exposing only some pins of a port (PB1, PB5) and for banks wider than any mask type. On the wire an index of a pin below 8 is one nibble, a level one bit, so for 8 pins the argument of read_inputs is 5 bytes and its list of levels 2, and the argument of write_outputs (one byte per PinLevel) 9. At most MAX_PORT_PINS (64) pins per call.

let bank = device.port(0);
if bank.capabilities().call().await?.simultaneous_write {
    // data lines 0..=3 and the strobe on pin 4, in one register write
    let levels = [(0, Level::High), (1, Level::Low), (2, Level::Low), (3, Level::High), (4, Level::High)]
        .into_iter()
        .map(|(pin, level)| PinLevel { pin: UNib32(pin), level })
        .collect::<Vec<_>>();
    bank.write_outputs(MaxLen::new(levels)?).call().await?;
}
let levels = bank.read_inputs(MaxLen::new(vec![UNib32(5), UNib32(6)])?).call().await?;

Timing of many pins beyond one write (a pattern, a waveform) is a signal generator, fast sampling of many pins a logic analyzer.

items.title: Observing a pin level (planned)
items.text: A property!(ro+observe level: Level) on Pin, at one of its reserved indices 4..=6, would let a host watch slow inputs without opening the event stream of every pin. It waits for array index bounds (API-29): Pin sits in the Bank::pin[] array, and observed properties under a resource array aren't supported yet (STD-31).

items.title: Types
items.text:
• Level - Low / High, sized, 1 bit on the wire.
  • Mode - PushPullOutput, OpenDrainOutput, Input, HighZ (like Input but may disable the input buffer to save power), Analog, Custom(u8); sized, 1 nibble.
  • Pull - None, Up, Down, Custom(u8); sized, 2 bits.
  • Speed - Slow, Medium, Fast, VeryFast, Custom(u8); sized, 1 nibble.
  • IoPinEvent - RisingEdge, FallingEdge, Custom(u8); sized, 2 bits.
  • GpioError<'i> - Common(CommonError) (common errors), DifferentModes; unsized (unib32 discriminant), evolvable, Display from the doc lines. Each method lists the variants it returns (#[errors]).
  • PinLevel - pin: UNib32 (index into Bank::pin[]), level: Level; one entry of Bank::write_outputs, final_structure.
  • IoPinEnabledEvents<'i> - which sources the event stream reports, its argument: rising: bool, falling: bool, and a custom: RefVec<'i, u8> list of custom source indices.
  • PinCapabilities<'i> - what one pin supports: modes: MaxLen<RefVec<'i, Mode>, 8>, pulls: MaxLen<RefVec<'i, Pull>, 4>, speeds: MaxLen<RefVec<'i, Speed>, 5>, events: bool (the event stream works on this pin), name: MaxLen<&'i str, 16> (e.g. "IO4", "PB5").
  • BankConfig - io_level: Option<Volt>; the argument and the answer of Bank::configure.
  • BankCapabilities<'i> - what a bank supports: io_levels: MaxLen<RefVec<'i, Volt>, MAX_IO_LEVELS>, io_level_min / io_level_max: Option<Volt> (an adjustable supply), push_pull / open_drain / input / individually_configurable_pins: bool, custom_mode / custom_pull / custom_speed: RefVec<'i, &'i str> describing any Custom(u8) variants, and simultaneous_read / simultaneous_write: bool (port access, false when an older device leaves them out).

Level and Mode also carry small helpers: Level::is_high() / is_low(), Mode::is_driving() (true for PushPullOutput and OpenDrainOutput).

All enums and structs are behind #[derive_shrink_wrap] with owned(feature = "std") and cfg_attr_borrowed(feature = "defmt", derive(defmt::Format)), so owned (*Owned) variants and defmt::Format are available by enabling the crate's std / defmt features.

items.title: Composing into a device API
items.text:
A device exposes one or more banks by implementing Bank as an array on its API root, see the examples/all_gpio_api crate:

#[ww_api_root]
pub trait AllGpioApi {
    ww_impl!(port[]: ww_gpio::Bank);
}

Because Bank itself contains pin[]: Pin, resources end up two levels deep and addressed by a [bank_index, pin_index] pair, e.g. port(0).pin(5).

items.title: Client usage (examples/all_gpio)
items.text:
The generated client wraps wire_weaver_client::Commander; see examples/all_gpio/src/lib.rs for the small AllGpio wrapper type. A few usage patterns from examples/all_gpio/examples:

Enumerate banks and pins, and read a bank's capabilities (info.rs):

let device = AllGpio::new().connect().await?;

let available_ports = device.port_valid_indices().read().await?;
for port_idx in available_ports.iter() {
    let name = device.port(port_idx).name().call().await?;
    let available_pins = device.port(port_idx).pin_valid_indices().read().await?;
    println!("Port {port_idx}: name: '{name}', pins: {available_pins:?}");
}

let capabilities = device.port(0).capabilities().call().await?;

Read every pin's mode sequentially (mode.rs) - simple, but one round trip per call:

for port in ports.iter() {
    for pin in 0..=15 {
        let mode = device.port(port).pin(pin).mode().call().await?;
    }
}

The same, but firing all calls concurrently with futures::future::join_all (mode_parallel.rs) - independent requests get assembled into as few USB packets as possible by the client, giving a large speedup (940ms -> 55ms on USB Full Speed in this example, 361ms -> 38ms on High Speed) without changing anything server-side:

let modes = (0..=15)
    .map(|pin| device.port(port).pin(pin).mode().call())
    .collect::<Vec<_>>();
let modes = join_all(modes).await;

mode_mega_parallel.rs takes this further, flattening the bank/pin loop into a single join_all over every pin of every bank at once, for the best-case latency (17ms on USB High Speed in this example).

items.title: MCU server implementation (examples_mcu/nucleo_h743zi2/src/bin/all_gpio.rs)
items.text:
On the device side, ww_codegen! generates the dispatch code and leaves the actual register access to hand-written methods on the server state:

struct ServerState {
    bank: [Gpio; 11],
}

mod server_impl {
    wire_weaver::ww_codegen!(
        all_gpio_api :: AllGpioApi for super::ServerState,
        server = true, no_alloc = true, use_async = true,
        method_model = "_=immediate",
        property_model = "_=get_set",
        introspect = "no_docs",
    );
}

Each resource path becomes an async method named after the flattened path, e.g. port_pin_set_output_level, get_port_pin_pull / set_port_pin_pull (property get/set), or port_pin_event / close_port_pin_event (the stream opened with its sources, closed). The [bank_index, pin_index] addressing is passed in as index: [UNib32; 2]:

async fn port_pin_set_output_level(
    &mut self,
    _cx: &mut Context<'_, impl EventOut>,
    index: [UNib32; 2],
    level: Level,
) -> RpcResult<()> {
    let bank_idx = index[0].0 as usize;
    let pin_idx = index[1].0 as usize;
    let odr = self.bank[bank_idx].odr();
    let level = if level == Level::High { Odr::HIGH } else { Odr::LOW };
    odr.modify(|o| o.set_odr(pin_idx, level));
    Ready(())
}

Which indices are valid is reported through wire_weaver::ValidIndices, driving what port_valid_indices() / pin_valid_indices() return on the client:

fn valid_indices_root_port(&mut self) -> ValidIndices<'_> {
    ValidIndices::range_u32(0..self.bank.len() as u32)
}

fn valid_indices_root_port_pin(&mut self, index: [UNib32; 1]) -> ValidIndices<'_> {
    ValidIndices::range_u32(0..16)
}

port_read_inputs reads IDR once and picks the listed pins from it, port_write_outputs collects every entry into one BSRR value (set and reset bits) and writes it once, so the board reports simultaneous_read and simultaneous_write.

In this example, capabilities() and configure are hardcoded (3.3V without level control, push-pull/open-drain/input all supported, no custom modes), set_mode/mode and pull/speed are translated to/from the STM32 MODER / OTYPER / PUPDR / OSPEEDR registers, and the event stream never opens (port_pin_event answers Common(Unsupported), one Counted state serves every pin) since the example does not wire up EXTI interrupts.

items.title: ww_i2c
items.text:
ww_i2c is a global WireWeaver trait family for an I2C bus reachable through a device: a USB adapter, a dev board, or an instrument. A host can configure the bus, run write/read/transaction calls against a slave address, scan the bus, see and recover stuck lines, let the device poll a few registers on its own (I2cWatch), or watch every transaction on the bus without taking part in it (I2cMonitor). It is no_std by default and depends only on wire_weaver and ww_si (for the Second and Volt reference types).

Add it to a device API crate with:

[dependencies]
ww_i2c = "0.1"

items.title: Traits
I2c
items.text:
The most common call of a register-based sensor driver is a write-read: i2c_read with I2cReadKind::RepeatedStart (register address out, data in, one transaction). Several calls in one round trip are a multi-call of the client, not a method here - use i2c_transaction when the device itself must do several operations without releasing the bus in between (repeated starts).

#[ww_trait]
pub trait I2c {
    fn i2c_capabilities() -> I2cCapabilities<'i>;
    fn i2c_configure(config: I2cConfig) -> Result<I2cConfig, I2cError>;
    fn i2c_write(addr: I2cAddress, data: MaxLen<RefVec<'i, u8>, MAX_WRITE_LEN>, delay_after: Option<Second>)
        -> Result<I2cTransactionTimeRange, I2cError>;
    fn i2c_read(addr: I2cAddress, kind: I2cReadKind<'i>, len: u16, delay_after: Option<Second>)
        -> Result<I2cReadEnvelope<'i>, I2cError>;
    fn i2c_scan() -> Result<MaxLen<RefVec<'i, u8>, MAX_SCAN>, I2cError>;
    fn i2c_transaction(addr: I2cAddress, ops: MaxLen<RefVec<'i, I2cOp<'i>>, MAX_OPS>)
        -> Result<I2cTransactionResult<'i>, I2cError>;
    fn i2c_lines_state() -> I2cLinesState;
    fn i2c_wiggle_clock(count: u8) -> Result<I2cLinesState, I2cError>;
    fn i2c_set_pullups(enabled: bool) -> Result<(), I2cError>;
    fn i2c_pullups() -> bool;
}
  • i2c_capabilities - static description of what the adapter supports: modes, frequency range, IO levels, buffer sizes, 10-bit addresses, pull-ups, bus recovery; see I2cCapabilities under Types.
  • i2c_configure - sets the bus mode and, on adapters with level translators, the bus voltage, in one I2cConfig (io_level: None leaves the level as it is); answers with what was actually set: the SCL frequency the hardware settled on (never above the one asked for) and the IO level in effect.
  • i2c_write - start, address, data, stop; delay_after makes the next transfer to the same address wait (an EEPROM page write needs ~5 ms) while transfers to other addresses go ahead meanwhile.
  • i2c_read - plain read, or a register read (write a few bytes, repeated start, read) through I2cReadKind.
  • i2c_scan - 7-bit addresses that acknowledged a one-byte read, ascending, skipping the reserved ranges (0x00..=0x07, 0x78..=0x7F).
  • i2c_transaction - several I2cOp writes/reads to one address with repeated starts in between and one stop at the end, like embedded_hal::i2c::I2c::transaction; the bytes of all reads come back concatenated, in order.
  • i2c_lines_state - levels of SCL and SDA now; both high on an idle bus, a line held low means a slave stuck mid-byte, missing/unpowered pull-ups, or a short.
  • i2c_wiggle_clock - clocks SCL up to count times (9 is enough for any stuck byte) until SDA is released, then sends a stop; returns the line levels afterwards (bus recovery).
  • i2c_set_pullups / i2c_pullups - the adapter's own pull-up resistors on SCL and SDA, on adapters that have switchable ones (see I2cCapabilities::pullups).

items.title: I2cWatch
items.text:
Autonomous reads: the device repeats configured reads on its own and reports only what the host asked for (every result, a change under a mask, or a mask/value match starting or stopping), so the host doesn't have to poll over the link. A device implementing it also implements I2c (it needs a master). Host transactions have priority: the device runs a watch read only when no host transaction is waiting, so host calls are spliced in between autonomous ones and see no more delay than one watch read.

#[ww_trait]
pub trait I2cWatch {
    #[counted]
    stream!(changes: I2cWatchEvent<'i>);
    fn watch_capabilities() -> I2cWatchCapabilities;
    fn watch_add(watch: I2cWatchConfig<'i>) -> Result<u32, I2cError>;
    fn watch_modify(slot: u32, watch: I2cWatchConfig<'i>) -> Result<(), I2cError>;
    fn watch_remove(slot: u32) -> Result<(), I2cError>;
    fn watch_list() -> MaxLen<RefVec<'i, u32>, MAX_WATCHES>;
}
  • watch_add / watch_modify / watch_remove / watch_list - manage watch slots (at most I2cWatchCapabilities::max_watches, see Types); modifying a watch forgets its previous result, so the next read is always reported.
  • changes - results, in the order the watches were read, as I2cWatchEvent. A counted stream (unit: result): the host opens it by calling it, the event head carries when each read started and how many results the device dropped (stream delivery).

I2cWatchReport (part of I2cWatchConfig) decides when a result is worth a report:

  • Always - every read.
  • Changed { mask } - when data & mask differs from the previous reported read's (mask as long as the read; all-ones to see any change).
  • Matches { bytes } - when data[i] & bytes[i].mask == bytes[i].value for every byte starts or stops being true (an alert bit set, a status reaching a state) - a transition, not every read while it holds. One I2cMatchByte { mask, value } per byte read, two bytes each on the wire; a mask of 0x00 ignores that byte.

An error is reported once, when the watch starts to fail, and the next successful read is reported unconditionally whatever the rule - and that recovery read becomes the new baseline, so a later unchanged read goes quiet again instead of being reported a second time. tests/io_i2c exercises all three rules plus this error/recovery sequence end to end against a mock server.

items.title: I2cMonitor
items.text:
Watches the bus without taking part: every transaction becomes one I2cRecord on the records stream. The same function as I2cMode::MonitorOnly (or the monitor flag of I2cMode::Master, to watch the adapter's own transfers too), for devices that only sniff and implement no I2c.

#[ww_trait]
pub trait I2cMonitor {
    #[stream(I2cRecord<'i>, counted)]
    fn records(io_level: Option<Volt>) -> Result<(), I2cError>;
}

records is a counted stream function: opening it starts monitoring (at io_level, as in I2cConfig; the adapter's pull-ups stay as they are, the watched bus has its own), closing it stops. Its unit is a transaction: the event head carries the time of each start condition and exactly how many records the device dropped and where (stream delivery).

items.title: Addresses
items.text: I2cAddress is 7-bit (0x50 for a 24C02 EEPROM, not 0xA0) or 10-bit, as in the I2C specification and embedded-hal (SevenBitAddress / TenBitAddress): I2cAddress::seven(0x50), I2cAddress::ten(0x350), both returning None above the respective range. It is bit-packed (SW-48, sub-byte fields): a 7-bit address takes one byte on the wire, exactly as a plain u8 would, and a 10-bit one 11 bits (2 bytes) - ww_i2c's own test suite checks both sizes against a real to_ww_bytes() call. An adapter without 10-bit support answers Common(Unsupported) (see I2cCapabilities::ten_bit_addresses). i2c_scan still only returns 7-bit addresses (a 10-bit scan is rarely useful and would need 1024 single-byte reads).

items.title: Sizes
items.text: Every byte buffer is bounded (MAX_WRITE_LEN, MAX_READ_LEN, MAX_WRITE_READ_LEN, MAX_OPS, MAX_SCAN, MAX_RECORD_LEN, MAX_WATCHES, MAX_WATCH_LEN, MAX_NAME_LEN, MAX_IO_LEVELS), so a device knows the largest request it has to take and the largest reply it has to build at compile time. A device may support less: its limits are in I2cCapabilities / I2cWatchCapabilities. Raising a bound later is a compatible change, lowering it is not (see evolution rules).

items.title: Time
items.text: Every transfer reports when it started and ended (I2cTransactionTimeRange), and every monitor record and watch result when it happened (the time in the event head of its counted stream), as ww_si::Seconds of device time: time since the device's clock started, in the prefix and number type the device picks (usually a u32 of microseconds). A fixed-width value wraps (a u32 of µs every 71.6 minutes) and the host unwraps it. All timestamps of one device come from the same clock, so I2C transfers line up with the device's other data.

items.title: Types
items.text:
• I2cConfig - mode: I2cMode, io_level: Option<Volt>; the argument and the answer of i2c_configure.
  • I2cMode - Disabled (pins released), Master { speed: Hertz, monitor }, Slave { addr, monitor } (data paths for slave mode are not defined yet), MonitorOnly.
  • I2cReadKind<'i> - Plain (start, address+read, len bytes, stop) or RepeatedStart { write } (start, address+write, write, repeated start, address+read, len bytes, stop), bounded by MAX_WRITE_READ_LEN.
  • I2cOp<'i> - Write(MaxLen<RefVec<'i, u8>, MAX_WRITE_LEN>) or Read(u16), one operation of i2c_transaction.
  • I2cTransactionTimeRange - start / end: Second (start and stop condition).
  • I2cReadEnvelope<'i> - duration: I2cTransactionTimeRange, data: MaxLen<RefVec<'i, u8>, MAX_READ_LEN>.
  • I2cTransactionResult<'i> - duration, read (every I2cOp::Read's bytes, concatenated in order).
  • I2cLinesState - is_scl_high / is_sda_high: bool, scl / sda: Option<Volt> (measured level, where the adapter can).
  • I2cCapabilities<'i> - io_levels, io_level_min / io_level_max, max_write_len, max_read_len, min_freq / max_freq: Hertz, driver_name (bounded by MAX_NAME_LEN), master_supported / slave_supported / monitor_supported, ten_bit_addresses, pullups, bus_recovery.
  • I2cWatchCapabilities - max_watches: u32 (at most MAX_WATCHES, 512), max_len (at most MAX_WATCH_LEN), min_period.
  • I2cWatchConfig<'i> - addr, kind: I2cReadKind<'i>, len, period: Second, report: I2cWatchReport<'i>.
  • I2cWatchReport<'i> - Always, Changed { mask }, Matches { bytes }, see I2cWatch above.
  • I2cMatchByte - mask, value: u8, one byte of a Matches rule; sized, two bytes.
  • I2cWatchEvent<'i> - slot, result: Result<MaxLen<RefVec<'i, u8>, MAX_WATCH_LEN>, I2cError>.
  • I2cRecord<'i> - end: Second (stop or repeated start; the start condition is the head's time), addr, read: bool, kind: I2cRecordKind, nack_at: Option<u16> (index of the first byte not acknowledged, Some(0) = the address), bytes (without the address).
  • I2cRecordKind - Complete, RepeatedStart (the next record continues the transaction), Truncated (more than MAX_RECORD_LEN bytes), BusError.
  • I2cError<'i> - Common(CommonError) (common errors), then Nack, Arbitration, Bus, Crc, Overrun, BufferTooBig, OutOfWatchSlots, InvalidWatchSlot; unsized (unib32 discriminant), evolvable, Display from the doc lines (see below).

All enums and structs are behind #[derive_shrink_wrap] with owned(feature = "std") and cfg_attr_borrowed(feature = "defmt", derive(defmt::Format)), so owned (*Owned) variants and defmt::Format are available by enabling the crate's std / defmt features.

items.title: Errors
items.text:
Every trait returns I2cError: CommonError as its #[common] Common variant (unsupported mode or IO level, invalid argument, in use, wrong state, no power, refused, timeout), then what is specific to I2C and a caller acts on: Nack (retry an EEPROM busy with a page write), Arbitration, Bus, Crc, Overrun, BufferTooBig (split the transfer), OutOfWatchSlots, InvalidWatchSlot. Each method lists the variants it returns with #[errors(..)], shown in its rustdoc and checked on the client. The enum is unsized, so a newer device's variant reads as Unknown(n) on an older host instead of failing the call.

match dev.i2c().i2c_write(addr, data.clone(), None).call().await {
    Err(CallError::Device(I2cErrorOwned::Nack)) => { /* not there, or busy */ }
    Err(CallError::Device(e)) if e.common().is_some() => { /* the same handling as for any other crate */ }
    r => { r?; }
}

items.title: Composing into a device API, and testing (tests/io_i2c)
items.text:
A device exposes the traits it implements on its API root, see tests/io_i2c_api:

#[ww_api_root]
pub trait IoI2cTest {
    ww_impl!(i2c: ww_i2c::I2c);
    ww_impl!(i2c_watch: ww_i2c::I2cWatch);
    ww_impl!(i2c_monitor: ww_i2c::I2cMonitor);
}

tests/io_i2c runs a mock server implementing all three traits on ww_device::Server (through tests_common::start_device, the same in-process harness tests/credit_sink and tests/streams use), simulating a tiny bus of addressable byte registers in a shared Model. The generated client drives it through the real host event loop end to end:

  • i2c_write_read_roundtrip, i2c_nack_and_zero_length, i2c_scan_and_lines - I2c write/read/scan/lines/pullups, and the Nack / Common(InvalidArgument) (zero length) error paths.
  • i2c_monitor_records_writes_and_reads - opening I2cMonitor::records turns transactions into I2cRecords on it.
  • i2c_watch_always_reports_every_read, i2c_watch_changed_reports_only_on_change, i2c_watch_matches_reports_on_transition_only, i2c_watch_error_reported_once_then_recovery_always_reports, i2c_watch_modify_remove_and_list - the three I2cWatchReport rules, the error-once-then-recovery sequence, and slot management.

Since nothing drives a real periodic timer in the mock, the test API adds one test-only method, tick_watches() -> u8, that runs a single watch-read cycle on demand (applying I2cWatchReport exactly like a real firmware's polling loop would) and returns how many watches reported - a real device would call the same internal logic from its own timer or event loop instead.

items.title: ww_indication
items.text:
Device indication control (STD-28): one global mode every indicator (LED, buzzer, ...) follows.

#[ww_trait]
pub trait Indication {
    property!(rw mode: Mode);
    #[optional]
    property!(rw brightness: Brightness);
    #[optional]
    fn identify(duration: Second) -> Result<(), CommonError<'i>>;
    #[optional]
    const NAMES: RefVec<'i, &'i str>;
}

mode is the only item a device must implement: AllOff, OnlyEssential (only what must stay visible: faults, power) or Normal. Everything else is optional, each its own item, so a device picks what its hardware or flash budget supports:

  • brightness — one Brightness setting (Lowest .. Highest, 5 levels) for every indicator; a device with no adjustable brightness leaves it out with omit = ["indication.brightness"].
  • identify(duration) — blinks every indicator for duration (a ww_si::Second) so the unit can be found on a bench or in a rack, then returns to mode. Errors on CommonError directly (no indication-specific error): Unsupported without a way to blink, Busy while already identifying.
  • NAMES — indicator names in the device's own order, a const item served without a handler. Left out by a device with no room to keep them.

Mode and Brightness are Unsized (the default): a later version may add a variant (an in-between brightness level, a new mode) without breaking a host built against an older ww_indication, which reads it as Unknown(u32) (SW-47).

tests/indication has two mock servers: one implementing only mode, one with every optional item.

items.title: ww_log
items.text:
ww_log is the log of a device: its defmt frames, decoded on the host with the firmware's ELF (LogDefmt), or text records for firmware without defmt (LogText). Both are reliable streams: the device keeps what it logged until the host has it, also while no host is connected, and tells the host exactly how many messages it dropped and where. It is no_std by default and depends only on wire_weaver.

[dependencies]
ww_log = "0.1"

#[ww_api_root]
pub trait MyDevice {
    ww_impl!(log: ww_log::LogDefmt);
}

The device side of LogDefmt is the ww_defmt_logger crate: the firmware's defmt global logger, which also tees every frame to RTT (see below).

items.title: LogDefmt
items.text:
#[ww_trait]
pub trait LogDefmt {
    const DEFMT: DefmtInfo<'i>;
    #[stream(DefmtFrames<'i>, reliable)]
    fn frames() -> Result<(), LogError<'i>>;
}

pub struct DefmtInfo<'i> {
    pub encoding: DefmtEncoding,                          // Raw, Rzcobs
    pub build_id: MaxLen<RefVec<'i, u8>, 32>,
}
pub struct DefmtFrames<'i> {
    pub bytes: MaxLen<RefVec<'i, u8>, 512>,               // one or more whole frames
}
  • DEFMT - the encoding defmt is built with (its encoding-raw / encoding-rzcobs cargo feature), and the GNU build id of the firmware: the host takes the ELF with this build id to decode the frames (the format strings are interned there, not sent).
  • frames - the log. Its unit is one defmt frame, so the stream head's units is the number of frames in an item and its lost is the exact number of log messages the host won't get. An item never holds half a frame: a decoder fed one item after the other never loses sync, also with raw encoding and after a loss.

Timestamps are defmt's own (defmt::timestamp!), inside each frame; the head's t stays off.

items.title: Logs from before the host connects
items.text:
The device starts the stream's session at boot, without a host, and keeps logging into the store. A host that wants these logs resumes that session from its start instead of opening the stream (opening starts a new session and empties the store):

let status = device.log().frames_status().read().await?;
let cursor = StreamCursor { session: status.session.unwrap(), pos: UVlq64(0) };
let mut frames = device.log().frames_resume(cursor).call().await?;

The backlog arrives as the backfill run while new logs come live, see stream reliability. When the store is full, its FullPolicy decides: with DropOldest it keeps the latest logs, which matter most after a fault, and the host gets the dropped ones as one gap. A store on SD or NOR flash (ww_stream's LogStore) keeps the logs across reboots and power cuts with nothing changed in the API.

items.title: Decoding on the host
items.text:
defmt-decoder does the decoding: Table::parse(&elf) for the table, a stream decoder fed with the bytes of each item, frames out of it until it needs more bytes. examples/defmt_log is a complete host program: it reads DEFMT, refuses an ELF whose build id differs from the device's (--force to use it anyway), resumes the session and prints decoded frames and gaps, something like:

INFO  heartbeat 41
--- 312 log messages lost (Device) ---
INFO  flood 189 of 500

items.title: The build id
items.text:
The linker writes a GNU build id when asked (-C link-arg=--build-id=sha1, a hash of the linked output: it changes with every byte of code); a section in memory.x puts it into flash where the firmware reads it at run time:

SECTIONS {
    .note.gnu.build-id : ALIGN(4)
    {
        __build_id_start = .;
        KEEP(*(.note.gnu.build-id));
        __build_id_end = .;
    } > FLASH
} INSERT AFTER .rodata;

ww_firmware_info::build_id() (its build-id feature) reads the id between the two symbols. examples_mcu/rp2 does all three steps (build.rs, memory.x, src/bin/usb_log.rs). Without the note, build_id is empty and a host can only guess the ELF.

items.title: The device side: ww_defmt_logger
items.text:
defmt allows one global logger, called from any context, interrupts included, and it can't wait; a reliable stream's store is async. ww_defmt_logger sits between them:

  1. global_logger!(LOG, 4096) makes a DefmtLogger with a ring of 4 KiB the #[defmt::global_logger]. A defmt macro takes a critical section (as defmt-rtt does), encodes the frame into the ring and, with the rtt feature, into an RTT up channel. The whole frame is committed at once; a frame that doesn't fit the free space (or is longer than 512 bytes) is dropped whole and counted.
  2. LOG.pump(&mut stream) in the event loop takes the committed frames out of the ring, without a critical section, packs up to 512 bytes of whole frames into one DefmtFrames item and pushes it into the store, units = frames. Frames the ring dropped become the stream's lost exactly where they were dropped.
ww_defmt_logger::global_logger!(LOG, 4096);

// at boot
let channels = rtt_init! { up: { 0: { size: 1024, mode: NoBlockSkip, name: "defmt" } } };
LOG.set_rtt_channel(channels.up.0);       // probe-rs and `cnt run` keep showing the logs
state.log_stream.start_session(1).await?; // keep logs until a host resumes

// the event loop
loop {
    if let Either::First(ready) = select(server.wait(), Timer::after_millis(5)).await
        && let Some(LinkEvent::Down(_)) = server.handle(ready, state).await
    {
        state.log_stream.detach();
    }
    LOG.pump(&mut state.log_stream).await?;
    if server.is_up() {
        state.poll_streams(&mut server.sink(), now_ms, &mut buf, 2048).await?;
    }
}
  • RAM: the ring (a power of two; each frame takes its encoded length plus 6 bytes) and about 1 KiB for packing an item. The ring only has to hold what is logged between two pumps; the store holds the rest.
  • Encoding: ww_defmt_logger::encoding() tells which one defmt is built with, for DEFMT. With rzCOBS the very first frame after boot starts with an extra 0x00 (defmt's resync marker), which decoders skip.
  • Contexts: frames from an interrupt never interleave with one being written. A defmt macro inside a defmt macro panics, as with defmt-rtt. defmt::flush() doesn't wait, the ring is emptied by pump only.
  • Other global loggers: none may be linked next to it: not defmt-rtt, not rtt-target's defmt feature.
  • Async server: a reliable stream needs use_async = true.

The ring is tested on the host with four threads logging into a 512-byte ring while another pumps: every frame arrives whole and in order, and received plus lost is exactly what was logged. examples_mcu/rp2's rp2_usb_log logs over USB and RTT at once (just run rp2 usb_log, host: examples/defmt_log, --flood 500 to overload it).

items.title: LogText
items.text:
For firmware without defmt: the log crate on embassy or std targets, ESP-IDF.

#[ww_trait]
pub trait LogText {
    #[stream(LogRecord<'i>, reliable)]
    fn records() -> Result<(), LogError<'i>>;
    property!(rw level: LevelFilter, LogError<'i>);
}

pub struct LogRecord<'i> {
    pub severity: Severity,               // Error, Warn, Info, Debug, Trace
    pub target: MaxLen<&'i str, 48>,      // module path
    pub message: MaxLen<&'i str, 256>,
    pub truncated: bool,                  // the message was cut at the device's limit
}
pub enum LevelFilter { Off, Error, Warn, Info, Debug, Trace }
  • records - one record per message, unit: record. The head's t carries the device time of the record. Logs from before the host connects come the same way as with LogDefmt, by resuming.
  • level - records less severe than this are not produced (LevelFilter::allows(severity)); filters compiled into the firmware still apply. Writing it may fail with Common(Unsupported) when the level is fixed at compile time.

Severity and LevelFilter are complete as they are (no_future_version): the five levels of log, tracing and defmt.

items.title: Errors
items.text: LogError has only Common(CommonError) for now (common errors): Busy when another host has the log open, Unsupported when the device logs elsewhere only. It stays an enum so variants can be added.

items.title: ww_logic_analyzer
items.text:
ww_logic_analyzer is a global WireWeaver trait family for timestamped capture of many digital channels on one common time base: an MCU with a DMA-able GPIO port or a PIO, up to a dedicated analyzer. It is no_std by default and depends on wire_weaver, ww_si (Hertz/Second/Volt), ww_gpio (Level) and ww_i2c (I2cAddress, for a protocol trigger stage).

Add it to a device API crate with:

[dependencies]
ww_logic_analyzer = "0.1"

It sits next to ww_gpio rather than inside it because GPIO is one pin, one call, no timing; here the whole point is timing: every sample of every channel lands on one grid. Protocol decoding (UART, I2C, SPI, CAN on top of captured edges) stays on the host; a device that decodes a protocol itself implements that protocol's own monitor (Uart::monitor, I2cMonitor, Spi::monitor) instead.

items.title: Traits
items.text: A device with only capture memory implements LogicAnalyzer; one that can stream while sampling adds LogicStream. Both follow the same conventions as the rest of the IO trait family.

items.title: LogicAnalyzer
items.text:
Triggered capture into device RAM, read out after — the same shape as ww_adc::AdcCapture: arm with a configuration, poll the status, read the data out, abort.

#[ww_trait]
pub trait LogicAnalyzer {
    fn capabilities() -> LaCapabilities<'i>;
    fn capture(config: CaptureConfig<'i>) -> Result<CaptureActual, LaError>;
    fn rearm() -> Result<CaptureActual, LaError>;
    fn status() -> CaptureStatus;
    fn read_raw(range: SampleRange) -> Result<RawChunk<'i>, LaError>;
    fn read_transitions(channel: u8, from: u32) -> Result<TransitionsChunk<'i>, LaError>;
    fn abort();
}
  • capabilities - channels, rates, memory, storage and read encodings, and which triggers work (TriggerCapabilities).
  • capture - arms a capture, replacing the previous one and its data, and returns what was actually set. With Trigger::Now it starts at once; otherwise it samples pre_trigger samples continuously and keeps them, waits for the trigger, then takes the rest.
  • rearm - arms again with the last configuration, for repeated captures of the same event without resending it.
  • status - Idle, Armed, Triggered { t }, or Done { t_first, trigger_at, samples } once the data is ready — a host polls this until Done.
  • read_raw - samples of a sample range as raw words, at most MAX_READ_LEN bytes (Common(WrongState) before a capture is done, Common(InvalidArgument) outside it, Common(Unsupported) if the device only keeps transitions).
  • read_transitions - edges of one channel from a sample index on, up to MAX_EDGES or a full reply; TransitionsChunk::scanned_to says where the next call starts (same error set, plus LaError::NoSuchChannel).
  • abort - stops an armed or running capture and drops its data.

Reads are in samples, not bytes, and split by encoding, since a byte offset means nothing for transitions (their size depends on the signal). read_transitions is per channel: it is the cheapest shape for the device (one bit of every raw word, one pass, a fixed index buffer) and lets a host fetch only the channels it shows; a host fetching every channel sends one call per channel in one multi-call.

A capture's storage (raw words or transitions) is the device's choice (LaCapabilities::storage) and independent of how it is read out: either storage can be read back in either encoding the device lists.

items.title: LogicStream
items.text:
Continuous capture, streamed while the link keeps up:

#[ww_trait]
pub trait LogicStream {
    #[stream(StreamChunk<'i>, counted)]
    fn data(config: StreamConfig<'i>) -> Result<StreamActual, LaError>;
    fn stream_capabilities() -> StreamCapabilities<'i>;
}
  • data - a counted stream function: the host opens it with channels, rate and encoding and gets back what was actually set (or an LaError), then receives raw chunks or per-channel transition chunks as they fill. Closing the stream stops sampling, opening it again restarts it with the new configuration.
  • stream_capabilities - the highest raw rate per channel count the link carries, and the highest rate with Transitions (bounded by the edge rate fitting the link, not the sample rate).

The stream's unit is a chunk: the event head says exactly how many chunks the device dropped and where (stream delivery), and each chunk's own sample range (RawChunk::first, TransitionsChunk::from) tells which samples they covered. The head's t is the device time of a chunk's first sample.

items.title: Encodings
items.text:
Both traits, and ww_signal_generator's pattern sink, share two encodings so a capture can be replayed without conversion:

  • Encoding::Raw, [RawChunk] - every sample, a word of RawLayout::width bits (1, 2, 4, 8, 16 or 32, the smallest the device gives for the channel count). Bit i of a word is the i-th channel of the configuration's channel list; sub-byte words are packed starting at bit 0 of a byte, multi-byte words are little-endian — what a DMA from a GPIO port produces with no CPU work.
  • Encoding::Transitions, [TransitionsChunk] - per channel, its level at the start of the range and the sample indices where it toggles, as a DeltaOfDelta<u32>. A steady clock costs about one bit per edge, a quiet channel almost nothing (its start level and an empty list), so the edge rate limits a stream, not the sample rate: a busy signal sampled for clean edge timing costs the same at a high rate as at a low one.

Sample indices are u32, counted from a capture's first sample or from the start of a stream session (where they wrap and a host unwraps them, as with any fixed-width timestamp in the family).

items.title: Triggers
items.text:
pub enum Trigger<'i> {
    Now,
    Stages(MaxLen<RefVec<'i, TriggerStage<'i>>, MAX_STAGES>),
    External { edge: Edge },
}

Trigger::Stages is met stage after stage, each one after the one before; the capture triggers when the last one is. One TriggerStage::Pattern combines level, edge and pattern conditions on several channels at once (ChannelCondition { channel, when: Condition }, where Condition is Low / High / Rising / Falling / AnyEdge) — a level trigger is one condition High, an edge trigger one Rising. TriggerCapabilities says how many stages and conditions a device supports; zero stages means only Now and maybe External work.

Three protocol stages are matched on the decoded stream next to the capture, decoding only as much as the match needs, and combine with patterns and with each other like any other stage: TriggerStage::UartByte (a UART frame matching a value under a mask, met at the stop bit), TriggerStage::I2cAddress (an address byte matching, of a read/write/either, met at the ACK bit), TriggerStage::SpiFirstByte (the first byte after CS goes low, met at its last bit). TriggerCapabilities lists which protocol stages a device supports.

CaptureConfig::trigger_out pulses the device's trigger output when the capture triggers, so another analyzer, a scope, or a ww_signal_generator::PatternGenerator on another device can start on the same edge (Start::External); two devices synced through ww_timebase::Clock::configure_sync line their captures up on the shared time base for anything less exact than a sample.

items.title: Types
items.text:
• LaCapabilities<'i> - channels: MaxLen<RefVec<'i, ChannelInfo<'i>>, MAX_CHANNELS>, rates: MaxLen<RefVec<'i, RateLimit>, MAX_RATE_LIMITS> (highest rate per channel count), memory: u32, storage: Encoding, raw / transitions: bool (which encodings reads give), trigger: TriggerCapabilities.
  • ChannelInfo<'i> - name, gpio_pin: Option<u8> (the same pin's index in the device's ww_gpio::Bank), threshold: Option<VoltRange> (if the input threshold is adjustable).
  • RateLimit - channels: u8, max_rate: Hertz.
  • TriggerCapabilities - max_stages: u8, max_conditions: u8, edges: bool, uart_byte / i2c_address / spi_first_byte: bool, external: bool, trigger_out: bool.
  • CaptureConfig<'i> - channels: MaxLen<RefVec<'i, u8>, MAX_CHANNELS>, rate: Hertz, samples: u32 (total, pre_trigger included), pre_trigger: u32, trigger: Trigger<'i>, threshold: Option<Volt>, trigger_out: bool.
  • CaptureActual - rate: Hertz, samples: u32 (the memory may hold fewer than asked at this channel count), layout: RawLayout.
  • CaptureStatus - Idle, Armed, Triggered { t: Second }, Done { t_first: Second, trigger_at: Option<u32>, samples: u32 }; sized (unib32 discriminant).
  • SampleRange - first: u32, count: u32.
  • RawLayout - width: u8.
  • RawChunk<'i> - first: u32, samples: u32, data: MaxLen<RefVec<'i, u8>, MAX_READ_LEN>.
  • TransitionsChunk<'i> - channel: u8, level: Level, from: u32, scanned_to: u32, edges: DeltaOfDelta<'i, u32> (ascending, at most MAX_EDGES).
  • StreamChunk<'i> - Raw(RawChunk<'i>) or Transitions(TransitionsChunk<'i>).
  • StreamCapabilities<'i> - raw_rates: MaxLen<RefVec<'i, RateLimit>, MAX_RATE_LIMITS>, transitions_rate: Option<Hertz>.
  • StreamConfig<'i> - channels, rate: Hertz, encoding: Encoding, flush_interval: Option<Second>, threshold: Option<Volt>.
  • StreamActual - rate: Hertz, layout: RawLayout.
  • Trigger<'i>, TriggerStage<'i>, ChannelCondition, Condition, Edge - see Triggers.
  • LaError<'i> - Common(CommonError) (common errors) (Busy: a stream runs while a capture is asked for, or the other way round, on devices that share one sampler), NoSuchChannel; unsized (unib32 discriminant), evolvable, shared by both traits.

All enums and structs are behind #[derive_shrink_wrap] with owned(feature = "std") and cfg_attr_borrowed(feature = "defmt", derive(defmt::Format)), so owned (*Owned) variants and defmt::Format are available by enabling the crate's std / defmt features.

items.title: Composing into a device API
items.text:
#[ww_api_root]
pub trait MyProbe {
    ww_impl!(la: ww_logic_analyzer::LogicAnalyzer);
}

ChannelInfo::gpio_pin cross-references the same pin's index in the device's own ww_gpio::Bank::pin, so a host or a generic tool can show which logic-analyzer channel is which GPIO pin. A ww_signal_generator::PatternGenerator on the same or another device replays a capture directly: it accepts the same StreamChunk encodings this crate produces, so a host reads a capture out in whichever encoding the generator lists and feeds the chunks straight to its pattern sink — see ww_signal_generator.

items.title: ww_memory
items.text:
ww_memory gives a host low-level access to memory or registers of a device: read and write words at addresses, and optionally watch addresses for changes. It is no_std by default and depends only on wire_weaver.

[dependencies]
ww_memory = "0.1"

items.title: Traits
Errors
items.text: MemoryError<'i> starts with #[common] Common(CommonError) (common errors), then WrongAddress (outside address_range, or a range running past its end) and OutOfWatchSlots. Each method lists the variants it returns with #[errors(..)].

items.title: Number types as features
items.text:
NumericValue holds any number, and is as big as its biggest variant: 32 bytes on a PC and 24 on a Cortex-M with u128 in it. Each variant except U8 is behind a cargo feature of its name, so firmware enables only what it uses:

# host: std enables every number type
ww_numeric = "0.2"
# firmware: 8 bytes per value, no 64 or 128-bit code
ww_numeric = { version = "0.2", default-features = false, features = ["u16", "f32"] }

Features: nibble, u16, u32, unib32, u64, i32, f32, un, in, u128, i8, i16, i64, i128, f64, uvlq32, uvlq64, and all. ww_si has the same ones and passes them on.

The wire format is the same for every set. A value of a type that is not enabled is read as Error::EnumVariantDisabled; see #[cfg(..)] on enum variants.

items.title: Variable-length numbers
items.text:
For values that are usually small but have no useful bound (counters, lengths, timestamps in ww_si::Second), three variants grow with the value:

Variant Encoding Bytes on the wire, with discriminant UNib32(UNib32) nibbles, 3 bits each, right after the discriminant 5: 45; 300: 4C D4 UVlq32(UVlq32) bytes, 7 bits each, big endian 5: 82 05; 300: 82 82 2C UVlq64(UVlq64) same, up to 10 bytes 5: 92 05; u64::MAX: 11 bytes

UVlq32 and UVlq64 have discriminants 16 and 17, which take two nibbles.

items.title: Conversions
items.text: From<u16>, From<f32>, From<UVlq32>, .. for NumericValue (each behind its type's feature), so APIs can take impl Into<NumericValue>. to_f64() and as_f32() give the value as a float, to_i128() the exact value of an integer variant, unsigned_bits() the width at which an unsigned counter wraps (U32 and UVlq32: 32).

items.title: ww_onewire
items.text:
ww_onewire is a global WireWeaver trait for 1-Wire masters: reset the bus, find the devices on it (paged or bit-level search), and run addressed transactions, with strong pull-up for parasite-powered parts. It is no_std by default and depends only on wire_weaver and ww_si (for the Second type OneWireTransaction::strong_pullup uses as a duration).

Add it to a device API crate with:

[dependencies]
ww_onewire = "0.1"

items.title: The protocol, briefly
items.text:
A 1-Wire bus is a single data line shared by a master and one or more slaves, each identified by an 8-byte ROM id (RomId): a family code, a 48-bit serial number, and a CRC8 of the other seven bytes. Every operation starts with a reset pulse and a presence pulse from any slave listening (OneWire::reset); OneWire::transaction does this implicitly. A slave is picked with its RomId (Match ROM) or, on a bus with one device, skipped entirely (rom: None, Skip ROM).

Finding the ROM ids on a bus (there is no broadcast "who's there") is a bit-level search: a reset, the Search ROM command (0xF0) written through OneWire::transaction with an empty read, then up to 64 calls to OneWire::triplet, one per ROM bit, walking a binary tree of every bit position where connected devices disagree. OneWire::search runs this on the device and returns whole ids a page at a time, which is what most hosts want; OneWire::triplet exposes the same primitive for a host that wants to drive the tree walk itself (e.g. to stop early once it has found the family code it is looking for).

items.title: Trait
items.text:
#[ww_trait]
pub trait OneWire {
    fn transaction(t: OneWireTransaction<'i>) -> Result<MaxLen<RefVec<'i, u8>, OW_MAX>, OneWireError>;

    fn reset() -> Result<bool, OneWireError>;

    fn search(from: Option<SearchState>, family: Option<u8>) -> Result<SearchPage<'i>, OneWireError>;

    fn capabilities() -> OneWireCapabilities<'i>;

    fn configure(config: OneWireConfig) -> Result<OneWireConfig, OneWireError>;

    fn triplet(direction: bool) -> Result<Triplet, OneWireError>;
}
  • transaction - reset, ROM select (or skip ROM), write, read read_len bytes, optional strong pull-up after the last byte. The common way to talk to one known device.
  • reset - reset pulse on its own; true when a device answered with a presence pulse (not an error - an empty bus is a normal false).
  • search - paged ROM search: start with from: None, continue with each page's next until it comes back None. family, when given, only returns ids whose first byte matches.
  • capabilities - pins the bus can be put on, IO levels, and whether overdrive / strong pull-up are supported.
  • configure - puts the bus on one of capabilities().pins at a given speed and IO level (io_level: None leaves it as it is), or disables it; answers with what was actually set, as the configure of the other IO crates does.
  • triplet - one search step at bit level, for a search run on the host instead of the device (see The protocol, briefly).

items.title: Strong pull-up
items.text: Parasite-powered parts (no separate Vcc pin) draw their supply from the data line and need it actively driven high for the duration of certain operations (EEPROM writes, DS18B20 temperature conversions) rather than left to the bus pull-up resistor. OneWireTransaction::strong_pullup asks the device to do this for the given duration right after the transaction's last byte; OneWireCapabilities::strong_pullup says whether it can.

items.title: Types
items.text:
• RomId - bytes: [u8; 8]: family code, 48-bit serial, CRC8, most to least significant.
  • OneWireTransaction<'i> - rom: Option<RomId> (None = skip ROM), write: MaxLen<RefVec<'i, u8>, OW_MAX>, read_len: u16, strong_pullup: Option<Second>.
  • SearchState - where a paged search left off: last_rom: RomId, last_discrepancy: u8 (the classic Dallas/Maxim search state, carried from one page to the next).
  • SearchPage<'i> - roms: MaxLen<RefVec<'i, RomId>, MAX_ROMS>, next: Option<SearchState> (None when all devices were found).
  • Triplet - one triplet step's result: id_bit, cmp_bit (both set when every remaining device agrees on this bit, both clear at a fork), direction (the bit this step actually drove onto the bus).
  • OneWireConfig - enabled: bool, pin: u8 (index into OneWireCapabilities::pins), speed: OneWireSpeed, io_level: Option<Volt>; the argument and the answer of configure.
  • OneWireSpeed - Standard / Overdrive; sized, 1 bit.
  • OneWireCapabilities<'i> - pins: MaxLen<RefVec<'i, MaxLen<&'i str, 16>>, MAX_PINS> (by name), io_levels: MaxLen<RefVec<'i, Volt>, MAX_IO_LEVELS>, io_level_min / io_level_max: Option<Volt>, overdrive: bool, strong_pullup: bool.
  • OneWireError<'i> - Common(CommonError) (common errors), NoPresence, CrcMismatch, ShortCircuit; unsized (unib32 discriminant), evolvable.

Constants: OW_MAX (256, largest write or read of one transaction), MAX_ROMS (16, most ROM ids in one search page), MAX_PINS (8, most pins a bus can be put on).

All enums and structs are behind #[derive_shrink_wrap] with owned(feature = "std"), so owned (*Owned) variants are available by enabling the crate's std feature (on by default).

items.title: Composing into a device API
items.text:
A device with one 1-Wire bus implements OneWire once, flat, on its API root:

#[ww_api_root]
pub trait MyAdapter {
    ww_impl!(onewire: ww_onewire::OneWire);
}

items.title: Testing (tests/io_onewire)
items.text: tests/io_onewire (with its tests/io_onewire_api companion) is a worked, in-process example: a mock bus server driven by the generated client through tests_common::start_device. The mock implements the actual Dallas/Maxim search algorithm against a handful of simulated RomIds (not just canned answers), so search's paging and triplet's bit-level walk are both exercised for real, including the family filter and a full 64-bit triplet-driven search that reconstructs a known RomId.

items.title: ww_pwm
items.text:
Part of the IO trait family. ww_pwm is a global WireWeaver trait pair for PWM outputs and pulse measurement: setting frequency, duty cycle and polarity on one or more channels, and (on devices with a capture timer) measuring frequency, duty cycle, pulse width or edge count on others. It is no_std by default and depends only on wire_weaver and ww_si (for the Hertz and Second quantities).

Add it to a device API crate with:

[dependencies]
ww_pwm = "0.1"

items.title: Traits
items.text:
Trait What it is for Who implements it Pwm channel[] of PWM outputs: frequency, duty, polarity. Every device with PWM PwmCapture channel[] of inputs measuring frequency, duty, pulse width, edges. Devices with timer capture

Measuring pulses is its own trait, not a mode of Pwm's channels: it needs a timer in capture/input mode, which most devices with PWM output don't have spare on every channel, so a plain PWM driver implements Pwm only.

items.title: Pwm
items.text:
#[ww_trait]
pub trait Pwm {
    ww_impl!(channel[]: PwmChannel);

    fn capabilities() -> PwmCapabilities<'i>;
}

#[ww_trait]
pub trait PwmChannel {
    fn set_output(output: PwmOutput) -> Result<PwmActual, PwmError>;
    fn set_duty(duty: u16) -> Result<u16, PwmError>;
    fn stop(idle_high: bool) -> Result<(), PwmError>;
    fn state() -> PwmState;
}
  • channel[] - one PWM output per channel; channel n is channels[n] of capabilities().
  • capabilities() - the channels (name, group, whether a channel also captures), and the frequency and duty range, see PwmCapabilities under Types.
  • set_output - starts or changes a channel's output (frequency, duty, polarity, edge- or center-aligned) and returns what was actually set, the nearest the hardware can do.
