Channels sharing a timer (PwmChannelInfo::group) share its frequency: setting a different frequency on another channel of the same group fails with PwmError::SharedTimer.
  • set_duty - changes only the duty, keeping the frequency, and returns the duty actually set. Fails with Common(WrongState) if the channel is currently idle.
  • stop - stops the output, leaving the pin high or low.
  • state - the channel's current output, or PwmState::Idle.

items.title: PwmCapture
items.text:
#[ww_trait]
pub trait PwmCapture {
    ww_impl!(channel[]: PwmCaptureChannel);
}

#[ww_trait]
pub trait PwmCaptureChannel {
    #[stream(CaptureValue, counted)]
    fn capture(config: CaptureConfig) -> Result<CaptureConfig, PwmError>;

    fn set_capture(config: CaptureConfig) -> Result<CaptureConfig, PwmError>;
    fn read_capture() -> Result<CaptureSample, PwmError>;
}
  • channel[] - one capture input per channel; channel n is the same index as Pwm's own channel[], see PwmChannelInfo::capture.
  • capture - a counted stream function: the host opens it with what to measure (CaptureMode) and the measurement window (CaptureConfig::gate), gets back what was actually set, then one CaptureValue per window until it closes the stream. Its unit is a measurement; the event head carries the end of each window as its time and how many measurements the device dropped (stream delivery).
  • set_capture - picks what to measure and the window without a stream, for polling with read_capture, and returns what was actually set.
  • read_capture - the last measurement, without waiting on the stream. Fails with Common(WrongState) before the first measurement completes.

items.title: Types
items.text:
• PwmOutput - what to set: freq: Hertz, duty: u16 (0..=65535 = 0..100 %), inverted: bool, phase_correct: bool (center-aligned instead of edge-aligned counting).
  • PwmActual - what was actually set: freq: Hertz, duty: u16.
  • PwmState - Idle or Output(PwmActual); unib32 discriminant.
  • PwmCapabilities<'i> - channels: MaxLen<RefVec<'i, PwmChannelInfo<'i>>, MAX_CHANNELS>, min_freq / max_freq: Hertz, duty_bits: u8 (the hardware's duty resolution).
  • PwmChannelInfo<'i> - name: MaxLen<&'i str, MAX_NAME_LEN>, group: u8 (channels sharing a timer share this), capture: bool (also reachable through PwmCapture, at the same index).
  • CaptureConfig - mode: CaptureMode, gate: Second (the measurement window, or how long PulseWidth waits for one pulse to start).
  • CaptureMode - Off, Frequency, DutyCycle, PulseWidth, EdgeCount; sized, unib32 discriminant.
  • CaptureSample - t: Second (end of the window), value: CaptureValue.
  • CaptureValue - Frequency(Hertz), DutyCycle(u16), PulseWidth(Second), EdgeCount(u32); the variant always matches CaptureConfig::mode. unib32 discriminant.
  • PwmError<'i> - Common(CommonError) (common errors), SharedTimer; unsized (unib32 discriminant), evolvable. Each method lists the variants it returns (#[errors]).

All enums and structs are behind #[derive_shrink_wrap] with owned(feature = "std") and cfg_attr_borrowed(feature = "defmt", derive(defmt::Format)), so owned (*Owned) variants and defmt::Format are available by enabling the crate's std / defmt features. Hertz and Second don't derive PartialEq (their NumericValue can carry f32); compare their prefix and value fields directly where needed.

items.title: Composing into a device API
items.text:
A device exposes PWM outputs and, if it can measure, capture inputs as separate resources on its API root, see the tests/io_pwm_api crate:

#[ww_api_root]
pub trait IoPwmTest {
    ww_impl!(pwm: ww_pwm::Pwm);
    ww_impl!(pwm_capture: ww_pwm::PwmCapture);
}

Because Pwm and PwmCapture both contain their own channel[], resources end up two levels deep: pwm.channel(0).set_output(..), pwm_capture.channel(0).set_capture(..).

items.title: Mock server (tests/io_pwm)
items.text:
tests/io_pwm is a small in-memory PWM device used for end-to-end tests: it tracks each channel's actual output in a Model shared with the test, and a capture channel's last configured mode and measurement, instead of driving real hardware. It shows the handler shape ww_codegen! expects for a trait nested in an array (pwm_channel_set_output, pwm_capture_channel_read_capture, ...) and how to send a measurement on a channel's counted capture stream from the device's event loop, with the ww_stream::tx::Counted state the server keeps per channel (stream_pwm_capture_channel_capture):

api_impl::stream_data_ser()
    .pwm_capture()
    .channel(idx)
    .capture_send_blocking(&mut self.capture[idx as usize], &value, 1, Some(t), out)?;

See tests/io_pwm/src/lib.rs for the full mock server and client-side test calls (capabilities, set_output / set_duty / stop / state, set_capture / read_capture, and the capture stream opened with its configuration, an invalid one refused, and closed).

items.title: ww_self
items.text:
ww_self is WireWeaver's own AST: a self-describing model of an API (its traits, methods, properties, streams) and of the data types it uses, serializable with shrink_wrap like any other wire type. The codegen builds one from a #[ww_trait]/#[ww_api_root] definition at compile time, a device can send its own as introspection data, and tools (the dynamic client, the ww CLI, the Python bindings) walk it to call methods, decode values and show an API without any generated code for it. It lives in the wire_weaver repo root, not ww_stdlib/, but is versioned and published the same way; add it with:

[dependencies]
ww_self = "0.2"

items.title: The API model
items.text:
• ApiBundle<'i> - one API as serialized/introspected: magic (ww_self::MAGIC), ww_self_version (the ww_self version the bundle was built with, so a reader knows which format it's in), root: ApiLevel<'i> (the entry point), a deduplicated types: RefVec<TypeLocation<'i>> and traits: RefVec<ApiLevelLocation<'i>> (referred to by index from elsewhere in the model), ext_crates: RefVec<FullVersion<'i>> (every external crate a type or trait in the bundle comes from), and root_omitted (ids of the root's optional items this device leaves out).
  • ApiLevel<'i> - one trait's worth of API: docs, crate_idx (into ext_crates), trait_name, and items: RefVec<ApiItem<'i>>.
  • ApiItem<'i> - one item of a level: id, kind: ApiItemKind<'i>, multiplicity (Flat or Array { index_type_idx } for a ww_impl!(x[]: ..) array), since (the version it was added in), ident, docs, and optional (#[optional]/#[optional(group)], see optional items).
  • ApiItemKind<'i> - what kind of item: Method { args, return_ty, errors }, Property { ty, access, write_err_ty }, Stream { ty, is_up }, Trait { trait_idx, omitted } (a nested level), FlowSink { ty, flow } (a credit sink), or StreamFn { ty, delivery, args, return_ty } (a stream opened by calling it, with its own arguments and Delivery: Plain, Counted or Reliable).
  • TypeLocation<'i> / ApiLevelLocation<'i> - either InLine (the actual Type/ApiLevel, plus which ext_crates entry it's from) or Skipped{FullVersion,CompactVersion} (name/id and version only, plus a signature hash) - how a device leaves out a definition the host is expected to already know (from a published crate), to save flash, while still letting the host check it's the exact same definition.

items.title: The type and value model
items.text:
• Type<'i> - every shape a value on the wire can have: Bool, NumericAny (any ww_numeric number type), String, Vec, Array { len, ty }, Tuple, Struct(ItemStruct), Enum(ItemEnum), Option { some_ty }, Result { ok_ty, err_ty }, Box (self-referential types), Range/RangeInclusive, MaxLen { max_len, ty }, Delta/DeltaOfDelta/XorFloat (the compressed number sequences of shrink_wrap, SW-31/SW-32), OutOfLine { type_idx } (a reference into ApiBundle::types, how recursive and shared types stay out of the inline tree), and Flag (a relocated Option/Result presence bit, #[flag] - marks a named field, never appears in a value).
  • Value<'i> - a value matching some Type: Bool, Numeric(NumericValue), String, Vec/Array/Tuple (of Values), Struct { fields: FieldsValue }, Enum { variant, fields }, Option, Result, Range/ RangeInclusive (of NumericValue). This is what a dynamic client builds from wire bytes plus a Type, without generated Rust types for the API at hand.
  • ItemStruct<'i> / ItemEnum<'i> - a struct's/enum's own size: ElementSize (the same size assumption #[derive_shrink_wrap] picks), crate_idx, docs, ident, and fields/(repr: Repr, variants: RefVec<Variant>).
  • Field<'i> / Variant<'i> - ident, ty, docs, since; a Field also carries its default: Option<Value> (for a #[default = ..] field) and relocates its own presence flags with #[flag] the same way ww_version::Version does.

Every enum in this model is no_future_version (SW-47): rather than tolerating an unknown future variant the usual shrink_wrap way, a bundle names its own ww_self_version and a reader is expected to walk the whole model, so a newer kind of item or type can't silently be skipped - that tolerance is handled one layer up instead (introspection version negotiation, INT-8).

items.title: Dynamic access helpers
items.text:
With the std feature, owned types (TypeOwned, ValueOwned, ApiBundleOwned, ...) get methods for walking the model without generated code:

  • ApiBundleOwned::get_item(id_chain) / get_trait / get_ty / crate_name / crate_version - resolve an item path, a nested trait, an out-of-line type, or an ext_crates entry by index.
  • TypeOwned::get_in_line(bundle) - follows an OutOfLine reference to the actual Type.
  • TypeOwned::human_name / human_definition - a Rust-like name ("Option<Vec<u8>>") or full definition, with or without the owning crate's name, for display in a tool.
  • TypeOwned::is_lifetime / is_unsized / is_byte_slice / max_len - what the type needs structurally (does it borrow, is its size written to the FIFO, is it Vec<u8>/MaxLen<Vec<u8>, N>, what bound a MaxLen carries).
  • TypeOwned::is_common_error / ValueOwned::common_error / doc_message - recognise ww_error::CommonError (by crate and type name, any version, even when its definition was left out) inside an API's own error enum, and turn an error variant's first doc line into a message with its fields filled in (doc_message, used for Display on generated error types; fill in ww_self::common does the {field} substitution).
  • ww_self::errors - per-method #[errors(..)] lists (API-32): ApiItemKindOwned::error_list, error_list_docs (one doc line per entry, "any CommonError" for a bare Common), error_list_contains (whether a returned error value matches the list), error_value_name.
  • ApiItemKindOwned::as_stream_fn / as_stream - see any device-to-host stream (a plain stream!, a #[stream] method, or a StreamFn) uniformly as a StreamFnRef (item type, Delivery, arguments, return type), or as a stream/sink with its direction and flow control.

items.title: Signatures, and putting skipped definitions back
items.text:
ww_self::signature computes a signature for a trait or type: a truncated SHA-256 (SIGNATURE_LEN, 8 bytes) of a canonical bundle holding just that definition and everything it refers to, in-line, with indices renumbered in the order of first use - so the signature depends only on the definition, not on where it sat in the original bundle or what else was alongside it. trait_signature/type_signature take a Resolve callback to look up Skipped* definitions (e.g. from a crate's published snapshot) along the way.

ww_self::inline::inline_skipped uses the same signatures to put Skipped* locations back: it resolves each one, checks its signature matches what was stored, and replaces it in place (appending whatever the restored definition itself refers to). Anything not found, or found with a different signature, comes back as a NotInlined (kind, crate/version if known, name, reason) instead of being substituted silently.

items.title: Visiting the model
items.text: ww_self::visit::Visit (read-only) and ww_self::visit_mut::VisitMut (mutable) are exhaustive visitor traits over every node kind above, generated from one define_visitor! macro definition: each has a default per-node method (visit_type, visit_api_item_kind, ...) that recurses into its children, plus leaf methods (visit_ident, visit_docs) that do nothing by default - override just the node kinds you care about and call the matching free function (visit::visit_api_bundle, ...) to keep recursing into the rest. Canonical (behind signature) and the remapping pass in inline are both built this way, overriding only visit_type/ visit_api_item_kind/etc. to rewrite the handful of index fields (type_idx, trait_idx, crate_idx) that need remapping.

items.title: How it relates to the rest
items.text: wire_weaver_core's codegen (transform/codegen) builds an ApiBundle from the trait source it parses and hands it to both the server (introspection data a device can send) and client codegen; wire_weaver_client uses it for the dynamic client, compatibility/evolution checks against a cached bundle, and the generated client's own layout; wire_weaver_cli and wire_weaver_py walk it to print an API tree, introspect a live device, and expose it to Python. wire_weaver_snapshots stores published crates' bundles so devices can skip their definitions and hosts can still resolve and verify them via the signatures above.

items.title: ww_si
items.text:
ww_si gives device APIs typed physical values: a quantity is an SI prefix plus a ww_numeric NumericValue in whatever number type the device picks. The API says "this is a voltage", each device decides whether that is a u16 of mV or an f32 of V, and the host reads them all.

use ww_si::{Prefix, Volt};

let v = Volt::millivolts(3300u16);     // Volt { prefix: Milli, value: U16(3300) }
let w = Volt::volts_f32(3.3);          // Volt { prefix: Unit,  value: F32(3.3) }
assert_eq!(v, w);                      // compares values, not representations
assert_eq!(v.to_f64(), 3.3);           // in V
assert_eq!(w.to_i128_in(Prefix::Milli), Some(3300));

Volt::millivolts(3300u16) is 3 bytes on the wire: the prefix and number type nibbles, then the u16.

items.title: Features
items.text:
Everything is a cargo feature, so a firmware compiles only what it uses. std (the default) enables all of them.

Feature What time Second, Hertz, HertzPerSecond, Baud electrical Ampere, Volt, Ohm, Farad, Siemens, Henry, Coulomb, Watt, Weber, Tesla mechanical Meter, KiloGram, Newton, Pascal, Joule, Litre, VolumetricFlow, Speed .. Yank angle Radian, Degree, Steradian, AngularVelocity, AngularAcceleration thermal Kelvin, DegreeCelsius chemical Mole, Katal photometric Candela, Lumen, Lux radiation Becquerel, Gray, Sievert, ElectronVolt logarithmic DeciBel, DeciBelmW quantities all of the groups above host host helpers: Unwrapper u16, f32, .. all number types of NumericValue, passed on to ww_numeric (see ww_numeric) 
# firmware with voltages and timestamps, stored as u16, u32 and f32
ww_si = { version = "0.1", default-features = false, features = ["time", "electrical", "u16", "u32", "f32"] }

The bytes on the wire are the same for every feature set.

items.title: Constructors and conversions
items.text:
Every quantity has new(prefix, value), taking any enabled number type (u16, f32, UVlq32, ..), and:

  • to_f64() / to_f32(): the value in the base unit (V, A, Hz, s);
  • to_f64_in(prefix): in another prefix, Volt::volts_f32(3.3).to_f64_in(Prefix::Milli) is about 3300.0;
  • to_i128_in(prefix): as an integer, exact for integer storage (truncated toward zero when going to a bigger prefix), rounded for floats; None when it doesn't fit.

Named constructors exist for the quantities the IO traits use most:

Type Constructors Volt volts, millivolts, microvolts, kilovolts, volts_f32 Ampere amperes, milliamperes, microamperes, nanoamperes, amperes_f32 Hertz hertz, millihertz, kilohertz, megahertz, gigahertz, hertz_f32 Second seconds, milliseconds, microseconds, nanoseconds, picoseconds, seconds_f32 Baud baud, kilobaud, megabaud, baud_f32

PartialEq and PartialOrd compare values across prefixes and number types: Volt::millivolts(1000u16) == Volt::volts(1u8). Two integers are compared exactly, even 60 orders of magnitude apart; otherwise through f64.

The quantity! macro is a shorthand for literals: quantity!(3300 mV u16), quantity!(400 kHz u32), quantity!(115200 Bd u32).

Baud is a symbol rate, the baud rate of a UART or a protocol decoder, kept apart from Hertz so a baud rate is never taken for a clock frequency (and a tool shows 115200 Bd, not 115.2 kHz).

items.title: Second as a timestamp
items.text:
A Second that marks when something happened (an ADC sample, the start and end of an I2C transaction) is the device's time since its clock started. A device has one clock, so the timestamps of all its traits line up, and ww_timebase::Clock::now() reads it in full. The device picks the prefix and the storage, and keeps them the same for a given stream or method.

Fixed-width unsigned storage holds the time modulo 2^bits, so it wraps:

Storage Wraps after (µs) Wraps after (ms) U16 65.5 ms 65.5 s U32, UVlq32 71.6 min 49.7 days U64, UVlq64 584 000 years never

Timestamps are never signed or floats. On the host, Unwrapper (feature host) gets the full time back. It is anchored on a full-width reading of the same clock, then takes each timestamp as the value with the same low bits closest to the previous one:

use ww_si::{Second, Unwrapper};

let mut unwrapper = Unwrapper::new(Second::microseconds(5_000_000_123u64)).unwrap(); // Clock::now()
let full = unwrapper.unwrap(Second::microseconds(705_032_827u32)).unwrap();        // U32 µs from a stream
assert_eq!(full, Second::microseconds(5_000_000_123u64));

That works while consecutive timestamps are less than half a wrap period apart; re-anchor with anchor(now) after a longer pause. Use one Unwrapper per stream. U64 and signed values pass through unchanged. The anchor and the timestamps can be in different prefixes.

items.title: Prefixes
items.text: Prefix covers every SI prefix from Quecto (10⁻³⁰) to Quetta (10³⁰), From<Prefix> for i8 gives the power of ten. The most used ones (Unit, Milli, Micro, Nano, Pico, Kilo, Mega, Giga) take one nibble on the wire.

items.title: ww_signal_generator
items.text:
ww_signal_generator is a global WireWeaver trait family for driving outputs: digital patterns on many pins at a fixed rate, and analog waveforms on DACs. It is no_std by default and depends on wire_weaver, ww_si (Hertz/Second/Volt), ww_logic_analyzer (reuses its chunk encodings and Edge) and ww_adc (reuses SampleFormat and Linear for DAC tables).

Add it to a device API crate with:

[dependencies]
ww_signal_generator = "0.1"

It is the reverse of ww_logic_analyzer: that crate samples many digital channels on one clock, this one drives them. A square wave from a timer pin is ww_pwm, not this crate; WaveformGenerator is for actual DACs (an MCU's DAC with a DMA table, a DDS chip, a lab function generator).

items.title: Traits
items.text: A device with a pattern generator (DMA-to-GPIO, a PIO program) implements PatternGenerator; one with analog outputs implements WaveformGenerator. A device can have both, neither, or only one.

items.title: PatternGenerator
items.text:
Digital channels driven from a pattern at a fixed rate, all switching on the same tick:

#[ww_trait]
pub trait PatternGenerator {
    fn capabilities() -> PgCapabilities<'i>;
    fn configure(config: PgConfig<'i>) -> Result<PgActual, PgError>;
    #[credit]
    sink!(pattern: StreamChunk<'i>);
    fn start() -> Result<(), PgError>;
    fn stop();
    fn status() -> PgStatus;
}
  • capabilities - channels, rates, pattern memory, which encodings it accepts (raw / transitions), and which start conditions work (external_start, analyzer_start).
  • configure - sets channels, rate, repetition (Repeat::Once / Times(n) / Forever), idle levels and the start condition, and returns what was actually set; drops a pattern already loaded.
  • pattern - the pattern data, appended in order; Open starts a new pattern, Close marks it complete. The sink's credit is the device's free pattern memory, so a host can never overrun it.
  • start - starts output now, or arms it to wait for PgConfig::start. Started before the pattern is complete, it plays what it has while the sink keeps filling, and stops with PgStatus::Underrun if the host falls behind.
  • stop - stops output; channels go to their idle levels.
  • status - Idle, Loading { samples }, Ready, Running { repeat, t_start }, Done { t_start }, Underrun.

Replaying a capture. The pattern sink takes ww_logic_analyzer::StreamChunk — Raw words or per-channel Transitions — the very item type LogicAnalyzer::read_raw / read_transitions and LogicStream produce. A host replays a capture by reading it out in an encoding the generator accepts (PgCapabilities::raw / ::transitions) and feeding the chunks to the sink unchanged, with the capture's rate and channel mapping carried over into PgConfig.

Start conditions (Start): Now (on start()), External { edge } (the external trigger input), or AnalyzerTrigger (this device's own LogicAnalyzer triggering) — a stimulus and its response sharing one time base. PgCapabilities::external_start / analyzer_start say which work.

Pins. While a pattern plays, its channels belong to the generator: ww_gpio::Pin::set_mode / set_output_level on the same pin answer PgError::InUse; reading the level still works.

items.title: WaveformGenerator
items.text:
DAC outputs, one sub-trait per channel:

#[ww_trait]
pub trait WaveformGenerator {
    ww_impl!(channel[]: WaveformChannel);
    fn capabilities() -> WgCapabilities<'i>;
    fn start_together(channels: MaxLen<RefVec<'i, u8>, MAX_CHANNELS>) -> Result<(), WgError>;
}

#[ww_trait]
pub trait WaveformChannel {
    fn set(waveform: Waveform) -> Result<WaveformActual, WgError>;
    fn stop(level: Volt) -> Result<Volt, WgError>;
    fn state() -> WaveformState;
    #[credit]
    sink!(table: MaxLen<RefVec<'i, u8>, MAX_TABLE_CHUNK>);
}
  • capabilities - the channels and their ranges, rates, resolution and table formats (WgChannelInfo).
  • start_together - starts every already-set channel in the list on the same sample clock tick, so their phases line up against each other (WgError::Unsupported if the channels don't share a clock).
  • WaveformChannel::set - starts or changes one output's waveform and returns what the DAC actually does (clamped levels, the frequency its sample clock divides to).
  • stop - stops and holds a level, returning the level actually held.
  • state - Stopped { level }, Held { waveform } (set, waiting for start_together), or Running { waveform, actual }.
  • table - raw DAC codes of a Shape::Arbitrary waveform, appended in order (Open / Close bracket one table); the credit is the channel's free table memory.

Shapes (Waveform { shape, freq, amplitude, offset, phase }, amplitude peak-to-peak, phase against the other channels in start_together): Sine, Square { duty }, Triangle, Sawtooth { rising }, Dc (offset only), and Arbitrary { format, once } — the table sink's codes played once per period, or once and held with once; fed faster than it plays, a once table is a streamed DAC output. Table codes are raw, converted to volts by WgChannelInfo::code_to_volt (a Linear, the same pair ww_adc uses the other way round).

items.title: Types
items.text:
• PgCapabilities<'i> - channels: MaxLen<RefVec<'i, PgChannelInfo<'i>>, MAX_CHANNELS>, rates: MaxLen<RefVec<'i, RateLimit>, MAX_RATE_LIMITS>, memory: u32, raw / transitions: bool, external_start / analyzer_start: bool.
  • PgChannelInfo<'i> - name, gpio_pin: Option<u8> (the same pin's index in the device's ww_gpio::Bank).
  • PgConfig<'i> - channels: MaxLen<RefVec<'i, u8>, MAX_CHANNELS>, rate: Hertz, repeat: Repeat, idle: u32 (bit i is the idle level of channels[i]), start: Start.
  • Repeat - Once, Times(u32), Forever.
  • Start - Now, External { edge: Edge }, AnalyzerTrigger.
  • PgActual - rate: Hertz, width: u8 (the raw word width the generator expects).
  • PgStatus - Idle, Loading { samples: u32 }, Ready, Running { repeat: u32, t_start: Second }, Done { t_start: Second }, Underrun; sized (unib32 discriminant).
  • PgError<'i> - Common(CommonError) (common errors), NoSuchChannel; unsized (unib32 discriminant), evolvable, used by PatternGenerator.
  • WgCapabilities<'i> - channels: MaxLen<RefVec<'i, WgChannelInfo<'i>>, MAX_CHANNELS>.
  • WgChannelInfo<'i> - name, min / max: Volt, max_freq: Hertz, max_sample_rate: Hertz, bits: u8, table_len: u32, code_to_volt: Linear, formats: MaxLen<RefVec<'i, SampleFormat>, MAX_FORMATS>.
  • Waveform - shape: Shape, freq: Hertz, amplitude: Volt, offset: Volt, phase: u16 (0..=65535 = 0..360°).
  • Shape - Sine, Square { duty: u16 } (0..=65535 = 0..100%), Triangle, Sawtooth { rising: bool }, Dc, Arbitrary { format: SampleFormat, once: bool }.
  • WaveformActual - freq: Hertz, amplitude: Volt, offset: Volt.
  • WaveformState - Stopped { level: Volt }, Held { waveform: Waveform }, Running { waveform: Waveform, actual: WaveformActual }; sized (unib32 discriminant).
  • WgError<'i> - Common(CommonError) (common errors), NoSuchChannel; unsized (unib32 discriminant), evolvable, shared by WaveformGenerator and WaveformChannel.

All enums and structs are behind #[derive_shrink_wrap] with owned(feature = "std") and cfg_attr_borrowed(feature = "defmt", derive(defmt::Format)), so owned (*Owned) variants and defmt::Format are available by enabling the crate's std / defmt features.

items.title: Composing into a device API
items.text:
#[ww_api_root]
pub trait MyBench {
    ww_impl!(la: ww_logic_analyzer::LogicAnalyzer);
    ww_impl!(pattern: ww_signal_generator::PatternGenerator);
    ww_impl!(dac: ww_signal_generator::WaveformGenerator);
}

A device with both ww_logic_analyzer and PatternGenerator can replay what it just captured: read the capture out in a shared encoding and feed it straight to the pattern sink, see ww_logic_analyzer.

items.title: ww_spi
items.text:
Part of the IO trait family. ww_spi is a global WireWeaver trait for talking to the SPI devices on a bus remotely: full-duplex transfers, transactions with CS held across several operations, plain writes, and watching a bus without taking part. It is no_std by default and depends only on wire_weaver and ww_si (for the Hertz, Second and Volt quantity types).

Add it to a device API crate with:

[dependencies]
ww_spi = "0.1"

items.title: Traits
items.text:
Spi is one bus: configure it, full-duplex transfers, transactions with CS held, writes, and, on adapters with the hardware for it, every frame on the bus on the optional monitor stream. A device with several buses nests it as an array, ww_impl!(spi[]: ww_spi::Spi), monitoring included:

#[ww_api_root]
trait MyAdapter {
    ww_impl!(spi: ww_spi::Spi);
}

// an adapter without monitoring hardware
ww_codegen!(my_adapter_api::MyAdapter for Server, server = true, omit = ["spi.monitor"]);

items.title: Spi
items.text:
#[ww_trait]
pub trait Spi {
    fn transfer(data: MaxLen<RefVec<'i, u8>, SPI_MAX>) -> Result<MaxLen<RefVec<'i, u8>, SPI_MAX>, SpiError>;

    fn transaction(ops: MaxLen<RefVec<'i, SpiOp<'i>>, MAX_OPS>) -> Result<MaxLen<RefVec<'i, u8>, SPI_MAX>, SpiError>;

    fn write(data: MaxLen<RefVec<'i, u8>, SPI_MAX>) -> Result<(), SpiError>;

    fn capabilities() -> SpiCapabilities<'i>;

    fn configure(config: SpiConfig) -> Result<SpiConfig, SpiError>;

    fn set_cs(active: bool) -> Result<(), SpiError>;

    #[optional]
    #[stream(SpiFrame<'i>, counted)]
    fn monitor(config: SpiMonitorConfig) -> Result<(), SpiError>;
}
  • transfer - full duplex: writes data, returns as many bytes as were read. CS is asserted for the call and released after (CsMode::Auto); with CsMode::Manual the bus must already be selected through set_cs.
  • transaction - CS asserted once for every op of ops, released at the end; returns the bytes of every SpiOp::Read and SpiOp::Transfer, concatenated in order. This is how a command-then-response exchange (write a register address, then read it) stays under one CS assertion instead of two separate transfer calls.
  • write - like transfer, ignoring what comes back.
  • capabilities - frequency range, word sizes, master/slave support, IO levels; see Types below.
  • configure - sets the bus (role, frequency, mode 0-3, bit order, word size, CS mode, IO level) in one SpiConfig and answers with what was actually set: the frequency the hardware settled on, never above what was asked, and the IO level in effect (io_level: None leaves it as it is). SpiRole::Disabled releases the pins.
  • set_cs - asserts or releases CS, only meaningful with CsMode::Manual.
  • monitor - #[optional], a counted stream function: the host opens it with the bus settings needed to decode frames (mode, bit order, word size, IO level) and receives one SpiFrame per CS assertion seen on the bus, in order, until it closes the stream. The monitor doesn't drive CS or the clock itself, it only listens. Its unit is a frame: the event head carries when CS was asserted and how many frames the device dropped (stream delivery). A device without monitoring hardware leaves it out, and a host sees that in the device's introspection.

items.title: Types
items.text:
• SpiConfig - role: SpiRole, freq: Hertz, mode: SpiMode, bit_order: BitOrder, word_bits: u8, cs: CsMode, io_level: Option<Volt>; the argument and the answer of Spi::configure.
  • SpiMonitorConfig - mode, bit_order, word_bits, io_level: the subset of SpiConfig a monitor needs to decode frames, the argument of Spi::monitor.
  • SpiRole - Disabled, Master, Slave. Data paths for slave mode are not defined yet.
  • SpiMode - Mode0..Mode3, the usual CPOL/CPHA numbering; sized, 2 bits.
  • BitOrder - MsbFirst, LsbFirst; sized, 1 bit.
  • CsMode - Auto (asserted per transfer/transaction, released after), Manual (only Spi::set_cs), None (not driven by this device).
  • SpiOp<'i> - one operation of a Spi::transaction: Write, Read(u16), Transfer, Delay(Second).
  • SpiFrame<'i> - one frame seen by Spi::monitor: end: Second (CS released; asserted is the head's time), truncated, mosi / miso: MaxLen<RefVec<'i, u8>, SPI_MAX>.
  • SpiCapabilities<'i> - min_freq / max_freq: Hertz, min_word_bits / max_word_bits: u8, master / slave: bool, io_levels: MaxLen<RefVec<'i, Volt>, MAX_IO_LEVELS>, io_level_min / io_level_max: Option<Volt> (an adjustable supply), max_len: u32 (largest transfer this device does, at most SPI_MAX).
  • SpiError<'i> - Common(CommonError) (common errors), BufferTooBig; unsized (unib32 discriminant), evolvable. Each method lists the variants it returns (#[errors]).

SPI_MAX (512 bytes) bounds every transfer, write and the reads of one transaction concatenated; MAX_OPS (16) bounds the operations of one Spi::transaction. Both are compatible to raise later, not to lower.

items.title: ww_timebase
items.text:
ww_timebase is a global WireWeaver trait for a device's clock: reading device time, and synchronising it with other devices over a sync line (IRIG-B, PPS, ...). It is no_std by default and depends only on wire_weaver, ww_si (for the Second timestamp type) and ww_date_time (for set_time_of_day). It is part of the IO trait family.

Add it to a device API crate with:

[dependencies]
ww_timebase = "0.1"

items.title: Device time (D6)
items.text: Every device has exactly one free-running clock. Every timestamp it reports elsewhere in its API (captures, stream items) is a ww_si::Second since that clock started, in whatever fixed width fits the field, so it wraps (a U32 of microseconds wraps every 71.6 minutes). There is no separate Ticks type and no unbounded UVlq64: the width is picked per field, and Clock::now() always returns the full-width value so a host can unwrap a truncated timestamp and correlate device time with its own.

items.title: Clock
items.text:
#[ww_trait]
pub trait Clock {
    fn now() -> Second;

    fn info() -> ClockInfo<'i>;

    stream!(time_map: TimeMapPoint);

    fn configure_sync(config: SyncConfig) -> Result<(), ClockError>;

    fn sync_config() -> SyncConfig;

    fn sync_status() -> SyncStatus;

    fn set_time_of_day(t: DateTime) -> Result<(), ClockError>;
}
  • now() - device time now, full width.
  • info() - static description of this clock: its resolution, what it calls itself, and which SyncFormats it supports.
  • time_map - local time mapped to the shared sync time, sent about once a second while synced and on every SyncState change, so a host can line up this device's timeline with others and see the unsynced spans.
  • configure_sync / sync_config - switch sync off, or make this device the master on the sync line, or a slave locking to one, in a given SyncFormat; sync_config() reads back the last accepted configuration.
  • sync_status() - current sync state, with the offset and local time of the last lock, when known.
  • set_time_of_day - time of day a sync master sends on the sync line, set from its host; has no effect on a slave or while sync is off.

items.title: Types
items.text:
• ClockInfo<'i> - resolution: Second, source: MaxLen<&'i str, 32> (e.g. "RP2350 TIMER0"), sync_formats: MaxLen<RefVec<'i, SyncFormat>, 8> (empty without a sync line).
  • SyncConfig - Off, Master { format: SyncFormat }, Slave { format: SyncFormat }; unib32 discriminant, evolvable.
  • SyncFormat - IrigB, Pps; unib32 discriminant, evolvable.
  • SyncStatus - state: SyncState, offset: Option<Second> (local minus shared time at the last lock), last_lock: Option<Second>.
  • SyncState - Free, Acquiring, Locked, Holdover; unib32 discriminant, evolvable.
  • TimeMapPoint - one time_map item: local: Second, shared: Second, state: SyncState.
  • ClockError<'i> - Common(CommonError) (common errors); unsized (unib32 discriminant), evolvable.

All enums and structs are behind #[derive_shrink_wrap] with owned(feature = "std"), so owned (*Owned) variants are available by enabling the crate's std feature.

items.title: Composing into a device API
items.text:
A device exposes its clock once at the root (or nested, if grouped with other traits):

#[ww_api_root]
pub trait DeviceApi {
    ww_impl!(clock: ww_timebase::Clock);
    // ... other traits
}

items.title: Server and client usage (tests/io_timebase)
items.text:
There is no dedicated example crate yet (no device in this repo has a sync line); tests/io_timebase is the reference mock server and client, driven through tests_common::start_device like a real device over USB. A sync master, locking immediately, then publishing a time_map point:

client
    .clock()
    .configure_sync(SyncConfig::Master { format: SyncFormat::IrigB })
    .call()
    .await?; // one `?`: a `ClockError` arrives as `CallError::Device`

let mut time_map = client.clock().time_map().call().await?;
let point = time_map.recv().await?;
assert_eq!(point.state, SyncState::Locked);

On the server side, a handler sends a time_map update at any point it decides the sync state changed, same as any other stream item:

fn clock_configure_sync(
    &mut self,
    cx: &mut Context<'_, impl BlockingEventOut>,
    config: SyncConfig,
) -> RpcResult<Result<(), ClockError>> {
    // ... update state ...
    api_impl::stream_data_ser()
        .clock()
        .time_map_send_blocking(&point, cx)
        .unwrap();
    Ready(Ok(()))
}

See tests/io_timebase/src/lib.rs for the full mock (a real Instant-backed clock, an IrigB-only sync line to exercise ClockError::Unsupported, and a slave that locks right away instead of staying Acquiring).

items.title: ww_uart
items.text:
Part of the IO trait family. ww_uart is a WireWeaver trait for bridging a UART (serial port) to the host, and for watching both lines of a serial link without driving them. It is no_std by default and depends on wire_weaver and ww_si (for Baud rates, the Volt reference-voltage type and Second timestamps).

Add it to a device API crate with:

[dependencies]
ww_uart = "0.1"

items.title: Traits
items.text: Uart is one port: configure it, receive on rx, send on the tx credit sink, and, on ports with the hardware for it, watch both lines of a link between two other devices on the optional monitor stream. It composes with the rest of the API using ww_impl! and is nested as an array when a device has more than one UART (ww_impl!(uart[]: ww_uart::Uart), as examples/uart_api does); monitoring comes with each element, no second array or trait to keep in step.

items.title: Uart
items.text:
#[ww_trait]
pub trait Uart {
    #[counted]
    stream!(rx: RxChunk<'i>);

    #[credit]
    sink!(tx: MaxLen<RefVec<'i, u8>, UART_TX_MAX>);

    fn capabilities() -> Capabilities<'i>;

    fn configure(config: UartConfig) -> Result<UartConfig, Error>;

    fn set_pin_level(pin: Pin, is_high: bool) -> Result<(), Error>;
    fn send_break(duration: Second) -> Result<(), Error>;
    fn tx_pending() -> u32;

    #[optional]
    #[stream(MonitorChunk<'i>, counted)]
    fn monitor(config: MonitorConfig) -> Result<MonitorConfig, Error>;
}
  • rx - received bytes, chunked as they arrive (see RxChunk below). A chunk ends when the line stays idle for more than UartConfig::idle_chars character times, when it is full, or on a line error, so each chunk is one burst of back-to-back characters (a frame of most protocols, or the part of it that fit). A counted stream, opened by calling it: its unit is a byte, so the event head carries each chunk's byte position, the device time of its first byte, and exactly how many bytes the device dropped before it (stream delivery); the chunk itself says when its last byte arrived, if the device measures it (Time below).
  • tx - bytes to send, a credit sink (API-28): the host tracks the device's TX buffer (Capabilities::tx_buffer) and never sends more than it holds, so a large write (e.g. a file piped to the UART) can't overrun it.
  • capabilities() - what this device supports: baud rate range, flow control modes, IO levels, buffer sizes.
  • configure - the whole line configuration in one UartConfig (baud rate, data bits, parity, stop bits, mode, back-feed detector, IO level, the idle time that ends a chunk), answered with what was actually set: the hardware rounds the baud rate to what its divider can do and the idle time to what its receiver can time, and io_level: None keeps the level and is answered with the level in effect. One call instead of a property per setting, so a port never runs with half a configuration.
  • set_pin_level - manual control of a pin, only in Mode::Test; every other mode answers Common(WrongState).
  • send_break - holds TX low for duration (a break condition), after the bytes already queued.
  • tx_pending() - bytes queued for sending and not sent yet.
  • monitor - #[optional], a counted stream function: the host opens it with the line settings of the watched link (baud rate, data bits, parity, stop bits, IO level) and gets back what was actually set (as Uart::configure does), then both directions of the link (rePort: RX and CTS/RX2) in one stream, in the order they arrived: each MonitorChunk says which MonitorLine it came from, so a request and its answer stay in order. Closing the stream stops receiving. The unit is a byte of either line. Most bridges can't sniff a link they aren't part of: such a device leaves it out with omit = ["uart.monitor"] in its ww_codegen!, and a host sees that in the device's introspection.

items.title: Time
items.text:
Every received chunk, on rx and on monitor, says when it arrived, on the device's one clock (ww_timebase::Clock) that also timestamps everything else the device captures:

What Where first byte arrived (end of its stop bit) the event head's t always set last byte arrived RxChunk::end: Option<Second> set by devices that measure it

The bytes of a chunk came back to back, so the time of each one follows from the first. Byte i (from 0) of a chunk of n bytes arrived at:

  • first + i * (end - first) / (n - 1) when end is set. This takes up the sender's baud rate error: UARTs accept 2-3 % off the nominal rate, which adds up to milliseconds over a long burst, so a device that can time the last byte does.
  • first + i * frame_bits / baud when it isn't: frame_bits is start + data + parity + stop bits (UartConfig::frame_bits(), 10 for 8N1) and baud the rate configure answered. The last byte is then at first + (n - 1) * frame_bits / baud.

All are ww_si::Seconds since the device's clock started, in the prefix and number type the device picks (usually a u32 of microseconds, which wraps every 71.6 minutes; the host unwraps it around Clock::now()). With them a host:

  • lines up serial traffic with the device's other data: a GPIO edge, an ADC sample, an I2C transaction;
  • tells a request and its answer apart in time on a monitor link, and measures the turnaround between them;
  • sees the gaps on the line: a chunk ends on a silence of more than idle_chars character times, so the next chunk's first byte comes at least that much after the previous chunk's last one.

On the client the head's time is the t of StreamEvent::Item (rx.recv_event()), next to the chunk:

let actual = client.uart().configure(config).call().await??;
let char_time = actual.frame_bits().unwrap() as f64 / actual.baud_rate.to_f64();
let mut rx = client.uart().rx().call().await?;
loop {
    match rx.recv_event().await? {
        StreamEvent::Item { t: Some(first), value, .. } => {
            let n = value.bytes.len();
            // measured, or one character time per byte after the first
            let last = value.end.map(|end| end.to_f64())
                .unwrap_or(first.to_f64() + (n - 1) as f64 * char_time);
            println!("{n} bytes from {:.6} s to {last:.6} s", first.to_f64());
        }
        StreamEvent::Gap { units, .. } => println!("{units} bytes lost"),
        _ => {}
    }
}

A device that can't time each byte (a DMA that hands over a block when the line goes idle) times the block's end from the idle interrupt, sends it as end, and takes the first byte a character time per byte earlier at the configured baud rate, as examples_mcu/usb_stm32h725ig does.

idle_chars defaults to IDLE_CHARS_DEFAULT (2): a gap of one character time would split the output of senders that pause briefly between characters (a CPU feeding its UART byte by byte, a USB-serial bridge between its USB packets), more would merge the frames of protocols that keep only a short gap between them (Modbus RTU separates frames by 3.5 character times, which 2 still splits). A protocol with its own rule sets it in UartConfig.

items.title: Types
items.text:
• ww_si::Baud - a baud rate (Baud::baud(115_200u32)), in the number type and prefix the caller picks, like every other ww_si quantity.
  • Mode - Asynchronous (no flow control), HardwareFlowControl (RTS/CTS), SoftwareFlowControl (XON/XOFF), HighZ (all pins High-Z), Test (manual pin control through set_pin_level).
  • Pin - Tx, Rx, Rts, Cts, used by set_pin_level.
  • StopBits - Stop1, Stop2.
  • Parity - None, Odd, Even.
  • DataBits - Eight, Seven, Nine, Six, Five.
  • UartError<'i> - Common(CommonError) (common errors); unsized, evolvable. Each method lists the variants it returns (#[errors]); line errors of received data are RxFlags of the chunk, not errors.
  • RxChunk<'i> - end: Option<Second> (when the last byte arrived, if the device measures it), flags: Option<RxFlags>, bytes: MaxLen<RefVec<'i, u8>, UART_CHUNK_MAX>; when the first byte arrived is the time in the event head, see Time.
  • MonitorChunk<'i> - line: MonitorLine (A or B, 1 bit), chunk: RxChunk<'i>.
  • RxFlags - parity_error, framing_error, overrun, break_detected, seen while receiving a chunk.
  • UartConfig - baud_rate: Baud, data_bits, parity, stop_bits, mode, prevent_back_feed: bool, io_level: Option<Volt>, idle_chars: u8 (idle character times that end a chunk); the argument and the answer of configure. frame_bits() is the bits of one character on the line (start + data + parity + stop).
  • MonitorConfig - baud_rate, data_bits, parity, stop_bits, io_level, idle_chars of the link Uart::monitor watches; the argument and the answer of monitor.
  • Capabilities<'i> - min_baud_rate / max_baud_rate: Baud, io_levels: MaxLen<RefVec<'i, Volt>, MAX_IO_LEVELS>, io_level_min / io_level_max: Option<Volt> (an adjustable supply), hw_flow_control / sw_flow_control / high_z_mode / test_mode / back_feed_detector: bool, rx_buffer / tx_buffer: u32 (device receive and transmit buffer sizes, in bytes).

All enums and structs are behind #[derive_shrink_wrap] with owned(feature = "std"), so owned (*Owned) variants are available by enabling the crate's std feature; the plain configuration enums (Mode, Pin, StopBits, Parity, DataBits) also derive PartialEq/Eq.

items.title: Composing into a device API
items.text:
A device exposes a UART by implementing Uart on its API root:

#[ww_api_root]
pub trait MyDeviceApi {
    ww_impl!(uart: ww_uart::Uart);
}

// a port without monitoring hardware
ww_codegen!(my_device_api::MyDeviceApi for Server, server = true, omit = ["uart.monitor"]);

tests/io_uart_api is exactly this shape (used by tests/io_uart's mock server and in-process tests); a device with more than one UART nests it as an array instead (ww_impl!(uart[]: ww_uart::Uart), see examples/uart_api).

items.title: Client usage (examples/uart)
items.text:
The generated client wraps wire_weaver_client::Commander; see examples/uart/src/lib.rs for the small UartBridge wrapper type (connecting over USB with a fixed VID/PID). Sending bytes through the tx credit sink (examples/uart/examples/simple.rs):

let device = UartBridge::new().connect().await?;
let mut tx = device.uart(0).tx().await?;
tx.send_bytes(b"abc000def").await?;

Receiving chunks from rx and configuring the port look the same as any other nested trait, method and stream (see streams); for a non-array uart resource (as in tests/io_uart_api) the same calls drop the index: client.uart().rx(), client.uart().configure(config).

items.title: ww_uid
items.text:
ww_uid lists the unique ids of a unit: a chip's factory id, a MAC address, an EUI-64. One trait implemented once can carry several, which one-trait-per-id could not (a trait cannot be implemented twice on one server).

#[ww_trait]
pub trait Uid {
    const IDS: MaxLen<RefVec<'i, UniqueId<'i>>, 4>;
}

IDS is a const item, served without a handler and read by a host once per connection. Ids are read from the chip at boot, so a server provides them as a fn (const_model = "IDS=fn", fn uid_ids(&self) -> MaxLen<RefVec<'_, UniqueId<'_>>, 4> for uid: Uid). At most 4 ids.

items.title: The primary id
items.text: The first id is the primary id. A device puts its hex (lower case, no separators) into the USB serial number string and a host shows it in ww list. When the unit reboots into a ROM bootloader that reports the same id (RP2350 BOOTSEL, STM32 DFU) the host finds it again by it; see follow reboot.

items.title: UniqueId
items.text:
• kind: UidKind - ChipUnique, Mac48, Eui64, Uuid, Other(name).
  • source: UidSource - InternalIc, ExternalIc, Firmware, HardwareStraps, Other(name).
  • value - up to 16 bytes.

Both enums are public and evolvable: a variant from a newer version reads as Unknown(u32).

items.title: ww_user_info
items.text:
A name and notes the user gives a unit, shown by ww list.

#[ww_trait]
pub trait UserInfo {
    const CAPABILITIES: UserInfoCaps;
    property!(rw name: MaxLen<&'i str, 32>, UserInfoError<'i>);
    #[optional]
    property!(rw notes: MaxLen<&'i str, 256>, UserInfoError<'i>);
}

CAPABILITIES (name_max, notes_max, persistent) says what this device keeps: a device may keep less than the bounds of 32 and 256 bytes, and a device without room for notes leaves them out with omit = ["user.notes"] (notes_max is then 0). It is a const item, usually a Rust const in the server's consts impl.

items.title: Errors
items.text: A write returns UserInfoError: Common(CommonError) (see ww_error) or TooLong { max } with what the device keeps. Common(Busy) means storage can't be touched right now, Common(Fault) that saving failed. The property syntax has no per-property #[errors] list yet, so the doc comment names the variants a device returns.

items.title: Persistence
items.text:
• When persistent, a write is saved before the call answers: Ok means it survives a power cut.
  • A device writes its storage only when the value changed, so a host may write the same value again freely (flash wear).
  • A failed write leaves the old value in place.

items.title: ww_version
items.text:
ww_version is SemVer for no_std targets: a nibble-packed Version/FullVersion pair that compiles into every #[ww_trait]/#[ww_api_root] to identify an API's crate and version on the wire, plus CompactVersion for identifying it even more cheaply once it has a global type id. It is no_std by default and depends only on shrink_wrap and ww_global (for GlobalTypeId).

Add it to a device API crate with:

[dependencies]
ww_version = "0.2"

items.title: Types
items.text:
• Version<'i> - major / minor / patch: UNib32, optional pre / build: Option<&'i str> (the -alpha.1 and +zstd.1.5.0 parts of a SemVer string); final_structure. pre participates in compatibility checks, build is metadata only.
  • FullVersion<'i> - crate_id: &'i str, version: Version<'i>; final_structure. Identifies an API crate by name and version, the same two pieces of information that make a crate's identity on crates.io.
  • CompactVersion - gid: GlobalTypeId, major / minor / patch: UNib32; final_structure. Stands in for a FullVersion once the API has a global type id, for requests made often or over a bandwidth-limited link.
  • VersionTriplet - plain major / minor / patch: UNib32, no crate name; final_structure. For comparing versions where a name isn't needed.
  • ApiHashPair<'i> - no_docs / with_docs: ApiHash<'i>; final_structure. Two hashes of a device's ApiBundle, with and without doc strings, so a client can detect any change to the API (not just ones that bumped the version) while still being able to drop doc strings to save flash and fall back to a cached full ApiBundle for compatibility checks.
  • ApiHash<'i> - hash: RefVec<'i, u8>; final_structure. One hash value, Debug-formatted as hex.

Every struct derives PartialEq, Eq (except ApiHash, no Eq) and Clone; the borrowed variants also derive Copy. Enabling std adds owned (*Owned) counterparts (String instead of &str, Vec<u8> instead of RefVec).

items.title: Compatibility checks
items.text: Version::is_protocol_compatible implements SemVer's own rule: once major >= 1, two versions are compatible when major matches; below 1.0, minor must match too (pre-1.0 minor is the breaking position, same convention this project's own crates follow). pre is not compared by this rule - it answers "can these talk to each other", not "are these the exact same build". FullVersion::is_protocol_compatible additionally requires the same crate_id, and CompactVersion::is_protocol_compatible the same gid.

items.title: Reading the current crate's version
items.text: Version, FullVersion and CompactVersion all have a const fn new(..) (plus Version::full for pre/build and CompactVersion/VersionTriplet likewise), but code using WireWeaver's codegen rarely builds one directly. wire_weaver::full_version!() and wire_weaver::compact_version!(gid) (from wire_weaver_derive) expand to a FullVersion/Option<CompactVersion> built from the calling crate's own Cargo.toml version (CARGO_PKG_NAME, CARGO_PKG_VERSION_*) at compile time. #[ww_trait] and #[ww_api_root] use exactly these macros to emit a <TRAIT>_FULL_GID: FullVersion and <TRAIT>_COMPACT_GID: Option<CompactVersion> constant next to every API trait - compact_version! returns None unless the trait was given a global type id (#[ww_trait(gid)]).

items.title: On the wire
items.text:
Version packs major/minor/patch as UNib32 (one nibble each for values below 8) with the two Option presence flags for pre/build relocated next to them via #[flag], so 0.1.2 with no pre-release or build metadata is 2 bytes total; a fully populated version only grows by exactly the bytes its pre/build strings need. final_structure on every type here means no reverse-length is written for the type itself when it's the last field of something else - see size assumptions.

ww_client_server's own Request/Event model uses CompactVersion for the common case of addressing a global trait by id (2 extra bytes when every number is ≤ 7) and falls back to FullVersion only for the one-off case of calling into an arbitrary crates.io trait by name - see ww_client_server.

items.title: Features
items.text: Feature What std (default) owned (*Owned) type variants, plus hex-based Display for ApiHashOwned defmt defmt::Format on the borrowed types serde serde::Serialize/Deserialize (owned types for Version/FullVersion; directly on CompactVersion/VersionTriplet, which hold no borrowed data) semver TryFrom<semver::Version>/TryInto<semver::Version> for VersionOwned

items.title: Following a reboot: RP2350 BOOTSEL
items.text:
A device that updates in place can leave the job to the chip's boot ROM: the app reboots into the ROM bootloader, the host writes the new image, the ROM boots it. On the RP2350 (and RP2040) that is BOOTSEL mode, where the ROM offers a UF2 drive and PICOBOOT, the USB interface picotool speaks. Nothing of WireWeaver runs there, so the host has to find the same unit again after each reboot, talk PICOBOOT to it, and find it once more when the new firmware is up. This is CLT-21 in the features, and the "update stage 1" of the rePort.

app (WireWeaver)        boot ROM (BOOTSEL)               app (WireWeaver), new image
 serial = chip id  ──►   serial = chip id   ──►            serial = chip id
 BootControl::reboot     PICOBOOT: erase, write,
   (Updater)               verify, REBOOT2

items.title: What the firmware does
items.text:
• Report the chip id as the USB serial number, in the boot ROM's format: the 64-bit id (GET_INFO SYS chip info, or OTP), 16 hex digits, high word first. wire_weaver_client::follow::rp2350_serial(chip_id) makes the same string on the host. Matching ignores case, as all device filters do.
  • Implement ww_dfu::UpdateNode and BootControl (the lean app of the ww_dfu scenarios), with Role::App, Profile::InPlace, Offers { boot_control: true, .. }. reboot(Updater) replies first, then calls the ROM's reboot into BOOTSEL (rom_reboot(REBOOT2_FLAG_REBOOT_TYPE_BOOTSEL, ..)) a few tens of milliseconds later, so the reply leaves.
  • Keep PICOBOOT enabled in BOOTSEL (don't pass BOOTSEL_FLAG_DISABLE_PICOBOOT_INTERFACE, don't disable it in OTP).

items.title: What the host does
items.text:
follow::rp2_update() and the wire_weaver_client::ww_picoboot re-export need the picoboot Cargo feature of wire_weaver_client (off by default, pulls in ww_picoboot and its nusb-backed PICOBOOT transport): most host apps that only talk WireWeaver over USB never flash an RP2040 / RP2350 boot ROM, so they shouldn't pay for it. follow::rp2_update_with() and follow::Follow/Bus/Found stay available without it — that is what tests/follow_reboot runs against a simulated device.

use wire_weaver_client::follow;
use wire_weaver_client::ww_picoboot::{Image, image::family};

let serial = device_info.serials[0].clone(); // as listed, before the reboot
app.boot().reboot(BootTarget::Updater).call().await?;
drop(app);

let image = Image::from_uf2(&std::fs::read("app.uf2")?, &[family::RP2350_ARM_S])?;
let back = follow::rp2_update(&serial, &image, &mut ()).await?; // DeviceInfo of the app that came back
let app = App::config(|c| c.usb().serial_eq(serial)).connect().await?;

rp2_update waits for the BOOTSEL device with the serial number (10 s), opens its PICOBOOT interface, writes and verifies the image, sends REBOOT2 as picotool load -x does (FLASH_UPDATE at the image's base, 500 ms delay) and waits for a WireWeaver device with the same serial number (10 s). A timeout says what was there instead, e.g. the app still running because it ignored the reboot request.

The pieces work on their own too:

  • follow::Follow waits on any follow::Bus (UsbBus lists real USB devices): gone() until no device has the serial number (needed when the device reboots into the same kind of firmware; it has to stay off the bus longer than Follow::poll, 50 ms, which USB re-enumeration always does), back() with a predicate on follow::Found (WireWeaver, RpBootsel, Other), back_in_bootsel(), back_in_wire_weaver().
  • follow::rp2_update_with() takes the bus and the PICOBOOT opener as arguments: that is how the tests run it on a simulated device.
  • ww_picoboot is the PICOBOOT host on its own: usb::open(Some(serial)) gives a Picoboot with flash() (erase the touched 4 KiB sectors, write 256-byte pages, read back, with a progress callback), read, write, flash_erase, chip_id, reboot2. Image comes from a UF2 file (blocks of the given families; picotool's RP2350-E10 dummy block is skipped) or a raw binary at an address. No libusb: nusb, pure Rust. It lives in its own repo, picoboot_host (crate name picoboot_host, re-exported here as ww_picoboot), with no WireWeaver dependency of its own.

items.title: From the command line
items.text:
ww bootsel list                                   # boot ROMs in BOOTSEL mode with their serial numbers
ww bootsel info -s E661                           # chip id over PICOBOOT
ww bootsel flash app.uf2 -s E661                  # erase, write, verify, reboot into the new image
ww bootsel flash app.uf2 -s E661640843522C2F --wait 10 --follow
                                                  # after the app was asked to reboot(Updater): wait for the
                                                  # boot ROM, flash, wait for the app to come back
ww bootsel reboot -s E661 [--bootsel]

-s / --serial selects the device as for every other command (flag, WW_SERIAL, ww.toml), a part of the serial number is enough when only one device matches; --wait and --follow need the full one. A raw binary (any extension other than .uf2) is written at --addr, 0x10000000 by default. On Linux the boot ROM (2e8a:000f) needs a udev rule for access without root, as picotool does.

Asking the app to reboot from the CLI needs calls to ww_dfu::BootControl on any device, whatever its API version: CLT-10 and API-20 (the rePort design's WW-2). Until then the host program that knows the device's API does it.

items.title: Tests without hardware
items.text: ww_picoboot::sim::SimRp2350 (feature sim) is a boot ROM at the level of PICOBOOT's USB transfers: command packets, data phases, zero-length status packets, stalls on refused commands, IF_RESET / IF_CMD_STATUS, flash that only clears bits when programmed. tests/follow_reboot puts it under a simulated RP2350 device whose app (the dfu_lean_app_api server on the in-process simulated USB) boots from that flash and reports the image version, and runs the whole sequence: v1 → reboot(Updater) → BOOTSEL under the same serial → v2 written over PICOBOOT → v2 runs. What only hardware shows: real enumeration times, the ROM's exact serial number string, REBOOT2 behaviour with partition tables, Windows and macOS drivers.

items.title: Transport protocols
items.text:
Several transport protocols are supported:

  • USB (nusb on host side, embassy on embedded, no drivers needed on Windows/Mac/Linux)
  • RTT over a debug probe (rtt-target on embedded, probe-rs on host side), see RTT
  • WebSocket (host side, for devices on a network), see WebSocket
  • UDP (for devices on a network, best for telemetry), see UDP
  • TODO: CAN Bus (using CANOpen)

Others could be easily implemented, possibly reusing the same code.

USB and UDP transports support multiple events per packet/datagram. Many small messages can be accumulated over a time window conserving bandwidth and allowing much higher message throughput per unit of time that would otherwise be possible with one message per packet/datagram.

items.title: RTT
items.text:
RTT (SEGGER Real-Time Transfer) turns the debug probe that is already attached to a dev board into a transport: an up channel (device → host) and a down channel (host → device) are ring buffers in the device's RAM, read and written by the probe over SWD / JTAG. No USB peripheral, no UART wiring, and it works next to defmt logging, which uses another RTT channel.

Useful when a board has no USB, when the USB peripheral is taken by something else, or to try an API out before any transport hardware exists.

items.title: Device side
items.text:
Device support is in ww_device behind the rtt feature, on top of the rtt-target crate. Create the channels with rtt_init!, hand one pair to rtt_server() and run the same Server loop as for USB:

use ww_device::rtt::{RttBuffers, RttConfig, rtt_server};
use ww_device::{EmbassyClock, LinkConfig};

const MAX_MESSAGE_LEN: usize = 1024;
static RTT_BUFFERS: StaticCell<RttBuffers<MAX_MESSAGE_LEN>> = StaticCell::new();

let channels = rtt_init! {
    up: {
        0: { size: 1024, mode: NoBlockSkip, name: "defmt" }
        1: { size: 2048, mode: NoBlockSkip, name: "ww_up" }
    }
    down: {
        0: { size: 2048, mode: NoBlockSkip, name: "ww_down" }
    }
};
rtt_target::set_defmt_channel(channels.up.0);

let link_config = LinkConfig::new(
    blinky_api::BLINKY_API_FULL_GID,
    server_impl::api_hash(),
    ww_client_server::COMPACT_VERSION,
);
let mut server = rtt_server(
    link_config,
    channels.up.1,
    channels.down.0,
    EmbassyClock,
    RttConfig::default(),
    RTT_BUFFERS.init(RttBuffers::new()),
);
server.run(&mut state).await;

examples_mcu/rp2/src/bin/ww_rtt.rs (just run rp2 ww_rtt) and examples_mcu/nucleo_g0b1re/src/bin/ww_rtt.rs (just run nucleo ww_rtt) are complete examples, serving the same blinky API as usb_blinky. examples/blinky has the matching host side: cargo run -p blinky --features rtt --example blinky_rtt -- --chip STM32G0B1RETx.

items.title: Sizing
items.text:
• MAX_MESSAGE_LEN is the longest message the device accepts and the longest reply it can serialize, reported to the host as is. RttBuffers takes 3 * MAX_MESSAGE_LEN plus a few bytes of framing overhead.
  • RTT channel buffers are separate, allocated by rtt_init!. A chunk (one or more messages, up to MAX_MESSAGE_LEN plus framing) is written to the up channel in one go, and in NoBlockSkip mode a write that does not fit is skipped entirely, so the up channel must be at least MAX_MESSAGE_LEN + 5 bytes, better twice that. NoBlockTrim works too. BlockIfFull must not be used: it spins forever when no host reads.
  • The down channel only needs to hold what the host writes between two polls.

items.title: Timing
items.text:
RTT has no notion of a connection and cannot wake the device: the down channel is polled every RttConfig::poll_interval (1 ms by default), which bounds the request latency, and the same interval is used to retry a write into a full up channel. A host that is gone shows up as an up channel that stays full for RttConfig::write_timeout (500 ms), and in any case as the link's peer timeout (10 s without a message).

A probe polls the target on its own schedule, so the round trip is set by the host side (probe-rs polling interval, SWD clock) rather than by the device.

items.title: Framing
items.text:
RTT is a byte stream: what the device writes as one chunk may be read by the host in any number of pieces, and the other way around, so the framer is used in stream mode — every message is a Full one, never split across chunks (Tx::write_full), and the receiver cuts messages out of the stream by their length (StreamTx / StreamRx in ww_device). The configuration is RttHead / RttChecksum / RttTail from ww_link: U2Head, no checksum and no tail, since the ring buffers are in RAM and cannot corrupt bytes, and NoBlockSkip writes are atomic, so nothing is lost mid-message either.

Without a delimiter there is nothing to re-synchronize on: a message larger than the receiver's buffer is skipped, but the bytes that follow are misinterpreted until the transport is reset. The device reports its MAX_MESSAGE_LEN during link setup, a host must never send more than that.

Many small messages are still packed into one chunk, accumulated for the window the device asks for in DeviceInfo (1 ms by default); control messages are flushed right away.

items.title: Host side
items.text:
wire_weaver_client connects over RTT with the rtt feature, through probe-rs. Select it with ClientConfig::rtt(target, speed_hz), where target is the probe-rs chip name (the same one probe-rs run --chip takes) and speed_hz is the SWD / JTAG clock (None for the probe's default):

let config = ClientConfig::new().rtt("RP2040".into(), None);
  • Probe selection: with a single probe connected, it is used. Otherwise, pick one with usb_vid_pid(..), serial_eq(..) or serial_contains(..) placed after .rtt(..). Filters before it describe the device behind the probe, which is not known before connecting, and are not used to select the probe, so a driver crate's config works as is: Blinky::default_config().rtt("RP2040".into(), None).serial_contains("820102657".into()). The device API is checked during link setup as usual. WireWeaver USB is not tried when RTT is selected.
  • Attaching does not reset the core, a running firmware is attached to as is. probe-rs halts it for a few milliseconds to clear hardware breakpoints, on attach and on detach. RAM is scanned for the RTT control block, which takes a noticeable time on chips with a lot of RAM (about 1.5 s for 144 KiB on an STM32G0 through an ST-LINK V2-1). In case the firmware has just started and has not initialized RTT yet, the scan is retried for 2 s, and at least once, however long a single scan takes. To skip the scan, pass the firmware's ELF file with .rtt_elf(path) (the address of the _SEGGER_RTT symbol is taken from it, attaching then takes tens of milliseconds), or the address itself with .rtt_control_block_at(address). If the running firmware doesn't match the file, RAM is scanned anyway after 0.5 s, with a warning; a file that can't be read or has no RTT fails the connection. Then channels named ww_up and ww_down are looked up, so these names must be used on the device side. Connecting returns only once all this is done. Whatever is left in the up channel from a previous host is dropped. Nothing else may use the probe at the same time, e.g., a probe-rs run or a debugger session showing defmt logs: a probe can only be opened once.
  • Polling: probe-rs is a blocking API and RTT cannot notify the host, so a dedicated thread polls the up channel and writes to the down channel, sleeping 1 ms whenever there was nothing to do. Each poll is a few probe USB transfers, so the round trip is a few milliseconds, depending on the probe.

items.title: Limitations
items.text:
• defmt logs go to another up channel of the same control block, but can't be read while the client holds the probe.
  • A message larger than the other side's buffer is skipped, but the stream is out of sync until the link is set up again (see Framing). Both sides advertise and respect their maximum message length, so this only happens on a bug.

items.title: See also
items.text:
• ww_link — session lifecycle, messages, how the device runs it
  • ww_framer — head layout, write_full for stream media
  • USB — the primary transport

items.title: UDP
items.text: Connects the host to a device on a network over UDP: low overhead and no connection state, for telemetry-heavy devices, where a lost stream event now and then is better than a stall while TCP retransmits.

items.title: Host side
items.text:
Enable the udp feature of wire_weaver_client and select the device by address:

let blinky = Blinky::config(|c| c.udp_addr("192.168.1.10:9000"))
    .connect()
    .await?;

Host names are resolved when connecting (my-device.local:9000), the first address is used. IPv6 works too ([fe80::1%2]:9000).

Everything above the medium is the same as with USB or WebSocket: link setup, version check, introspection, pings, timeouts, streams. There is no discovery, so device filters (serial, label, ...) are not checked before connecting.

The host socket is connected to the device address: datagrams from anyone else are dropped by the OS, and if nothing listens on the device port, the ICMP error fails the connection right away (on Linux and macOS) instead of after the link setup retries.

items.title: Wire format
items.text:
Each datagram is one ww_framer frame, with ww_link's UDP configuration: UdpHead (U2Head), UdpChecksum (CRC-16 on split messages only) and UdpTail (none). Same as over USB, small messages accumulated by the event loop share a datagram and big ones are split across several.

The host sends datagrams of at most ww_link::UDP_MAX_DATAGRAM_LEN (1452 B: Ethernet MTU minus IPv6 and UDP headers, so that nothing is fragmented over IPv4 or IPv6), the device must be able to receive datagrams of this size. The host accepts datagrams of any size, the device picks its own frame size.

items.title: Reliability
items.text:
Nothing is retransmitted:

  • a lost request (or its reply) times out, as a request to a busy device would;
  • a lost stream event is gone;
  • a message split across datagrams is dropped if any piece of it is lost or reordered, the framer detects it from the remaining length and the CRC, and continues with the next one;
  • link setup survives losses, GetDeviceInfo is retried;
  • if the device goes away silently, the peer timeout ends the session.

Keep messages that must not be lost small enough to fit in one datagram, or use WebSocket if the device can run TCP.

items.title: Device side
items.text:
The udp feature of ww_device is the device end: ww_device::udp::UdpSink / UdpSource send and receive datagrams on any DatagramSocket (receive from anyone, send to an address), and FramedTx / FramedRx do the framing on top, as over USB. They run the same Server loop. The embassy-net feature adds EmbassyNetUdpSocket on an embassy-net UDP socket, and udp_server() puts it all together:

let socket = UdpSocket::new(stack, rx_meta, rx_buf, tx_meta, tx_buf);
let socket = EmbassyNetUdpSocket::bind(socket, 9000).unwrap();
let conn = UDP_CONNECTION.init(UdpConnection::new(socket));
let mut server = udp_server(link_config, conn, EmbassyClock, UDP_BUFFERS.init(UdpBuffers::new()));
server.run(&mut state).await;

UDP has no connections, so the device serves one host (peer) at a time and replies to it only:

  • a host is adopted when it starts link setup: the first message of its datagram is Nop or GetDeviceInfo, which the host sends alone before anything else;
  • datagrams from other hosts are dropped, unless they start link setup: then the new host replaces the current one, as if another process opened a USB device. The device reports LinkEvent::Down(DownReason::Transport), starts over and handles the datagram that started the takeover, so the new host connects without waiting for a retry;
  • a host that is gone is noticed by the peer timeout, there is nothing to close.

There is no authentication, anyone who can reach the port can take over. Put the device on a trusted network, or use a medium with access control.

  • No allocation: UdpBuffers<MAX_MESSAGE_LEN> holds the reassembly, tx datagram and scratch buffers (3 * MAX_MESSAGE_LEN + 2 * UDP_MAX_DATAGRAM_LEN bytes). Datagrams are received straight into the framer.
  • Device datagrams are UDP_MAX_DATAGRAM_LEN at most too. The socket's own buffers must fit at least one such datagram each way.
  • server.wait() is cancel-safe, so it can be selected on together with anything else.
  • EmbassyNetUdpSocket gives up on a send after 1 s (set_send_timeout), e.g., when the network interface is down, so the link goes down instead of blocking the event loop.
  • The medium is not Send (the peer is kept in a Cell), as with the other embassy based media; on tokio, run it on a LocalSet. wire_weaver_client/src/udp.rs has a device on tokio::net::UdpSocket in its tests.

examples_mcu/rp2 has a complete example, ww_udp_ncm: the board shows up on the host as a USB CDC-NCM Ethernet adapter, runs embassy-net with a static address and a small DHCP server, so the host is configured automatically, and serves the blinky API at 192.168.7.1:9000. Run it with just run rp2 ww_udp_ncm from examples_mcu/rp2, then blink from the host with cargo run -p blinky --features udp --example blinky_udp.

items.title: USB
items.text: USB is the primary transport for embedded devices: fast, always available on a dev board, and — because WireWeaver uses a vendor-specific interface with plain bulk or interrupt endpoints — it needs no drivers on Windows, macOS or Linux. The host side is nusb, a pure-Rust USB library, so there is no libusb to ship either.

items.title: What you get
items.text:
• Plug and play: connect by VID:PID, by physical port (bus + port chain, survives re-enumeration), by serial string, or just "any WireWeaver device". Hot-plug is handled — a device that disappears fails outstanding requests and can be re-connected without touching the rest of the application.
  • High message rate: many small requests and events are packed into one USB packet, so throughput is bounded by bandwidth, not by packets per second. Large messages are transparently split across packets and reassembled.
  • Full duplex: sending and receiving never block each other on the host, so a device that is busy answering cannot stall the host and vice versa (see ww_link for why this matters).
  • Version and identity check during link setup, before any application data flows.
  • Tracing: with the usb-tracing feature every packet in both directions is published over iceoryx2 for external inspection.
let client = ClientConfig::new()
    .usb_vid_pid(0xC0DE, 0xCAFE)      // or .usb_port_chain(..), .serial_eq(..), .usb()
    .connect().await?;

items.title: How it works
items.text:
application        wire_weaver_client                  device
 ───────────        ────────────────────────────        ──────────────────
 Request bytes ──► TxCore ──► ww_link msg ──► framer ──► OUT endpoint ──► embassy-usb
 Event bytes   ◄── RxCore ◄── ww_link msg ◄── framer ◄── IN endpoint  ◄── ...

The USB transport plugs into the generic event loop through a small message-level interface: it receives (kind, bytes) pairs from the tx side and hands decoded (kind, bytes) pairs to the rx side. Everything USB specific lives in the implementation of that interface.

items.title: Device layout
items.text:
Interface 0 with a pair of bulk (or interrupt) endpoints, 0x01 OUT and 0x81 IN; a vendor-specific class keeps the OS from attaching its own driver. Max packet size is read from the endpoint descriptor — 64 B on full speed, 512 B (Bulk) / 1024 B (Interrupt) on high speed — and used as the framer frame size. Nothing else is assumed about the descriptor.

TODO: Interrupt vs Bulk

items.title: Device identity strings
items.text:
Everything needed to tell devices apart is in string descriptors, which the OS reads during enumeration and exposes to anyone listing devices, so the host does not need to open a device to know what it is (on Linux, listing doesn't even need the udev rule):

Descriptor Contents Manufacturer (iManufacturer) Vendor name Product (iProduct) Device description, e.g. Nucleo G0B1RE blinky Serial (iSerialNumber) Unique serial number, e.g. MCU UID WireWeaver interface (iInterface) API id: ww:<crate>@<version> h=<hash>[ l=<user label>]

For example: ww:blinky_api@0.1.0 h=042c28cc0c9da99b l=Nucleo on the desk. h= is the first 8 bytes of the API hash without docs, the same one reported during link setup. l= is optional and always last, so the label may contain anything, including spaces. Unknown key=value fields are ignored by the parser, so more can be added later. See wire_weaver::api_id for the encoder and parser.

The API id is an interface string rather than the product or serial string so that the product stays human-readable and the serial stays stable across firmware updates (Windows keys device instances by serial). Interface strings are available without opening the device on Linux (sysfs), macOS (IOKit) and Windows (for composite devices, which usb_init() always configures). The host falls back to the product string if no interface string is an API id.

On the device, server codegen emits the API_ID constant, built entirely at compile time, and it is passed to usb_init():

let (usb, server) = usb_init(driver, buffers, timings, link_config, server_impl::API_ID, |config| {
    config.product = Some("Nucleo G0B1RE blinky");
    config.serial_number = Some(embassy_stm32::uid::uid_hex());
});

A user label is only known at runtime (e.g., loaded from flash), with_label appends it into a buffer without any formatting, truncating it to the 126 UTF-16 characters a USB string descriptor can hold:

static API_ID_BUF: StaticCell<[u8; 126]> = StaticCell::new();
let api_id = wire_weaver::api_id::with_label(server_impl::API_ID, label, API_ID_BUF.init([0; 126]));

A changed label becomes visible after re-enumeration. The control buffer must hold the longest string descriptor (2 + 2 * 126 bytes), UsbBuffers has 256 bytes for it.

On the host, DeviceInfo (used for filtering and in AmbiguousDeviceChoice errors) is filled from these strings, so .user_label_eq(..) and .implements_api(..) filters work without opening devices. wire_weaver_client::list_usb_devices() lists all devices reporting an API id, the same as ww list (install the CLI with cargo install --git https://github.com/vhrdtech/wire_weaver wire_weaver_cli):

$ ww list
LOCATION             PRODUCT               SERIAL                    API               HASH              LABEL
usb 003-1 c0de:cafe  Nucleo G0B1RE blinky  21002200175036344B333720  blinky_api@0.1.0  042c28cc0c9da99b  Nucleo on the desk

Filters can be combined: --api blinky_api@^0.1 (name with an optional SemVer requirement), --label <label>, --product <substring>, --serial <substring>, --usb-path 003-1, ... --all also lists devices without an API id, and --plain prints one line per device for scripts. See Command line tool for all options and for keeping the selection in a project ww.toml.

items.title: Framing
items.text:
Messages are packed into packets with ww_framer using the USB configuration from ww_link: U2Head (1–2 byte heads), a CRC-16 per message, no tail. Packet boundaries are significant: the framer relies on USB delivering each transfer as sent, and a short packet marks the end of a frame. The CRC is not there for the wire (USB already checks packets) but to reject stale or reordered packets after a reconnect.

Small requests are accumulated for the window the device asks for in DeviceInfo (typically a few hundred µs) and flushed as one packet; control messages (link setup, ping, disconnect) are flushed immediately.

items.title: nusb transfer queues
items.text:
USB transfers are fire-and-forget: the host submits a buffer and gets a completion later. To keep the bus busy, several transfers must be in flight at once, especially for IN where the host has to be listening before the device can push anything. The transport keeps two independent queues, each driven by a small task that submits buffers and forwards completions over a channel:

Direction In flight Purpose IN (rx) 64 Pre-submitted read buffers; the device can burst up to 64 packets before the host must catch up. OUT (tx) 4 A small pool of write buffers; a write waits for a completion when all four are on the wire.

Buffers are allocated once through nusb (so they can be DMA-friendly where the platform supports it) and recycled: a completed IN buffer is resubmitted right after its payload is staged into the framer; a completed OUT buffer goes back into the pool. There are no timeouts on individual transfers — a device that stops responding is detected by the link-level peer timeout (10 s without any message), which keeps a device that is legitimately busy for a moment (flash erase, say) from being cut off.

items.title: Reconnection
